If you are interested in document AI, not just OCR, here are some of our recommendations.

Sources indicate that visual document retrieval is to retrieve the most relevant top-k documents when given a text query. If you have previously worked with retriever models, the difference is that you search directly on a stack of PDFs. Aside from using them standalone, you can also build multimodal RAG pipelines by combining them with a vision language model (find how to do so here). You can find all of them on Hugging Face Hub.

According to recent reports, there are two types of visual document retrievers, single-vector and multi-vector models. Single-vector models are more memory efficient and less performant; meanwhile, multi-vector models are more memory hungry and more performant. Most of these models often come with vLLM and transformers integrations, so you can index documents using them and then do a search easily using a vector DB.

Sources indicate that if you have a task at hand that only requires answering questions based on documents, you can use some of the vision language models that had document tasks in their training tasks. We’ve observed customers trying to convert documents into text and passing the output to LLMs, but if your document has a complex layout, and your converted document outputs charts and so on in HTML, or images are captioned incorrectly, the LLM will miss out. Instead, feed your document and query to one of the advanced vision language models like Qwen3-VL not to miss out on any context.

In this blog post, we wanted to give you an overview of how to pick your OCR model, existing cutting-edge models and capabilities, and the tools to get you started with OCR.If you want to learn more about OCR and vision language models, we encourage you to read the resources below.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Today, we are announcing that Sentence Transformers is transitioning from Iryna Gurevych’s Ubiquitous Knowledge Processing (UKP) Lab at the TU Darmstadt to Hugging Face.
  • SentenceBERT or SBERT) is a popular open-source library for generating high-quality embeddings that capture semantic meaning.
  • Sources indicate that "Sentence Transformers has been a huge success story and a culmination of our long-standing research on computing semantic similarities for the whole lab.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Today, we are announcing that Sentence Transformers is transitioning from Iryna Gurevych’s Ubiquitous Knowledge Processing (UKP) Lab at the TU Darmstadt to Hugging Face. Hugging Face's Tom Aarsen has already been maintaining the library since late 2023 and will continue to lead the project. At its fresh home, Sentence Transformers will benefit from Hugging Face's robust infrastructure, including continuous integration and testing, ensuring that it stays up-to-date with the latest advancements in Information Retrieval and Natural Language Processing.

Sentence Transformers (a.k.a. SentenceBERT or SBERT) is a popular open-source library for generating high-quality embeddings that capture semantic meaning. Since its inception by Nils Reimers in 2019, Sentence Transformers has been widely adopted by researchers and practitioners for various natural language processing (NLP) tasks, including semantic search, semantic textual similarity, clustering, and paraphrase mining. After years of development and training by and for the community, over 16,000 Sentence Transformers models are publicly available on the Hugging Face Hub, serving more than a million monthly unique owners.

Sources indicate that "Sentence Transformers has been a huge success story and a culmination of our long-standing research on computing semantic similarities for the whole lab. Nils Reimers has made a very timely discovery and has produced not only outstanding research outcomes, but also a highly usable tool. This continues to impact generations of students and practitioners in natural language processing and AI. I would also like to thank all the users and especially the contributors, without whom this project would not be what it is today. And finally, I would like to thank Tom and Hugging Face for taking the project into the future.".

"We're thrilled to officially welcome Sentence Transformers into the Hugging Face family! Over the past two years, it’s been amazing to see this project grow to massive global adoption, thanks to the incredible foundation from the UKP Lab and the amazing community around it. This is just the beginning: we’ll keep doubling down on supporting its growth and innovation, while staying true to the open, collaborative spirit that made it thrive in the first place.".

Sentence Transformers will remain a community-driven, open-source project, with the same open-source license (Apache 2.0) as before. Contributions from researchers, developers, and enthusiasts are welcome and encouraged. The project will continue to prioritize transparency, collaboration, and broad accessibility.

The Sentence Transformers library was introduced in 2019 by Dr. Nils Reimers at the Ubiquitous Knowledge Processing (UKP) Lab at Technische Universität Darmstadt, under the supervision of Prof. Dr. Iryna Gurevych. Motivated by the limitations of standard BERT embeddings for sentence-level semantic tasks, Sentence-BERT used a Siamese network architecture to produce semantically meaningful sentence embeddings that could be efficiently compared using cosine similarity. Thanks to its modular, open-source design and strong empirical performance on tasks such as semantic textual similarity, clustering, and information retrieval, the library rapidly became a staple in the NLP research toolkit, spawning a range of follow-up work and real-world applications that rely on high-quality sentence representations.

In 2020, multilingual support was added to the library, extending sentence embeddings to more than 400 languages. In 2021, with contributions from Nandan Thakur and Dr. Johannes Daxenberger, the library expanded to support pair-wise sentence scoring using Cross Encoder and Sentence Transformer models. Sentence Transformers was also integrated with the Hugging Face Hub (v2.0). For over four years, the UKP Lab team maintained the library as a community-driven open-source project and provided continued research-driven innovation. During this period, the project's development was supported by grants to Prof. Gurevych by the German Research Foundation (DFG), German Federal Ministry of Education and Research (BMBF), and Hessen State Ministry for Higher Education, Research and the Arts (HMWK).

In late 2023, Tom Aarsen from Hugging Face took over maintainership of the library, introducing modernized training for Sentence Transformer models (v3.0), as well as improvements of Cross Encoder (v4.0) and Sparse Encoder (v5.0) models.

The Ubiquitous Knowledge Processing (UKP) Lab at Technische Universität Darmstadt, led by Prof. Dr. Iryna Gurevych, is internationally recognized for its research in natural language processing (NLP) and machine learning. The lab has a long track record of pioneering work in representation learning, large language models, and information retrieval, with numerous publications at leading conferences and journals. Beyond Sentence Transformers, the UKP Lab has developed a number of widely used datasets, benchmarks, and open-source tools that support both academic research and real-world applications.

Hugging Face would like to thank the UKP Lab and all past and present contributors, especially Dr. Nils Reimers and Prof. Dr. Iryna Gurevych, for their dedication to the project and for entrusting us with its maintenance and now stewardship. We also extend our gratitude to the community of researchers, developers, and practitioners who have contributed to the library's success through model contributions, bug reports, feature requests, documentation improvements, and real-world applications. We are excited to continue building on the strong foundation laid by the UKP Lab and to work with the community to further advance the capabilities of Sentence Transformers.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that we’re excited to announce a new collaboration between Hugging Face and VirusTotal, the world’s leading threat-intelligence and malware analysis platform. This collaboration enhances the security of files shared across the Hugging Face Hub, helping protect the machine learning community from malicious or compromised assets.

TL;DR - Starting today, every one of the 2.2M+ public model and datasets repositories on the Hugging Face Hub is being continuously scanned with VirusTotal.

In a recent development, AI models are powerful but they’re also complex digital artifacts that can include large binary files, serialized data, and dependencies that sometimes carry hidden risks. As of today HF Hub hosts 2.2 Million Public model artifacts. As we continue to grow into the world’s largest open platform for Machine Learning models and datasets, ensuring that shared assets remain safe is essential.

By collaborating with VirusTotal, we’re adding an extra layer of protection and visibility by enabling files shared through Hugging Face to be checked against one of the largest and most trusted malware intelligence databases in the world.

In a recent development, whenever you visit a repository page or a file or directory page, the Hub will automatically retrieve VirusTotal information about the corresponding files. Example.

This provides valuable context to owners and organizations before they download or integrate files from the Hub.

If you’d like to learn more about this integration or explore ways to contribute to a safer open-source AI ecosystem, reach out to security@huggingface.co.

Together, we can make AI collaboration not just open but secure by design.

Lianlian DigiTech and Visa revealed on November 18, 2026 the launch of LianLian XCard and a live business purchase completed with a payment credential designed specifically for an authorised AI agent, extending their collaboration into business spending and expense management.

Sources indicate that the companies described the purchase as an Asia Pacific first for a live B2B transaction using an agent-specific tokenised payment credential. LianLian XWorker, an AI agent registered in Visa’s Agentic Directory, obtained the credential through Visa Intelligent Commerce Connect and completed an office-supply order. The directory includes AI agents and merchants that Visa has verified as legitimate participants in agentic commerce.

Unveiled at Singapore FinTech Festival 2026, XCard is powered by Visa Intelligent Commerce and designed for spending across teams and projects. Eligible clients can apply through XWorker, while customers can link a LianLian XPay wallet to let authorised AI agents pay with XCard within business-defined parameters.

It has been revealed that visa Intelligent Commerce brings together agent identification, tokenisation, authentication and transaction controls for AI-initiated payments. Intelligent Commerce Connect supplies a single integration through the Visa Acceptance Platform for permissioned transactions across payment schemes, token providers and agent ecosystems.

Industry observers note that the new credential adds an agent-specific payment capability to that framework. Together with agent identification and business-defined controls, it enables a manufacturer to determine what an authorised agent may purchase and how payment is made. The arrangement ties payment authority to a recognised agent and places the business’s purchasing and payment rules around the transaction.

The launch builds on a July 24, 2026 announcement featuring LoopXPay, Lianlian’s earlier purchasing agent. In that transaction, LoopXPay identified a purchasing requirement, recommended and compared suppliers, ordered a product sample and paid within a single workflow. It operated under predefined spending controls and approval parameters and was registered in Visa’s Agentic Directory.

The earlier journey demonstrated sourcing through settlement; the latest purchase adds a dedicated agent payment credential and uses XWorker for a separate office-supply order. Visa and Lianlian said the approach can reduce manual purchasing for small and medium-sized businesses while preserving oversight, and that they will continue exploring applications in procurement, supplier payments and other B2B workflows.

XCard’s controls include card limits and transaction thresholds. The festival’s launch-session record describes multi-currency payments, real-time spending controls and centralized expense management, as well as native support for autonomous payments by AI agents. Those features connect agent-initiated purchases to a broader system for managing team and project expenditure.

Lianlian DigiTech mentioned selected AI-related benefits are planned for eligible customers. They are future additions, not part of the functionality described as available at launch.

The launch links two requirements for business use of agentic commerce: verifying that an agent is authorised to transact and enforcing the tech giant’s spending policy when it does. XCard supplies the card and expense-management layer, while XWorker and Visa’s credential system handle the agent-initiated payment. Whether those permissions can be carried consistently into the broader procurement and supplier-payment workflows the companies are exploring is the central question for the next phase of their collaboration.

In a recent development, we've completely overhauled our dataset infrastructure with LeRobotDataset v3.0, featuring a upcoming chunked episode format and streaming capabilities. This is a game-changer for handling massive datasets like OXE (Open X Embodiment) and Droid, bringing unparalleled efficiency and scalability.

Sources indicate that we've also provided a conversion script to easily migrate your existing v2.1 datasets to the new v3.0 format, ensuring a smooth transition. Read more about it in our previous blog post. Open-source robotics keeps leveling up!

Working with LeRobot datasets just got a whole lot easier! We've introduced a powerful set of utilities for flexible dataset editing.

With our fresh lerobot-edit-dataset CLI, you can now:.

Check out the LIBERO dataset and our docs to get started!

Industry observers note that we've integrated Meta-World, a premier benchmark for testing multi-task and generalization abilities in robotic manipulation, featuring over 50 diverse manipulation tasks. This integration, along with our standardized use of gymnasium ≥ 1.0.0 and mujoco ≥ 3.0.0, ensures deterministic seeding and a robust simulation foundation.

Train your policies with the Meta-World dataset today!

We're making robot control more flexible and accessible, enabling fresh possibilities for data collection and model training.

Industry observers note that getting data from a robot to a model (and back!) is tricky. Raw sensor data, joint positions, and language instructions don't match what AI models expect. Models need normalized, batched tensors on the right device, while your robot hardware needs specific action commands.

Recent findings suggest that we're excited to introduce Processors: a fresh, modular pipeline that acts as a universal translator for your data. Think of it as an assembly line where each ProcessorStep handles one specific job—like normalizing, tokenizing text, or moving data to the GPU.

It has been revealed that you can chain these steps together into a powerful pipeline to perfectly manage your data flow. We've even created two distinct types to make life easier:.

Industry observers note that this system makes it simple to connect any policy to any robot, ensuring your data is always in the perfect format for every step of the way. Learn more about it in our Introduction to Processors documentation.

In a recent development, whether you're fine-tuning a policy or running large-scale experiments, LeRobot now handles all the complexities of distributed training for you. This means you can drastically reduce training time, cutting it in half with 2 GPUs, down to a third with 3 GPUs, and beyond.

Check out the documentation to accelerate your robot learning!

Learn how to create your own plugin in our documentation.

Thanks to our powerful new pipeline system, you can now teleoperate your follower arm right from your phone (iOS/Android). The phone acts as a teleoperator device, and our RobotProcessor pipeline handles all the transformations, allowing you to drive robots in different action spaces (like end-effector space) with ease. Check out the examples!

Beyond these major features, this release is packed with numerous bug fixes, documentation improvements, updated dependencies, more examples and better infrastructure to make your experience with LeRobot smoother and more reliable.

Sources indicate that zellij is a relatively new entrant in the terminal-multiplexer category. Like GNU Screen and tmux it gives users the ability to manage a workspace inside a terminal with split panes, provides session management, and so forth; but Zellij also includes a web server for browser access to a terminal session, is extensible via a plugin API, and is likely more beginner-friendly than its predecessors. Its most recent release, version 0.46, adds a standalone terminal emulator, a built-in inbox for notifications, and a settings screen so users can configure the application without fussing with configuration files. While the low version number might suggest that it is not yet ready for serious use, it seems stable and full-featured enough to meet the needs of many users.

Redict deprecated in favor of Valkey

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (168 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Lwn

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Drew DeVault has unveiled that Redict, a fork of Redis that was created in response to Redis's 2024 license change, has been deprecated.
  • Industry observers note that I had hoped to rally the Redis diaspora around a copyleft initiative, to protect ourselves from future rug-pulls, and made Redict to serve this purpose.
  • We recommend that Redict people switch to valkey, which uses a permissive license but has better long-term prospects.

Drew DeVault has unveiled that Redict, a fork of Redis that was created in response to Redis's 2024 license change, has been deprecated. He recommends switching to Valkey, the permissively licensed Redis fork supported by the Linux Foundation. The two projects are mutually compatible, so switching should be as simple as changing which package is installed and renaming the configuration file.

Industry observers note that I had hoped to rally the Redis diaspora around a copyleft initiative, to protect ourselves from future rug-pulls, and made Redict to serve this purpose. However, with the valkey project's success, and Redis's return to a copyleft license, Redict was not able to build a sustainable community.

We recommend that Redict people switch to valkey, which uses a permissive license but has better long-term prospects. We advise against switching back to Redis; though it is once again open source, and copyleft, it uses a contributor license agreement which will facilitate another rug-pull when Redis has a bad financial quarter.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that synthesia unveiled on November 18, 2026 a custom connector that brings its AI video platform into Claude, allowing users to create and revise videos inside a conversation. It also works alongside other Claude connectors, so material from connected business tools can feed individual videos or automated workflows.

Consumers can start with a short prompt or source material such as a document, deck or spreadsheet. One request can summarize a Notion document and turn it into an explainer, while a Slack thread can also be condensed before video creation. An in-chat widget handles workspace, template, brand-kit and avatar selection before generation begins. Afterward, the user can ask in plain language for a newly introduced opening, a shorter version or a different tone.

The in-chat Synthesia player uses Syren, the manufacturer’s AI video agent for business, as its default creation tool. Controls cover the avatar or voiceover, the visual treatment and the video’s length and format. Versioning preserves each round of edits, allowing users to reverse a change or recover an earlier draft. For delivery, Claude can export the video at full quality; the video can also be opened in Synthesia.

Studio is the alternative when a script must remain exact or a template is required. It assigns an avatar to deliver the text without altering the wording, then opens a draft in Synthesia Studio’s editor so users can adjust individual scenes. The two paths separate prompt-led drafting from projects that need precise language or direct scene control.

Further examples use new help-center articles for how-to videos and GitHub release notes and merged pull requests for changelog videos.

Industry observers note that the Claude integration supports Starter, Pro and Enterprise looks. Users connect by adding a custom connector in Claude with Synthesia’s server address, leaving the OAuth fields blank, signing in to Synthesia and activating it through the plus menu in a fresh chat. Syren videos made in Claude draw on the same credits as videos made in Synthesia. Brand kits are an Enterprise-plan feature.

For enterprises, the central change is that connected business systems can supply both individual videos and repeatable production workflows inside Claude, while administrator setup, plan-based brand controls and Studio editing provide organizational and creative control over automated output.

huggingface_hub v1.0: Five Years of Building the Foundation of Open Machine Learning

📅 27 Oct 2025 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1908 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, TL;DR: After five years of development, huggingface_hub has reached v1.0 - a milestone that marks the library's maturity as the Python package powering 200,000 dependent libraries and providing core functionality for accessing over 2 million public models, 0.5 million public datasets, and 1 million public Spaces.
  • 🚀 We highly recommend upgrading to v1.0 to benefit from major performance improvements and new capabilities.
  • Major changes in this release include the migration to httpx as the backend library, a completely redesigned hf CLI (which replaces the deprecated huggingface-cli) featuring a Typer-based interface with a significantly expanded feature set, and full adoption of hf_xet for file transfers, replacing the legacy hf_transfer.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, TL;DR: After five years of development, huggingface_hub has reached v1.0 - a milestone that marks the library's maturity as the Python package powering 200,000 dependent libraries and providing core functionality for accessing over 2 million public models, 0.5 million public datasets, and 1 million public Spaces. This release introduces breaking changes designed to support the next decade of open machine learning, driven by a global community of almost 300 contributors and millions of people.

🚀 We highly recommend upgrading to v1.0 to benefit from major performance improvements and new capabilities.

Major changes in this release include the migration to httpx as the backend library, a completely redesigned hf CLI (which replaces the deprecated huggingface-cli) featuring a Typer-based interface with a significantly expanded feature set, and full adoption of hf_xet for file transfers, replacing the legacy hf_transfer. You can find the full release notes here.

We’ve worked hard to ensure that huggingface_hub v1.0.0 remains backward compatible. In practice, most ML libraries should work seamlessly with both v0.x and v1.x versions. The main exception is transformers, which explicitly requires huggingface_hub v0.x in its v4 releases and v1.x in its upcoming v5 release. For a detailed compatibility overview across libraries, refer to the table in this issue.

Every major library has a story. For huggingface_hub, it began with a simple idea: what if sharing machine learning models could be as easy as sharing code on GitHub?

In the early days of the Hugging Face Hub, researchers and practitioners faced a common frustration. Training a state-of-the-art model required significant compute resources and expertise. Once trained, these models often lived in isolation, stored on local machines and shared via (broken) Google Drive links. The AI community was duplicating work, wasting resources, and missing opportunities for collaboration.

The Hugging Face Hub emerged as the answer to this challenge. Initially, it was primarily used to share checkpoints compatible with the transformers library. All the Python code for interacting with the Hub lived within this library, making it inaccessible for other libraries to reuse.

Recent findings suggest that in late 2020, we shipped huggingface_hub v0.0.1 with a simple mission: extract the internal logic from transformers and create a dedicated library that would unify how to access and share machine learning models and datasets on the Hugging Face Hub. Initially, the library was as straightforward as a Git wrapper for downloading files and managing repositories. Five years and 35+ releases later, huggingface_hub has evolved far beyond its origins.

The early releases established the basics. Version 0.0.8 introduced our first APIs, wrapping Git commands to interact with repositories. Version 0.0.17 brought token-based authentication, enabling secure access to private repositories and uploads. These were humble beginnings, but they laid the groundwork for everything that followed.

In June 2022, version 0.8.1 marked a pivotal moment: we introduced the HTTP Commit API. Instead of requiring Git and Git LFS installations, users could now upload files directly through HTTP requests. The upcoming create_commit() API simplified workflows dramatically, especially for large model files that are cumbersome to use with Git LFS. In addition, a git-aware cache file layout was introduced. All libraries (not only transformers, but third party ones as well) would now share the same cache, with explicit versioning and file deduplication.

Recent findings suggest that this wasn't just a technical improvement. It was a philosophical shift. We were no longer building a Git wrapper for transformers; we were building purpose-built infrastructure for machine learning artifacts that could power any library in the ML ecosystem.

As the Hub grew from a model repository into a full platform, huggingface_hub kept pace with an expanding API surface. Core repository primitives matured: listing trees, browsing refs and commits, reading files or syncing folders, managing tags, branches, and release cycles. Repository metadata and webhooks rounded up the offering so teams could react to changes in real time.

Sources indicate that in parallel, Spaces emerged as a simple yet powerful way to host and share interactive ML demos directly on the Hub. Over time, huggingface_hub gained full programmatic control to deploy and manage Spaces (hardware requests, secrets, environment configuration, uploads). To deploy models on production-scale infrastructure, Inference Endpoints were integrated as well. Finally, the Jobs API came later (Q3 2025) to complete our compute offering.

The social and community layers became first-class citizens too: from APIs for pull requests and comments, to user and organization info, repository likes, following and followers, all the way through Collections to curate and share sets of related resources. Everyday ergonomics improved too: seamless authentication in Colab, resumable downloads, reliable uploads of large-scale folders, and more.

Recent findings suggest that then came version 0.28.0 and the Inference Providers ecosystem. Instead of a single inference backend, we partnered with multiple serverless providers (Together AI, SambaNova, Replicate, Cerebras, Groq, and more) to serve one API with transparent routing. We adopted a pay-per-request inference architecture that matched how people actually wanted to work.

It has been revealed that version 0.30.0 introduced Xet, a groundbreaking upcoming protocol for storing large objects in Git repositories. Unlike Git LFS, which deduplicates at the file level, Xet operates at the chunk level (64KB chunks). When you patch a large file in a dataset or a model, only the changed chunks are uploaded or downloaded, not the entire file.

Recent findings suggest that the migration was massive, starting with 20 petabytes across over 500,000 repositories. Yet it happened transparently, with full backward compatibility. One year later, all 77PB+ over 6,000,000 repositories have been migrated to the Xet backend, allowing for much faster (and smarter!) uploads and downloads. This happened with no user intervention, and no disruption to existing workflows 🔥.

Measuring the growth and impact of an open-source library is a tricky task. Numbers tell a story of their own:.

Recent findings suggest that but the real scale becomes clear when you look at the ecosystem. huggingface_hub is a dependency for over 200,000 repositories on GitHub and 3,000 packages on PyPI, powering everything from major third-party frameworks like Keras, LangChain, PaddleOCR, ChatTTS, YOLO, Google Generative AI, Moshi, NVIDIA NeMo, and Open Sora, to countless smaller libraries and tools across the ML landscape. Our own ecosystem (transformers, diffusers, datasets, sentence-transformers, lighteval, gradio, peft, trl, smolagents, timm, lerobot, etc.) benefits from this foundation as well.

In a recent development, the remarkable part? Most of the third-party integrations happened organically, and we played no role in them. The Hugging Face Hub empowers the ML community in countless ways, yet we're continually humbled by how far it has gone and how widely it's used.

According to recent reports, version 1.0 isn't just about reaching a milestone. It's about building the foundation for the next decade of open machine learning. The breaking changes we've made aren't arbitrary; they're strategic decisions that position huggingface_hub to scale with the explosive growth of AI while maintaining the reliability that millions of developers depend on.

Industry observers note that the most significant architectural change in v1.0 is our migration from requests to httpx. This isn't just dependency churn. It's a fundamental upgrade that brings the library into the modern era of HTTP.

Why httpx? The benefits are substantial: native HTTP/2 support for better connection efficiency and true thread safety that enables safe connection reuse across multiple threads. Most importantly, httpx provides a unified API for both synchronous and asynchronous operations, eliminating the subtle behavioral differences that existed between our sync and async inference clients.

The migration was designed to be as transparent as possible. Most consumers won't need to change anything. For those with custom HTTP backends, we've provided clear migration paths from configure_http_backend() to set_client_factory() and set_async_client_factory().

Additionally, hf_xet is now the default package for uploading and downloading files to and from the Hub, replacing the previously optional hf_transfer, which has now been fully removed.

Recent findings suggest that version 0.32.0 introduced Model Context Protocol (MCP) integration and tiny-agents, fundamentally changing how developers build AI agents. What once required complex framework integration now takes approximately 70 lines of Python.

Sources indicate that the MCPClient provides a standardized way for AI agents to interact with tools, while the tiny-agents CLI lets you run agents directly from the Hub. Connect to local or remote MCP servers, use any Gradio Space as a tool, and build conversational agents that feel natural and responsive.

Sources indicate that all of this is built on top of our existing InferenceClient and the dozens of Inference Providers it supports. We do believe Agents are the future, and huggingface_hub is there to provide the building blocks that enable AI builders to play with them.

Sources indicate that the CLI has evolved from a simple command-line tool into a comprehensive interface for ML operations. The streamlined hf command replaces the legacy huggingface-cli with a modern resource-action pattern:.

The CLI comes with a sandboxed installer, making it easy to upgrade without breaking existing dev environments:.

With autocompletion support and an installer that works across platforms, the CLI now feels as polished as any modern developer tool.

Version 1.0 removes legacy patterns that were holding us back. The Git-based Repository class is gone. HTTP-based methods like upload_file() and create_commit() are simpler, more reliable, and better suited for modern workflows. The HfFolder token management has been replaced with explicit login(), logout(), and get_token() functions. The old InferenceApi class has been superseded by the more feature-complete InferenceClient. hf_transfer has been fully replaced by hf_xet binary package.

According to recent reports, these changes weren't made lightly. Most deprecations were announced months in advance with clear warnings and migration guidance. The result is a cleaner, more maintainable codebase that can focus on forward-looking features rather than supporting deprecated patterns.

Recent findings suggest that we understand that breaking changes are disruptive. That's why we've invested heavily in making the migration as smooth as possible. Our comprehensive migration guide provides step-by-step instructions for every change with explanations of why each change was necessary.

In a recent development, most importantly, we've maintained backward compatibility wherever possible. HfHubHttpError, for example, inherits from both the old requests and upcoming httpx base HTTPError classes, ensuring that error handling continues to work across versions. With this release, we're fully committing to the future and we will focus exclusively on v1.0 and beyond, ensuring we can deliver the performance, features, and tools the community needs to interact with the Hugging Face Hub. Previous v0.* versions will remain available on PyPI, but they will only receive vulnerability updates.

Industry observers note that we’ve worked hard to ensure that huggingface_hub v1.0.0 remains backward compatible. In practice, most ML libraries should work seamlessly with both v0.x and v1.x versions. The main exception is transformers, which explicitly requires huggingface_hub v0.x in its v4 releases and v1.x in its upcoming v5 release. For a detailed compatibility overview across libraries, refer to the table in this issue.

To our 280+ contributors who built this library through code, documentation, translations, and community support, thank you!

We’re also deeply grateful to the entire Hugging Face community for their feedback, bug reports, and suggestions that have shaped this library.

Finally, a huge thank you to our users -from individual developers to large enterprises- for trusting huggingface_hub to power your workflows. Your support drives us to keep improving and innovating.

Please star us on GitHub ⭐ to show your support and help us continue building the foundation of open machine learning. It has been five years, but it is still only the beginning!

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We boosted load_dataset('dataset', streaming=True), streaming datasets without downloading them with one line of code!

Start training on multi-TB datasets immediately, without complex setups, downloading, no "disk out of space", or 429 “stop requesting!” errors.It's super fast! Outrunning our local SSDs when training on 64xH100 with 256 workers downloading data. We've improved streaming to have 100x fewer requests, → 10× faster data resolution → 2x sample/sec, → 0 worker crashes at 256 concurrent workers.

Loading data, especially at the terabyte scale, is a major pain in any machine learning workflow. We suffered this while training SmolLM3, at one point we had to wait 3 hours before each run to download enough data.

According to recent reports, streaming has always been possible in the datasets library, but large scale training with massive datasets remained a challenge. That changes today 🔥. We spent a few months improving the backend, focusing on streaming datasets to make it faster and more efficient.

First things first: our changes are backwards compatible. You can still stream any dataset from the Hub with the same simple streaming=True flag. It's as easy as ever. 🚀.

Thousands of AI developers around the world use datasets daily; they should just get improved performance with zero extra work.

Industry observers note that streaming was a lifesaver to quickly understand a dataset, but to train models, people were usually downloading the data locally, or using a cloud storage service such as S3. That's what we were doing for training SmolVLM, we had all of our data on S3 and were streaming directly from it.

We wanted to change that, so we decided to use streaming from the Hub when we were developing nanoVLM. Soon we found a big problem: our test run generated over 100,000 requests in under a minute, which got our IP blocked by the Hub! 😅 This happened because every DataLoader worker was initializing the dataset independently. As we dug deeper, we found that this creates a storm of redundant requests, many of which are unnecessary. Our changes ultimately reduced startup requests by a factor of 100. In total, our improvements delivered:.

Recent findings suggest that so, what changed? We focused on two phases: startup and streaming.

In a recent development, 1. Startup⚡️ The initial resolution of data files was creating a ton of requests. We made two major changes:.

2. Streaming 🏎️ To improve throughput during streaming itself, we've introduced two new features:.

This is how we can increase the minimum request size when streaming from 32MiB (default) to 128MiB and configure prefetching:.

Together, these improvements can double your data throughput, allowing you to train faster and more efficiently.

Industry observers note that hugging Face uses Xet: a dedupe-based storage which enables fast deduped uploads and downloads. Unlike traditional remote storage, data transfers are faster on Xet because duplicated data is only transferred once. For example: uploading a large scale dataset to Hugging Face leverages Xet which accelerates uploads. Once the dataset is uploaded, it can be streamed right away.

Deduplication for Parquet is enabled through Parquet Content Defined Chunking (CDC). Thanks to Parquet CDC and Xet deduplication, uploading datasets on Hugging Face is faster than on any traditional remote storage.

This is supported by our pyspark_huggingface package, a Spark Data Source to read/write HF datasets. It includes Parquet CDC and Xet support, accelerating data transfers on HF dramatically.

In a recent development, some data file formats are not supported in datasets, and sometimes there is a need for more control, so we made it easy to build custom streaming pipelines. This has been battle-tested in the LeRobot library to sample video frames, and in the WebDataset library to stream TAR archives.

We improved the HfFileSystem in the huggingface_hub library to efficiently read files from remote Hugging Face dataset repositories and stream data:.

Passing a HfFileSystem to a torch DataLoader reuses the cached results from .ls() and .glob() which eliminates the need for additional requests when listing data files.

We're now using these streaming enhancements in nanoVLM to train the next generation of SmolVLMs. With these tweaks, we achieve better performance from streaming than from training on our cluster's hierarchical hard disk setup. In fact, streaming is now as fast as reading the data from local SSDs! Previously, transferring data to local SSDs was the process that used to delay our trainings by three-hours. For more details, check out our GitHub.

Recent findings suggest that these powerful latest features landed in the datasets and huggingface_hub libraries. To take advantage of them, simply update your libraries and check out the documentation:.

To celebrate this, we preconcatenated and shuffled all the data sources in FineVision into FineVisionMax. You can use this single combined dataset to train your VLM – no need to handle multiple datasets manually!

And you can see how we do it at scale in nanoVLM!

#34386. Voice Cloning with Consent

📅 28 Oct 2025 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1445 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

Voice Cloning with Consent

📅 28 Oct 2025 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1445 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In this blog post, we introduce the idea of a 'voice consent gate' to support voice cloning with consent.
  • Industry observers note that realistic voice generation technology has gotten uncannily good in the past few years.
  • In a recent development, voice generation, and in particular the subtask of voice cloning, has notable risks and benefits.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In this blog post, we introduce the idea of a 'voice consent gate' to support voice cloning with consent. We provide an example Space and accompanying code to start the ball rolling on the idea.

Industry observers note that realistic voice generation technology has gotten uncannily good in the past few years. In some situations, it’s possible to generate a synthetic voice that sounds almost exactly like the voice of a real person. And today, what once felt like science fiction is reality: Voice cloning. With just a few seconds of recorded speech, anyone’s voice can be made to say almost anything.

In a recent development, voice generation, and in particular the subtask of voice cloning, has notable risks and benefits. The risks of “deepfakes”, such as the cloned voice of former President Biden used in robocalls, can mislead people into thinking that people have noted things that they haven’t said. On the other hand, voice cloning can be a powerful beneficial tool, helping people who’ve lost the ability to speak communicate in their own voice again, or assisting people in learning new languages and dialects.

So how do we create meaningful use without malicious use? We’re exploring one possible answer: a voice consent gate. That’s a system where a voice can be cloned only when the speaker explicitly indicates they consent. In other words, the model won’t speak in your voice unless you say it’s okay.

We provide a basic demo of this idea below:.

Sources indicate that the voice consent gate is a piece of infrastructure we're exploring that provides methods for ethical principles like consent to be embedded directly into AI system workflows. In our demo, this means the model only starts once the speaker’s consent phrase has been both spoken and recognized, effectively making consent a prerequisite for action. This turns an abstract principle into a concrete system condition, creating a traceable, auditable interaction: an AI model can only run after an unambiguous act of consent.

Industry observers note that such design choices matter beyond voice cloning. They illustrate how AI systems can be built to respect autonomy by default, and how transparency and consent can be made functional, not just declarative.

To create a basic voice cloning system with a voice consent gate, you need three parts:.

Our observation: Since some voice-cloning systems can now generate speech similar to a speaker’s voice using just one sentence, a sentence used for consent can also be used for voice cloning.

It has been revealed that the consent bit: To create a voice consent gate in an English voice cloning system, generate a short, natural-sounding English utterance (~20 words) for a person to read aloud that clearly states their informed consent in the current context. We recommend explicitly including a consent phrase and the model name, such as “I give my consent to use the < MODEL > voice cloning model with my voice”. We also recommend using an audio recording that cannot be uploaded, but that instead comes directly from a microphone, to make sure that the sentence isn’t part of an earlier recording that’s been manipulated. Pairing this with a novel (previously unsaid) sentence further helps to directly index the current consent context - supporting explicit, active, context-specific, informed consent. While this design reduces risks of reusing prior recordings, it’s not foolproof; a person could still generate a matching phrase using another TTS system. Future iterations could explore lightweight audio provenance checks, speaker-embedding similarity, or metadata from real-time capture to help verify that the consent audio originates from the intended speaker.

The suitable-for-voice-cloning bit: Previous work on voice cloning has shown that the phrases provided by the speaker must have phonetic variety, covering diverse vowels and consonants; have a “neutral” or polite tone, without background noise and with the speaker in a comfortable position; and have a clear start and end (i.e., don’t trim the clip mid-word).

To enact both of these aspects within the demo, we prompt a language model to create pairs of sentences: one expressing explicit consent, and another neutral sentence that adds phonetic diversity (covering different vowels, consonants, and tones). Each prompt utilizes a randomly-chosen everyday topic (like the weather, food, or music) to keep the sentences varied and comfortable to say, aiding in creating recordings that are clear, natural, and phonetically rich, while also containing an unambiguous statement of consent. This generation step is automated rather than pre-written so that each user receives a unique sentence pair, preventing reuse of the same text and ensuring that consent recordings are specific to the current session. In other words, the language model generates two fresh sentences per consent instance: one for explicit consent and one for phonetic variety. For example, the language model might generate: “I give my consent to use my voice for generating audio with the model EchoVoice. The weather is bright and calm this morning.” This approach ensures that every sample used for cloning contains verifiable, explicit consent, while remaining suitable as technical input for high-quality voice synthesis. (Note: It's not required that the language model be a "large" language model, which brings its own consent complications.).

Once the speaker’s input matches the generated text, the voice cloning system can start, using the speaker’s consent audio as the input.

Sources indicate that there are a few options for doing this, and we’d love to hear further ideas. For now, there’s:.

You can copy the code to suit your own use.

The code is modular so it can be sliced and diced in different ways to incorporate into your own projects. We’ll be working on making this more robust and secure over time, and we’re curious to hear your ideas on how to improve.

According to recent reports, handled responsibly, this technology doesn’t have to haunt us. It can instead become a respectful collaboration between humans and machines — no ghosts in the machine, just good practice. 🎃.

Not a big fan of trying to legislate every problem away but if malicious deep fakes are already illegal in most jurisdictions it seems that malicious voice cloning ought to be too.

Industry observers note that I think the problem with enforcement will be offshore usage (i.e. if a person from country X is illegally using a voice clone of a person from country Y, how will enforcement work?), as has already been shown with widespread global IP misuse. The second matter is going to be detection. Who is going to check that every single AI voice was or was not cloned with consent? Anything that would truly prevent misuse with robust checks would probably stifle the ability to iterate and develop quickly and anything that didn't stifle the ability to iterate and develop quickly probably wouldn't truly prevent misuse. The classic regulatory Catch-22.

It's problems like these that kind of necessitate a global response and whilst I'm usually not one to advocate for supranational law-making, it would be nice to see the so-called international community create a joint response or at least initiative on this topic because it's going to be a brutal wake-up call one day.

Sources indicate that at this point even just outreach and education on this topic would be helpful. In my time working with random developers and others in the OSS community, I've come across several suspicious requests from people I hardly know asking me for seemingly random recordings of my voice. Someone who doesn't understand the potential for misuse might provide such a recording and inadvertently have their voice used in scam campaigns.

In a recent development, I have tested it in local... its wonderful... We have to extend it to all the languages.

Recent findings suggest that @ZennyKenny 's point about suspicious voice recording requests hits home. We're living in an era where 'Can you say something for my ringtone?' has become the new 'Can I borrow your SSN for a second?' The consent gate approach at least makes the ask more obvious: 'Hey, can you explicitly consent to me cloning your voice while reading this phonetically diverse sentence about coffee?' Much harder to slip that one past someone!

Sources indicate that I saw your project and found it very interesting. I tried to contribute to it by adding a multilingual support and local sentence generation (with ollama and llama3:8b) and voice cloning using XTTS v2. I uploaded the code on GitHub, you can find it here: https://github.com/faridgnank02/voice-cloning.

Please let me know how you feel about it.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage News How Shopify Orchestrates AI-Powered Mobile App Development Without Overloading Developers' Machines.

Nov 17, 2026 2 min read.

To prevent AI development workflows from exhausting developer machines' resources, Shopify built Remote Dev, a remote mobile development environment that enables AI agents to independently build, test and maintain iOS and Android applications and in parallel.

In fact, according to Shopify engineers, running agentic workflows in parallel promptly hogs all resources available on development machines. They explain that "three or four workflows were enough to max out a laptop", on top of the resources already consumed by compilers, simulators, and emulators. Moreover, "if someone accidentally closed a laptop lid, the work stopped".

Recent findings suggest that shopify had previously built River to address the same challenge in web and backend development, but, being River a Linux-based solution, it could not be used for building iOS apps. To overcome this limitation, Shopify built Remote Dev:.

It has been revealed that with Remote Dev, we're no longer limited by how many builds and simulators our laptops can handle. Each River session gets its own environment, so we can have one agent debugging something on Android, another working on an iOS feature, and another testing a PR, all in parallel.

Remote Dev uses a fleet of remote Macs running Shopify's development environment and iOS simulators, accessible via SSH. Android emulators run on separate Linux VMs. This architecture allows developers to build and test both iOS and Android builds through the same SSH session.

Agents can work on multiple tasks in parallel, each with its own environment for maximum independence. They can also be accessed through a Slack channel backed by River. Thanks to this setup, Remote Dev can.

implement changes, build the app, run tests, interact with the simulators, collect screenshots, and create a PR. If something fails, it can inspect the logs, fix the problem, and try again, all while we focus on other tasks.

In a recent development, the platform supports automated workflows, including overnight runs that identify bugs, implement fixes, and submit PRs. Agents can also verify that a build is functional by navigating through the app, interacting with its UI, reproducing bugs, recording current behavior, implementing fixes, and running the same interaction to verify the fix.

Shopify notes that, after promoting internal adoption through demonstrations and storytelling, River's share of merged PRs increased from 6% to 61%.

In a recent development, commenting on Shopify's article, LinkedIn user Raiyan Jugbhery, in charge of software infrastructure and founder at SpendMe, argued that the key advantage of Remove Dev is its Xcode and iOS Simulator integration, noting that "a PR you still have to pull and verify on a Mac isn't really autonomous". However, he pointed out that the article does not explain "how they keep builds from queuing when several agents ask for a Mac at once", which he identified as a key concern.

Industry observers note that junaid Raza, solutions architect at Hoboetech, raised another concern. Allowing agents to run the simulator could lead to unreliable test results, as "give [the agent] a red test and enough retries and it'll sometimes rewrite the test until it passes". To prevent this, he suggests prohibiting runner agents from modifying the tests they execute.

Shopify says it aims to expand the platform with continuous application health monitoring, automated crash detection and fixes, and PR generation for identified issues, among other capabilities.

It has been revealed that subtle Medical announced on November 18, 2026 Japanese marketing certification for SubtleHD, its AI software for accelerating MRI sequences by up to 80% and enhancing images on existing scanners. The certification makes the software available to hospitals and imaging centers across Japan.

According to recent reports, the Japan Association for the Advancement of Medical Equipment issued the certification under the Pharmaceuticals and Medical Devices Act, Japan’s regulatory framework for medical products. SubtleHD can now be added to imaging workflows without providers purchasing a new MRI scanner.

In a recent development, subtleHD applies denoising and sharpening across body parts and integrates with existing MRI systems, according to Subtle Medical’s product documentation. The vendor-neutral software is designed to avoid new equipment purchases or original-equipment-manufacturer upgrades, with compatibility materials covering GE, Siemens, Hitachi and Philips systems across different field strengths.

One company-supplied example shows a coronal T1 knee sequence on a GE Signa HDxt 1.5T scanner dropping from an acquisition time of 6 minutes 42 seconds to 2 minutes 49 seconds, labeled as a 58% time saving. Other examples span brain, spine, shoulder, ankle, wrist and prostate imaging, showing that the company is targeting multiple clinical workflows rather than a single examination type.

In a recent development, subtle Medical positions the software as a way to add appointment slots, improve scheduling, reduce patient waits and make exams more comfortable, while extending the usefulness of existing magnets. That ties the product’s economics to additional capacity from installed equipment rather than a hardware purchase.

Japan has more than 57 MRI scanners per million people, the highest density among OECD countries, according to the release. That is approximately 50% higher than the United States and three times the OECD average. For Subtle Medical, that creates a substantial installed base for software designed to increase the capacity of machines already in use.

Sources indicate that the firm identifies high imaging volumes, a limited radiologist workforce and an aging population as pressures on Japanese radiology resources. Those conditions shift the emphasis from simply adding scanners to managing the workload passing through them, which is the workflow problem SubtleHD is intended to address.

Chief Commercial Officer Josh Gurewitz called Japan a “significant growth opportunity” as Subtle Medical expands internationally, and remarked the certification strengthens its Asia-Pacific presence.

It has been revealed that subtle Medical reports revenue growth of more than 50% in the year preceding the announcement, a doubled global sales team, an expanded international distribution network and deployments on more than 1,500 scanners worldwide. Those figures supply the commercial backdrop for Japan: the manufacturer is adding a market with extensive installed equipment while scaling the sales and distribution operation behind its international expansion.

For Japanese providers, the certification’s value will depend on whether sequence-level time savings become additional appointments and shorter waits across varied scanners and clinical protocols. That links the product’s commercial potential in Japan to a practical radiology problem: expanding examination capacity without relying solely on new hardware.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Simulation has been a cornerstone in medical imaging to address the data gap. However, in healthcare robotics until now, it's often been too slow, siloed, or difficult to translate into real-world systems. That’s now changing. With new advances in GPU-accelerated simulation and digital twins, developers can design, test, and validate robotic workflows entirely in virtual environments - reducing prototyping time from months to days, improving model accuracy, and enabling safer, faster innovation before a single device reaches the operating room.

That's why NVIDIA introduced Isaac for Healthcare earlier this year, a developer framework for AI healthcare robotics, that enables developers in solving these challenges via integrated data collection, training, and evaluation pipelines that work across both simulation and hardware.   • For fifteen years, the question was “Which app should I download?” Now it can be “What do I want my phone to do?” Sam Bright, Google’s VP and GM for Google Play and Developer Ecosystem, put it as a move from “there’s an app for that” to “there’s an app for me”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

On October 13th 2026, Google announced that Android people can now build their own apps with Google AI Studio and run them privately on their own phones through Google Play, with no public store listing required. The apps are “vibe-coded”: you describe what you want in plain language, and the AI writes it. The first release is limited to the US and to users aged 18 and over, and sharing with a small circle of trusted contacts is planned for the months ahead.

The shift is simple to say. For fifteen years, the question was “Which app should I download?” Now it can be “What do I want my phone to do?” Sam Bright, Google’s VP and GM for Google Play and Developer Ecosystem, put it as a move from “there’s an app for that” to “there’s an app for me”.

According to recent reports, think of a parent who wants one screen showing this week’s school pickup rota, the football schedule and the grocery list. No store has that app, because no store would ever build it. Today, that parent can describe it and have it on their phone by the evening.

I welcome this. It puts real creative power in the hands of people who never had it. But it also invites a question worth answering clearly: is a personal app the same thing as software? In my view, it is not.

A personal app might only need to work for one person. Software used by customers, employees or the public has to work reliably for people who depend on it. Both are software, but the responsibility changes when other people rely on what you build.

Industry observers note that A useful test: ask what happens at 3 a.m. when it fails. For a personal app, you might be able to fix it in the morning. For a service that people rely on, someone may need to respond immediately.

Not every app needs the same level of engineering, and not every task should be entrusted to an untested app. A gym-timer you built for yourself is a personal app. A system that holds your members’ payments, health data and contracts is software, and it carries obligations that a prompt cannot replace.

According to recent reports, personal apps do not appear in Play search or listings and are not shared with anyone except their creator. Sharing with trusted contacts is still to come. A popular app can later be moved to a public listing, but only after trust-and-safety reviews, and apps must still follow Google Play’s policies. Google’s own announcement frames the update around Play.

That is a design for individuals, families and small circles. It is not a design for a company rolling out a system to its staff and customers.

Here is what that looks like in practice:.

Sources indicate that these are meaningful, useful things, and until now most of them were never built because the cost was too high. That is the real gift here: the cost of building something small and personal has dropped to almost nothing.

Personalised apps will take some ground, and it is worth being clear about where.

It has been revealed that where they compete. Small, single-purpose utilities that people used to download because nothing else fitted: a custom unit converter, a simple expense log, a workout timer, a to-do list shaped exactly your way, a utility tool that you envisioned but didn’t know how to build. . Why pay a subscription for a tool that does 5% of what you need, when you can build one that does 100% of it?

Industry observers note that where they do not. Anything where trust, scale or accountability is the product: banking, payroll, healthcare records, logistics, identity. Nobody wants a one-off, unreviewed app holding their salary or medical history. Those systems need shared data, audit trails, integrations and people accountable when something goes wrong.

So the honest picture is not “apps replace software.” It is that the long tail of tiny needs finally gets served, while serious software is judged on what it was always meant to deliver: reliability, security and support. Incumbents who rely on being merely convenient should pay attention. Those who rely on being dependable have a clearer story than ever.

AI makes writing code fast. It does not make code correct. The 2025 Stack Overflow Developer Survey found that 84% of developers use or plan to use AI tools, yet 46% say they distrust the accuracy of AI output, against 33% who trust it. Even the people using these tools every day check the results.

According to recent reports, for a simple personal app, the consequences may be manageable, although privacy and security still matter. If your habit tracker miscounts a day, you fix it. For software that serves other people, the same slip can mean a leaked record or a wrong payment.

That is why serious teams treat quality as part of how software is made, not a final polish. The NIST Secure Software Development Framework describes this: practices for preparing the organisation, protecting the code, producing well-secured software and responding to vulnerabilities.

Sources indicate that the challenge grows as an app changes. A new feature can affect existing functions, data structures or access permissions. Without testing and version control, a small change can break something that previously worked.

An everyday comparison: a home cook can improvise a dinner for the family. A restaurant needs hygiene checks, supplier records and a process that works the same way every night. Both are cooking, but only one is held to a standard.

When you build something, “ownership” means three different things. It helps to ask all three questions before you commit.

According to recent reports, A personal app that is easy to build but hard to leave can become a quiet trap. Google’s private distribution model limits who can discover these apps, but privacy also depends on how the app handles data and permissions. The wider lesson holds for any AI builder: understand what you can export, what depends on the platform and what happens if you want to leave. Choose tools that let you keep your code, your data and your options.

Recent findings suggest that it is tempting to think that if AI writes the code, engineers become less crucial. The evidence points the other way. Google’s DORA 2025 research describes AI’s primary role as an amplifier: it magnifies an organisation’s existing strengths and weaknesses.

In a recent development, A team with good testing, clear ownership and sound design gets faster and better. A team without them gets faster at making mistakes. The biggest returns come from the surrounding system, not the tool itself.

Industry observers note that picture two teams given the same AI assistant. One reviews every change, tests it and monitors it in production. The other ships whatever the AI produces. Within a few months, the first has a product customers trust, and the second has a pile of problems nobody understands.

So the engineer’s job is moving from typing code to judging it: deciding what to build, checking what the AI produced, and keeping the whole system safe. That is a more valuable skill, not a lesser one.

Google’s announcement is good news. Anyone with an idea can now turn it into a working app on their own phone without any prior experience or knowledge of coding, and only by specifying the intent of what they want to build, without hiring a crew of human specialists. That widens who gets to build, and it will produce many small, useful things that never existed before.

According to recent reports, the lines worth keeping clear are these. A personal app can serve one person’s needs. Software that other people rely on carries greater expectations of reliability, security and support. Both deserve to exist, and each needs a different level of care.

It has been revealed that so here is my invitation. If you have ever thought “I wish there was an app for this,” stop wishing. Why not build one?
