📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that the status quo of AI chip usage, that was once almost entirely U.S.-based, is changing. China’s immense progress in open-weight AI development is now being met with rapid domestic AI chip development. In the past few months, highly performant open-weight AI models’ inference in China has started to be powered by chips such as Huawei’s Ascend and Cambricon, with some models starting to be trained using domestic chips.

In a recent development, there are two large implications for policymakers and AI researchers and developers respectively: U.S. export controls correlates with expedited Chinese chip production, and chip scarcity in China likely incentivized many of the innovations that are open-sourced and shaping global AI development.

According to recent reports, china’s chip development correlates highly with stronger export controls from the U.S. Under uncertainty of chip access, Chinese companies have innovated with both chip production and algorithmic advances for compute efficiency in models. Out of necessity, decreased reliance on NVIDIA has led to domestic full stack AI deployments, as seen with Alibaba.

In a recent development, compute limitations likely incentivized advancements architecturally, infrastructurally, and in training. Innovations in compute efficiency from open-weight leaders include DeepSeek’s introduction of Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA) and Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO). A culture of openness encouraged knowledge sharing and improvements in compute efficiency contributed to lower inference costs, evolving the AI economy.

Industry observers note that domestic silicon’s proven sufficiency has sparked demand and models are beginning to be optimized for domestic chips. In parallel, software platforms are shifting as alternatives to NVIDIA’s CUDA emerge and challenge NVIDIA at every layer; synergy between AI developers and chip vendors are creating a newly introduced, fast-evolving software ecosystem.

The shifting global compute landscape will continue to shape open source, training, deployment, and the overall AI ecosystem.

Utility of and demand for advanced AI chips has followed an upward trajectory and is predicted to continue to increase. Over the past few years all NVIDIA chips maintained dominance. Recently, fresh players are garnering attention. China has had long-term looks for domestic production, with plans for self-sufficiency and large monetary and infrastructural investments. Now, the next generation of Chinese open-weight AI models are starting to be powered by Chinese chips.

Industry observers note that broader trends worldwide are intensifying, with both the U.S. and China citing national security in chip and rare earth resource restrictions. As U.S. export controls tightened, the rollout of Chinese-produced chips seemingly accelerated. The rise of China’s domestic chip industry is fundamentally changing norms and expectations for global AI training and deployment, with more models being optimized for Chinese hardware and compute-efficient open-weight models picking up in adoption. In the last few months, Chinese-produced chips have already started to power inference for popular models and are beginning to power training runs.

The changes can affect everything from techniques used in training, to optimizing for both compute efficiency and specific hardware, to lower inference costs, to the recent open source boom. This could shift both U.S. trade policy and China's approach to global deployment, leading to a future of AI Advancements from an American-focused global ecosystem to one where China is at the center.

In a recent development, china’s domestic chip production has been in progress for years before the modern AI boom. One of the most notable advanced chips, Huawei’s Ascend, initially launched in 2018 but expanded in deployment starting in 2024 and increasingly throughout 2025. Other notable chips include Cambricon Technologies and Baidu’s Kunlun.

Sources indicate that in 2022, the Biden administration established export controls on advanced AI chips, a move targeting China's access to high-end GPUs. The strategy was intended to curb the supply of high-end NVIDIA GPUs, stalling China’s AI progress. Yet, what began as a blockade has paradoxically become a catalyst. The intent to build a wall instead laid the foundation for a burgeoning industry.

Sources indicate that chinese AI labs, initially spurred by a fear of being cut off, have responded with a surge of innovation, producing both world-class open-weight models like Qwen, DeepSeek, GLM, and Kimi, and domestic chips that are increasingly powering both training and inference for those models. There is a growing relationship between chip makers and open source, as the ability to locally run open-weight models also leads to mutually beneficial feedback. This is leading to e.g. more Ascend-optimized models.

China’s advancements in both open source and compute are shifting the global landscape. Martin Casado, partner at a16z, noted that a significant portion of U.S. startups are now building on open-weight Chinese models, and a recent analysis shows Chinese open-weight models leading in popularity on LMArena.

The vacuum created by the restrictions has ignited a full-stack domestic effort in China, transforming once-sidelined local chipmakers into critical national assets and fostering intense collaboration between chipmakers and researchers to build a viable non-NVIDIA ecosystem. This is no longer a hypothetical scenario; with giants like Baidu and Ant Group successfully training foundation models on domestic hardware, a parallel AI infrastructure is rapidly materializing, directly challenging NVIDIA’s greatest advantage: its developer-centric software ecosystem.

See the Appendix for a detailed timeline of chip controls and effects on hardware development and deployment.

Recent findings suggest that the 2022 ban, coinciding with the global shockwave of ChatGPT, triggered a panic across China's tech landscape. The safe default of abundant NVIDIA compute was gone. Claims of smuggling NVIDIA chips arose. Still, the ban had destroyed the trust from the research community, who, faced with the prospect of being left permanently behind, started to innovate out of necessity. What emerged was a latest, pragmatic philosophy where a “non-NVIDIA first” approach became rational, not merely ideological.

Recent findings suggest that chinese labs took a different path, focusing on architectural efficiency and open collaboration. Open source, once a niche interest, became the fresh norm, a pragmatic choice for rapidly accelerating progress through shared knowledge. This paradigm allows organizations to leverage existing, high-quality pre-trained models as a foundation for specialised applications through post-training, dramatically reducing the compute burden. A primary example is the DeepSeek R1 model, which required less than $300,000 for post-training on its V3 architecture, thereby lowering the barrier for companies to develop sophisticated models. While not the full base model, the cost reduction for the reasoning model is substantial. Algorithmic advances that improve memory such as Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA) with DeepSeek’s V3 model, likely incentivized by compute limitations, are a large part of January 2025’s “DeepSeek moment”.

According to recent reports, that moment also catalyzed a larger movement for Chinese companies, including those that were closed-source, to upend strategies and invest in compute-efficient open-weight models. These models’ lower costs could result from many variables and also are influenced by efficiency; as Chinese companies lowered compute and inference costs, they passed those lower costs to users, further evolving the overall AI economy.

In a recent development, deepSeek's (Open) Weight: In addition to high performance and low cost that created waves in early 2025, DeepSeek’s pioneering as an openly compute-efficient frontier lab is a large part of what has made the organization and its models mainstays. These advances can likely be attributed to innovating in a compute-scarce environment. Funded by investor Wenfeng Liang with a "pure pursuit of open source and AGI," DeepSeek became the most-followed organization on Hugging Face. Its highly detailed technical papers, including a groundbreaking _Nature_-published study on its R1 model, set a new standard for scientific communication. While a large draw is its open-weights over its API, in 2024, DeepSeek slashed its API prices to 1/30th of OpenAI's, triggering a price war. In 2025, DeepSeek-OCR further proved their prowess in compute efficiency and with the release of DeepSeek-V3.2-Exp, they passed on a further 50%+ discount to the users. Notably, DeepSeek’s-V3.2-Exp model was also released with day zero support for deploying on Chinese chips (Huawei’s Ascend and Cambricon). This release also marks emphasis on CUDA alternatives and exemplifies a full-stack hardware-software AI infrastructure in deployment.

It has been revealed that qwen's Ecosystem Dominance: Alibaba is on a path to control a full stack of high performance models and in-house designed chips, reducing reliance on NVIDIA. The company’s Qwen family became a primary resource for global open-source research. Its permissive Apache 2.0 license enabled commercial use, which was a barrier to comparable models that often used more restrictive customs licenses, leading to over 100,000 derivative models on Hugging Face. Alibaba recently unveiled improved chips for better inference, with its PPU being integrated into domestic infrastructure projects.

An Industry-Wide Tidal Wave of Low-Cost, High Efficiency:  More open-weight models released boasting SotA performance with significantly lower pricing. Zhipu AI returned with its GLM-4.5 and 4.6 open-weight releases, with both rapidly reaching top trending on Hugging Face and 4.6 becoming the top performing open-weight model on LMArena. GLM’s API pricing continually lowered, boasting cost-effectiveness that even offered a $3/month initiative as an alternative to Claude Code at 1/5 of the price. While full transparency on the pricing decisions is unclear, efficiency likely plays a strong role.

According to recent reports, seeds of Training Fully on Domestic Chips: While many upcoming chips are designed primarily for inference, more models are hinting at being trained on domestic chips. Ant Group pioneered training its Ling model on complex heterogeneous clusters of NVIDIA, Ascend, and Cambricon chips. Baidu successfully conducted continuous pre-training on a cluster of over 5,000 domestic Kunlun P800 accelerators, producing its Qianfan VL model.

The innovation was not confined to model weights alone; it went deep into the software and hardware stack.

In a recent development, architectural Exploration: Grassroots independent researchers such as Peng Bo, have championed Linear Attention as a potential successor to the Transformer. This approach, sometimes dubbed the "revenge of the RNN" and seen in models like RWKV, has been scaled into commercial grade models like MiniMax M1 and Qwen-Next by Chinese labs who willingly bet on high-risk, high-reward research. Meanwhile, DeepSeek has taken a different path by iterating on the original Transformer architecture. Their work introduces innovations like Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA) and DeepSeek Sparse Attention (DSA) introduced with its v3.2 model, which are designed to significantly reduce computational costs during inference without sacrificing performance, while also accelerating Reinforcement Learning (RL) exploration through faster rollouts. Highly performant proprietary models architectures are not public and are therefore difficult to compare.

It has been revealed that open Infrastructure: In a radical departure from corporate secrecy, labs shared their deepest engineering secrets. The Kimi team's work on the Mooncake serving system formalized prefill/decoding disaggregation. StepFun's Step3 enhanced this with Attention-FFN Disaggregation (AFD). Baidu published detailed technical reports on overcoming engineering challenges in its Ernie 4 training, while ByteDance's Volcengine contributed verl, an open-source library that puts production-grade RL training tools into the community's hands. What was once proprietary know-how became community knowledge, fueling a self-iterating flywheel of progress.

In a recent development, training breakthroughs: DeepSeek’s DeepSeekMath paper introduced a novel reinforcement learning (RL) methodology, Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), that significantly reduces compute costs compared to prior similar methods Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) while stabilizing training and even higher accuracy. GRPO has since been featured in a DeepLearning.AI course, built on by Meta’s researchers in their Code World Model, and lauded as having "in a large way accelerated RL research program of most US research labs" by OpenAI research lead Jerry Tworek.

With all the work aggregated, on public leaderboards like LMSYS's Chatbot Arena, models like DeepSeek R1, Kimi K2, Qwen and GLM-4.6 now frequently appear near the top alongside U.S. models. Innovation under constraints resulted in leaps.

Sources indicate that when AI models are trained and deployed, they are often optimized for certain types of chips. More than the hardware itself, NVIDIA’s software universe has been a reliable friend to the global AI ecosystem.

The deep-learning revolution, sparked by AlexNet's 2012 victory on NVIDIA GPUs, created a symbiotic relationship. NVIDIA’s Compute Unified Device Architecture (CUDA), cuDNN, and Collective Communications Library (NCCL) has long formed the bedrock of AI research. An entire ecosystem, including popular frameworks like PyTorch and Hugging Face transformers were heavily optimized on CUDA. An entire generation of developers grew up inside this ecosystem which created enormous switching costs.

Recent findings suggest that A software ecosystem reluctant to switch from existing platforms are now exploring elsewhere, which could be the first step away from U.S. reliance. The software side has evolved with the rise of new chips; developers are optimizing for and deploying their latest models on new parallel platforms.

Prior to 2022, domestic chips from companies like Cambricon and Huawei (Ascend) were rarely treated seriously. They were catapulted to the center of the domestic AI ecosystem in 2025 when SiliconFlow first demonstrated DeepSeek's R1 model running seamlessly on Huawei's Ascend cloud a couple weeks after the R1 release. This created a domino effect, sparking a market-wide race to serve domestic models faster and better on domestic chips.Fueled by the entire ecosystem and not just DeepSeek alone, the Ascend's support matrix promptly expanded. This proved domestic silicon was sufficient and ignited massive demand. Notably, Huawei's Ascend had zero-day integration with the release of DeepSeek v3.2–a level of collaboration previously unimaginable.

Researchers began co-developing with domestic chip vendors, providing direct input and solving problems collaboratively. This synergy creates a development ecosystem tailored for Large Language Models (LLMs) that evolves much faster than NVIDIA’s CUDA.

A new generation of younger researchers, trained in this multi-vendor world, emerged without the old biases that domestic hardware is inferior to Nvidia's chips. This collaborative approach has already resulted in adoption. The documentation for the DeepSeek-V3.1 model noting that its new FP8 precision format explicitly aims “for next-gen domestic chips,” a clear example of hardware-aware model co-design. Its successor, DeepSeek-V3.2, took this principle further by baking in TileLang-based kernels designed for portability across multiple hardware vendors.

Industry observers note that the CUDA ecosystem is now being challenged at every layer. Open-source projects like FlagGems from BAAI and TileLang are creating backend-neutral alternatives to CUDA and cuDNN. Communication stacks like Huawei Collective Communication Library (HCCL) and others are providing robust substitutes for NCCL. The ecosystem is substantially different from three years ago, which will have future reverberations globally.

Sources indicate that adaptations to geopolitical negotiations, resource limitations, and cultural preferences have led to leaps in both China’s development of highly performant AI and now competitive domestic chips. U.S. policy has changed throughout administrations, from prohibition to a revenue-sharing model, while China responds with a combination of industrial policy and international trade law. Researchers and developers have innovated and adjusted. The effects on open source, training, and deployment point to shifts in software dependencies, compute efficiency innovations that shape development globally, and a self-sufficient Chinese AI ecosystem.

China’s domestic AI ecosystem is accelerating, with companies like Moore Threads, MetaX, and Biren racing toward IPOs. Cambricon, once struggling, has seen its valuation soar. This newly introduced chip ecosystem’s expansion globally is yet to be decided.

In a recent development, the future of the global chip ecosystem, and therefore the future of AI progress, has become a key item for upcoming leadership talks. The question is no longer if China can build its own ecosystem, but how far it will go.

According to recent reports, before 2022, U.S. restrictions were targeted toward specific supercomputing entities. Policy then evolved as regulators and industry adapted.

The Initial Moves (October 2022):.

Chips such as Ascend are nascent while NVIDIA dominates the global and Chinese market.

According to recent reports, the Commerce Department’s Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) released its "advanced computing" controls in order to address U.S. national security and foreign policy concerns. The rule established a compute threshold with an interconnect-bandwidth trigger, immediately cutting off China's access to NVIDIA’s flagship A100 and H100 GPUs. China promptly filed a WTO dispute (DS615), arguing the measures were discriminatory trade barriers.

The Adjustment Era (Late 2022–2023):.

NVIDIA’s 95% share of the market in China began to quickly drop.

NVIDIA started to develop compliant variants for the Chinese market. The A800 (November 2022) and H800 (March 2023) were created with reduced chip-to-chip bandwidth to meet regulatory requirements and serve as alternatives to the A100 and H100s. The immensely popular consumer-grade RTX 4090 was also restricted, prompting the creation of a China-specific RTX 4090D.

Performance in Chinese domestic chips slowly improves.

According to recent reports, BIS comprehensively upgraded the framework. It removed interconnect bandwidth as a key test and introduced new metrics: Total Processing Performance (TPP) and performance density. This was a direct, successful strike against the A800/H800s. Debates expanded on export controls for the H20 and even model weights.

Adoption of Ascend, Cambricon, and Kunlun sharply increases following January’s “DeepSeek moment”.

Also in January, the Biden Administration established its AI Diffusion Rule, imposing further restrictions for both chips and select model weights amid security and smuggling concerns. In response, NVIDIA designed a fresh compliant chip, the H20. Leveraging NVIDIA’s increasing presence in political spheres, NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang began publicly explaining the strategic importance of selling U.S. chips worldwide. The U.S. then issued a licensing requirement in April 2025, charging NVIDIA $5.5 billion and effectively halting sales, before rescinding the AI Diffusion Rule in May 2025.

Alibaba unveils a newly introduced chip for inference.

It has been revealed that after intense negotiations, the Commerce Department began issuing licenses for the H20 with an unprecedented 15% revenue-sharing arrangement. But by the time the H20 was unbanned, the market had already started to change.

Day zero deployment begins for Ascend and Cambricon among fresh DeepSeek models.

Sources indicate that as the U.S. shifted to a revenue-sharing model, Beijing responded. Chinese regulators reportedly instructed firms to cancel NVIDIA orders, steering demand toward domestic accelerators under a "secure supply at home" narrative. This was followed by an anti-discrimination investigation into U.S. measures and an anti-dumping probe into U.S. analog ICs, centering chips in future leadership talks.

Agarwal said growth has increased Humyn’s working-capital needs because it pays workers and collection partners daily or weekly while typically waiting 30 to 60 days for AI-lab customers to pay, with borrowing bridging that gap and causing less dilution than a further equity sale.

The company uses its own two-camera hardware to record people performing everyday tasks. Agarwal said its software processes and labels the footage, tracking hand movements, interactions with objects and other details to turn raw recordings into data from which AI models can learn.

Collection extends across more than 20 countries in Latin America and Asia, with Brazil, India and South Korea as the main hubs, Agarwal said. Rather than relying on staged activities, Humyn records people doing their usual work or household chores, while local partners identify sites and supervise the process.

Humyn’s platform description sets out a broader pipeline spanning sound, sight, motion and touch. Speech audio, first-person video, motion traces from inertial measurement units and grip-force data pass through validation, processing, labelling and human review before being combined into a synchronized training signal. Listed outputs include MCAP, RLDS, LeRobot v3, ROS Bag, WAV, FLAC and JSON.

Gupta said Humyn has 12 paying customers spanning frontier AI labs, robotics companies and developers of world models, and that about 90% of its revenue comes from the United States. He declined to name specific customers.

Sources indicate that agarwal reported $10 million in revenue between April and October 2026, another $20 million in signed contracts, and a further $20 million in deals that have not been finalized. The last amount is prospective business rather than part of the signed-contract total.

Agarwal noted the tech giant has 51 full-time employees, most based in Bengaluru, alongside local partners across its collection countries.

The reported revenue and contracts point to early demand, while the payment cycle reveals the financial demands of meeting it. Humyn’s central operating constraint is to sustain a distributed collection network and its processing pipeline while covering the delay between paying for recordings and receiving customer revenue.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It's been fantastic to see the community dive into our fresh MiniMax M2, with many highlighting its impressive skills in complex agentic tasks.
  • If you've worked with LLM Agents, you've felt this pain: the same model can feel brilliant in one framework and useless in another.
  • In a recent development, when we designed M2, we knew we had to tackle this problem head-on.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It's been fantastic to see the community dive into our fresh MiniMax M2, with many highlighting its impressive skills in complex agentic tasks. This is particularly exciting for me, as my work was centered on the agent alignment part of its post-training. In this post, I'd like to share some of the key insights and lessons we learned during that process.

If you've worked with LLM Agents, you've felt this pain: the same model can feel brilliant in one framework and useless in another. An agent might crush a tool-use leaderboard but fail spectacularly at a simple, real-world task. This gap between benchmark performance and practical usability is one of the biggest challenges in the field.

In a recent development, when we designed M2, we knew we had to tackle this problem head-on. This led us to two core, and sometimes conflicting, objectives:.

It has been revealed that so, who do we align with? The answer is both. We align with benchmarks to build skill, but we must ultimately align with the user by ensuring those skills work everywhere.

While the methods for acing benchmarks are a deep topic for another day, I want to focus on that second, trickier objective: How do we train an agent for the wild?

Early in the project, we hit a frustrating wall. Agent performance was inconsistent, and we struggled to diagnose why. After many discussions, especially with Professor @Junxian He and @Wenhu Chen, we arrived at our first major conclusion: Agents require Interleaved Thinking.

This means that an agent's internal monologue—its "thinking"—can and should happen at any point during a task, not just once at the beginning like a standard reasoning model. This design is critical for two reasons:.

This principle became a cornerstone of M2's effectiveness.

Pro Tip for M2 Users: Because M2 relies on Interleaved Thinking, its context is its memory. For best performance, you must retain the full session history, including the thinking steps. We've noticed that much of the community feedback about performance gaps stems from accidentally discarding this vital context, which is a common practice with simpler reasoning models.

Our initial theory was simple: tool scaling is agent generalization.

Sources indicate that we started with a minimal set of tools (a Python interpreter, search engine, a browser) to build a baseline of tool-calling capability. The roadmap was clear: scale up the number and variety of tools, and the agent's ability to generalize to unseen tools would naturally follow.

At first, this worked. Our benchmark scores climbed to respectable levels. But as we dug deeper, we realized we were solving the wrong problem. The model aced the tests, but if we changed the environment even slightly—like swapping to a different scaffolding framework—its performance would plummet. We were still far from our goal of a "practically useful" model.

This led to our second, more profound realization: Agent generalization is not just about adapting to upcoming tools; it's about adapting to perturbations across the model's entire operational space.

This sounds abstract, so let's break it down. Think about everything that can change in a single agent task:.

It has been revealed that our work on M2 taught us an immense amount about agents, generalization, and data, but it has opened up more questions than it answered. Many of our ideas are still on the whiteboard. In the coming months, we will be exploring these frontiers even more deeply, and we can't wait to bring you the next generation of powerful and genuinely useful models.

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • InfoQ Homepage News Yelp Migrates Cassandra to EKS by Moving EBS Volumes.
  • Nov 18, 2026 4 min read.
  • Yelp has moved its Cassandra fleet from legacy self-managed Kubernetes clusters to Amazon EKS by re-pointing existing EBS volumes at new pods, rather than streaming data between nodes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage News Yelp Migrates Cassandra to EKS by Moving EBS Volumes.

Nov 18, 2026 4 min read.

Yelp has moved its Cassandra fleet from legacy self-managed Kubernetes clusters to Amazon EKS by re-pointing existing EBS volumes at new pods, rather than streaming data between nodes. A blog post by the site reliability team details a migration. It covered about 90 production clusters. There was zero downtime for customers and no data loss. The largest cluster, a 54-pod user-data store, took about 12 hours end to end.

Recent findings suggest that yelp had already moved its stateless workloads to EKS through its PaaSTA deployment layer, but Cassandra stayed behind. Kubernetes has no built-in way to migrate StatefulSets and their persistent volumes across clusters. The usual approach is to add nodes to the fresh cluster and shut down the old ones. This would temporarily double compute capacity but also lead to data transfer costs. For the largest clusters, streaming alone could have taken weeks. Yelp also considered a regional failover and rebuild, and a new Cassandra datacenter in EKS, but rated both as less transparent to customers.

Yelp's "Rolling PV Transplant" relies on the fact that an EBS volume is bound to an Availability Zone, not to a Kubernetes cluster, and that a PersistentVolume is effectively a pointer to a volume ID. The team pre-creates PVs and PVCs in EKS that reference the existing volume IDs, then creates an identical StatefulSet there, whose pods wait in ContainerCreating. The automation then deletes one pod at a time on the legacy cluster, waits for the volume to detach, and lets the EKS pod claim it. The pod rejoins the ring with the same data and token range, and the process repeats for the next pod. Cassandra's replication tolerates the few minutes each node is offline.

Yelp set a skipReconciliation: true flag on the custom resources in both clusters. This was done because two operators managed the same logical ring during the migration. The flag helped prevent them from conflicting over pod state. The flag was cleared on the EKS side at the end.

Recent findings suggest that across roughly 1,000 pods, about 1,000 TiB moved by pointer rather than over the wire. No node was ever decommissioned from the ring, so rollback was the same operation in reverse. Yelp used it a handful of times, for a missing subnet definition and a certificate mismatch, and restored pods within minutes. After a week of manual dev runs and a week of automation, one engineer ran the production rollout in about three weeks, migrating three to six clusters on a typical day.

The team had Claude generate the orchestration script, roughly 800 lines of bash, from its validated manual runbook, rather than asking it to design the procedure. The script needed minor adjustments after two days of testing.

According to recent reports, the approach relies on a previous Container Storage Interface migration by Yelp's Compute Infrastructure team. This work gave the Data Infrastructure team confidence in the volume detach and attach process. Yelp also used the technique for Kafka clusters, and states it applies to any AZ-pinned stateful workload on Kubernetes. The legacy clusters are now retired.

According to recent reports, the one failure specific to this technique was a stale VolumeAttachment object left behind by the AWS CSI controller after pod deletion. The EKS pod sat in Pending with no error, and deleting the object on the legacy cluster fixed it. Yelp advises building explicit timeouts for stalled detach and attach operations into any automation. Two other findings were unrelated to the mechanism. Backups failed with IAM AccessDenied errors for 48 hours because a new -eks role was not yet being assumed by scheduled jobs, and the alert only filed a ticket instead of paging. Pausing repairs for the migration also exposed one cluster whose repairs had been silently disabled for three months, leaving accumulated data inconsistencies. Teams planning a similar move should audit repair state, backup IAM roles and alert severity before starting.

Yelp's approach is not the only way to move Cassandra between EKS clusters. Monday.com's engineering team describes a different one in a post on zero-downtime Cassandra migration between EKS clusters. K8ssandra-managed clusters had to move without any downtime or data loss. So, the team created a workflow to add new Cassandra data centers, safely transfer data, and remove the old ones. That is the streaming model Yelp considered and rejected. The new cluster is brought up alongside the old one and receives data over the network, and the original is retired only afterwards. The team believes success relied more on control, automation, and handling failures than on speed. They automated long tasks like rebuilds and planned the migration in stages based on operator behavior.

The two migrations differ in what they trade away. Yelp's disk transplant skips data transfer and extra compute. It allows for a rollback by swapping the pointer. However, it relies on EBS volumes being linked to an Availability Zone, not a cluster. Monday.com's approach does not rely on that property, and it keeps the old environment intact until the end. The cost is a longer migration and the capacity to run both sides at once, which Yelp calculated would have taken weeks for its largest clusters.

Despite the different mechanics, the post-migration lessons are similar. Monday.com devotes part of its write-up to verifying that backups work after the migration, along with monitoring, dashboards and alerts. Yelp's own backups failed on an IAM role mismatch within 48 hours of its first production clusters landing in EKS. Teams planning either approach should treat those checks as part of the migration initiative, not as cleanup afterwards.

Presented by: David Iparraguirre - Senior Product Marketing Manager at Datadog, and Jessica Yang - Product Manager at Datadog.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

TechCrunch reported on November 18, 2026 that Unsiloed AI had raised $7.5 million in seed funding led by Felicis to develop technology that turns enterprise documents into structured data for AI agents.

Y Combinator, Orange Collective and Uncorrelated Ventures also participated, alongside angel investors Aarthi Ramamurthy and Beth Turner. CEO Aman Mishra said the proceeds will fund research and engineering hires, an expanded sales effort and proprietary datasets to improve the technology.

Y Combinator’s company profile lists Unsiloed as a San Francisco company founded in 2025 and a member of its Fall 2025 batch. It identifies Mishra as founder and CEO and Adnan Abbas as founder and CTO; the former IIT Kharagpur classmates developed the technology before joining the batch.

It has been revealed that unsiloed’s product overview describes a platform that converts PDFs, images and spreadsheets into JSON and Markdown for large language models and AI agents. Its three operations are Parse, which preserves document structure in Markdown; Extract, which returns requested fields against a JSON schema; and Split, which separates multi-document files and divides long documents into retrievable chunks.

Industry observers note that extracted fields can include confidence scores and citations pointing to their locations in the original document, allowing reviewers to check uncertain values before downstream use. The platform connects to S3, SharePoint, Drive, Snowflake and document-management systems, with enterprise deployment options in a virtual private cloud, on premises or in an air-gapped environment.

The founders describe a dual-stream architecture that keeps extracted content in one stream and document layout and hierarchy in another, followed by a decoder that applies industry-specific terminology and produces JSON or Markdown. Attention-guided heatmaps direct processing toward numerical columns, merged cells and section headers, while preserving multi-page tables and relationships between clauses.

It has been revealed that mishra described the underlying reliability concern: “The problem with LLMs is they’re inherently probabilistic. There is going to be some deviation induced. There is going to be some hallucination involved, and that has a massive negative impact downstream.”.

In a recent development, in Unsiloed’s own May 2026 evaluation, its parser scored 88.0 on olmOCR-Bench, a document-parsing benchmark, compared with 66.0 for Reducto Agentic and 39.9 for Unstructured. The evaluation used 8,413 unit tests across 1,403 PDF pages and unmodified version 0.4.27 of the olmocr scorer, covering tables, mathematical notation, reading order, long or tiny text and degraded scans.

Unsiloed also cautioned that strict string matching can flag harmless formatting or notation differences, while academic-oriented benchmarks can underrepresent charts, forms and other elements common in production documents.

It has been revealed that A separate organization-reported test of 542 financial documents produced 99.78% accuracy across roughly 84,000 extracted data points. The documents came from an enterprise customer, and the comparison included major AI models, Microsoft’s Azure Document Intelligence and the customer’s in-house extraction tool; the results had not been independently verified.

Mishra said Unsiloed is working with customers in finance, legal services and healthcare. An unnamed bank is using the software to process documents, while a law firm runs it on its own servers for contracts and old case files. Voice-AI startup Bolna AI uses it to ingest knowledge bases for building voice agents.

Industry observers note that its competitors include specialized document-processing startups Reducto and Unstructured, products from Microsoft and Amazon, and general-purpose AI models that businesses use for extraction. Mishra said pricing starts at one cent per page. He attributed the company’s cost control to directing computation toward the parts of a document that need the most attention instead of processing every section uniformly.

Recent findings suggest that unsiloed is pursuing that market with seven employees. The seed round gives it resources to expand; the immediate challenge is to turn early deployments and company-reported accuracy results into broader enterprise adoption against specialist providers and much larger platforms.

Customers who want greater control over their AI infrastructure can find a similar model library available in GKE AI/ML, or use pre-configured environments maintained by Hugging Face. Customers also run AI inference workloads with Cloud Run GPUs, enabling serverless open model deployments.

The common thread: we work with Google Cloud to build seamless experiences fully leveraging the unique capabilities of each service to offer choice to the customers.

Usage of Hugging Face by Google Cloud customers has grown 10x over the last 3 years, and today, this translates into tens of petabytes of model downloads every month, in billions of requests.

Whether you’re using Vertex, GKE, Cloud Run or just building your own stack in VMs in Compute Engine, you will benefit from faster time-to-first-token and simplified model governance.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Vero Security has raised $11 million in seed funding to help enterprises turn AI security policies into controls that operate while employees’ AI tools and agents are doing their work.

Industry observers note that the round was led by TLV Partners, with participation from GTM Capital, Maple Capital, and angel investors. Founded in 2025, Vero says multiple Fortune 500 companies already use its platform. It plans to invest the capital in product development, broader coverage of enterprise AI technologies and security workflows, and expansion of its U.S. commercial presence.

The startup is targeting a problem that grows with the usefulness of AI agents: software that can read tech giant files, connect to repositories, invoke tools, and execute code also needs boundaries that remain effective as those capabilities change.

Vero calls its market AI Security Engineering: the continuing work of discovering how AI is being used, assessing the associated risks, and keeping protections current. Its proposition is to take on more of that operational workload rather than leave security teams with another list of findings.

Security professionals define the policy and decide which changes the platform may implement automatically. Vero translates approved decisions into controls, coordinates fixes with the relevant owners, checks that work has been completed, and adjusts protections as tools and permissions evolve. Changes requiring a fresh risk decision return to a person with supporting analysis and a recommended action.

Industry observers note that A manufacturer might, for example, allow only developers to connect agents to corporate code repositories or execute code. Vero says one Fortune 1000 customer used that policy as its starting point, and the platform translated it into more than 15 controls spanning coding agents, identities, Model Context Protocol servers, skills, and runtime actions within minutes.

Sources indicate that the example illustrates the engineering work hidden inside a simple policy statement. Enforcing who may use an agent is only part of the task; the connected tools, credentials, and operations also have to reflect that decision.

At the center of the platform is Vero’s AI Runtime Governor. The organization indicates it inspects supported prompts, tool calls, and agent actions, applying policy when an operation is attempted rather than waiting for a later manual review.

Potential interventions include preventing a coding agent from reading unrelated secrets, blocking actions outside an approved policy, and stopping malicious skills or prompt injection from triggering unauthorized behavior.

Prompt injection occurs when material an AI system encounters contains instructions intended to redirect its behavior. For an assistant that only drafts text, the immediate consequence may be an unreliable answer. An agent with repository access or permission to execute commands can turn the same kind of manipulation into an operation against a real system.

According to recent reports, this makes runtime enforcement distinct from a policy written in an agent’s instructions. A rule asking software to avoid a sensitive resource expresses the intended behavior. An enforcement mechanism has to inspect the attempted access and apply the boundary along the execution path it supports.

In a recent development, vero’s website describes four connected functions: inventory, posture analysis, behavior detection, and enforcement. Inventory identifies agents and their owners; posture analysis examines configuration and reachable credentials; behavior detection examines activity during a session; enforcement applies the policy.

Its illustrated workflow follows an agent whose configuration exposes production credentials and whose approved skill later receives a malicious revision. The firm describes addressing the configuration problem, then blocking the harmful call when the changed skill tries to act.

In a recent development, the distinction is useful because an initial approval is a snapshot. A tool upgrade, new connection, or additional permission can change the risk after deployment. Continuous monitoring and action controls address a different moment from the original assessment.

Model Context Protocol, or MCP, is one of the connection mechanisms involved: it lets AI applications interact with external tools and data sources. Skills supply reusable instructions or procedures. Together with the agent’s credentials, these components help determine what it can actually do.

Vero says it operates through the endpoint, identity, AI, and security tools an enterprise already uses, without requiring employees to install something newly introduced. Its enforcement claims apply to supported prompts, tools, and actions; the practical scope of a deployment therefore follows the integrations and execution paths it covers.

Vero was founded by Elad Tessler, its CEO, and Daniel Meirov, its CTO. Tessler previously led product at Astrix Security, while Meirov was Sightfull’s first employee and led its R&D and product work. The founders met in Unit 8200, where they co-led a cyber operations unit of more than 100 people, according to the announcement. Vero has offices in Newly introduced York and Tel Aviv.

Industry observers note that GTM Capital indicates it invested after a structured evaluation involving its community of Fortune 500 CIOs and CISOs. The announcement describes those executives working directly with Vero before the firm committed.

The investment comes as runtime controls become a more prominent part of enterprise AI security. Other releases, including Sysdig’s AI Defense, also focus on observing agent behavior and enforcing boundaries during execution. Vero’s funding pitch emphasizes the ongoing operating work around those boundaries: implementing decisions, verifying remediation, and keeping the controls aligned with the policy.

Sources indicate that alongside the funding announcement, Vero is launching AISecurityEngineering.org, an open community and knowledge center with field guides, workshops, and an ASE credential track. The initiative is aimed at professionals establishing AI security practices while often carrying other responsibilities inside their organizations.

Recent findings suggest that the broader opportunity is to make security policy durable even when the software underneath it keeps changing. As enterprises give agents more useful access, the test for platforms such as Vero is whether they can consistently carry a security team’s decisions through to the actions those agents attempt.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, custom kernels are the backbone of high-performance deep learning, enabling GPU operations tailored precisely to your workload; whether that’s image processing, tensor transformations, or other compute-heavy tasks. But compiling these kernels for the right architectures, wiring all the build flags, and integrating them cleanly into PyTorch extensions can quickly become a mess of CMake/Nix, compiler errors, and ABI complications, which is not fun. Hugging Face’s kernels library makes it easy to build (with kernel-builder) and share these kernels with the kernels-community, with support for multiple GPU and accelerator backends, including CUDA, ROCm, Metal, and XPU. This ensures your kernels are fast, portable, and seamlessly integrated with PyTorch.

In a recent development, in this guide, we focus exclusively on ROCm-compatible kernels and show how to build, test, and share them using kernels. You’ll learn how to create kernels that run efficiently on AMD GPUs, along with best practices for reproducibility, packaging, and deployment.

This ROCm-specific walkthrough is a streamlined version of the original kernel-builder guide. If you’re looking for the broader CUDA-focused version, you can find it here: A Guide to Building and Scaling Production-Ready CUDA Kernels.

We will use the GEMM kernel from RadeonFlow_Kernels as an example. If you want to go straight to the guide, click here.

This section was written by the RadeonFlow GEMM kernel authors to introduce the kernel.Authors: ColorsWind, Zesen Liu, and Andy.

According to recent reports, the RadeonFlow GEMM kernel is a high-performance, FP8 block-wise matrix multiplication implementation optimized for the AMD Instinct MI300X GPU. GEMM (General Matrix Multiplication) is the core building block behind most deep learning workloads: given two matrices A and B, you compute their product C = A × B. Here it’s implemented in FP8, a low-precision floating-point format that trades a bit of accuracy for much higher throughput and lower memory bandwidth. This kernel was developed for the AMD Developer Challenge 2025, it was awarded the 🏆 Grand Prize in June 2025, recognizing its excellence in performance and innovation on AMD hardware.

The kernel operates on quantized inputs using the e4m3fnuz floating-point format and applies per-block scaling to preserve accuracy during low-precision computation. The e4m3fnuz format is an FP8 variant with 4 exponent bits and 3 mantissa bits, designed to be efficient for neural network workloads. Because FP8 has a much smaller dynamic range than FP16/FP32, we apply per-block scaling factors (a_scale and b_scale) so that each block of values is rescaled into a numerically “comfortable” range before and after computation, which helps preserve accuracy despite the low precision. It takes the following arguments:.

where a and b are the input matrices, a_scale and b_scale are the scaling factors for a and b respectively, and c is the output matrix:.

Industry observers note that the kernel is precompiled for specific matrix shapes and assumes a transposed memory layout (as required by the competition). To support additional shapes or alternative memory layouts, you must modify the kernel launcher.

So now that we have a high-performance ROCm kernel, the natural question is: how do we integrate it into a real PyTorch workflow and share it with others? That’s exactly what we’ll cover next, using kernels to structure, build, and publish the ROCm kernel.

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: Apriel-H1: The Surprising Key to Distilling Efficient Reasoning Models

📅 19 Nov 2025 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1585 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that we converted our 15B reasoning model to a Mamba hybrid achieving 2.1x throughput with minimal quality loss.
  • When MiniMax published their M2 post-mortem in October explaining why they abandoned efficient attention at 230B scale, the narrative briefly became "efficient attention is dead." Within days, Kimi Linear proved otherwise.
  • Sources indicate that our constraint was simple: we had a strong 15B reasoning model and needed to make it efficient without starting over.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that we converted our 15B reasoning model to a Mamba hybrid achieving 2.1x throughput with minimal quality loss. The key? A non-obvious insight about what data to distill on, and why intuition fails here.

When MiniMax published their M2 post-mortem in October explaining why they abandoned efficient attention at 230B scale, the narrative briefly became "efficient attention is dead." Within days, Kimi Linear proved otherwise. The real lesson: it depends on your constraints.

Sources indicate that our constraint was simple: we had a strong 15B reasoning model and needed to make it efficient without starting over. No infinite compute for 20T-token pretraining. No luxury of architectural co-design from day one. Just a practical question: can you retrofit efficiency into an existing model through distillation?

Spoilers: yes, but only if you ignore your intuition about what data to use.

Recent findings suggest that the Apriel-H1 family: seven checkpoints spanning 25-40 Mamba layers (out of 50 total), showing the complete efficiency-quality frontier. Our flagship Apriel-H1-15b-Thinker-SFT achieves 2.1x throughput with minimal quality loss: MATH500 and MTBench improve a few points (0.90 → 0.92 and 8.30 → 8.58, respectively), while GSM8k (0.97 → 0.95), GPQA (0.59 → 0.55), and AIME24 (0.70 → 0.65) regress slightly. Total training: 76.8B tokens.

In a recent development, apriel-H1-15b-Thinker-SFT (green) vs full-attention teacher (blue). Reasoning quality stays nearly flat across benchmarks while throughput increases 1.89-2.09x depending on context length.

According to recent reports, the full details are in our Apriel-H1 paper. Here, we focus on the key insight that made it work.

Here's what we initially thought would work: just distill on pretraining data and round it out with some SFT.

Recent findings suggest that the reasoning seemed solid. We're inserting completely new Mamba layers that have never seen data. These linear SSMs need to learn general-purpose token mixing from scratch. How can they become effective mixers unless they get exposure to the same broad distribution the original attention layers saw?

Recent findings suggest that so we tried it. Then we tried mixing pretraining and SFT data. It didn't work. The distilled hybrids lost reasoning quality, sometimes dramatically.

What actually worked: high-quality reasoning traces from the teacher's SFT dataset.

Distilling a reasoning model isn't about transferring general next-token prediction. The base model already has that, and we started from a strong 15B foundation. What we're preserving is specific and fragile: the teacher's multi-step reasoning patterns.

Recent findings suggest that those patterns emerge from intricate attention mechanisms. Retrieval heads pulling context from thousands of tokens back. Induction heads recognizing and continuing logical chains. Long-range dependencies connecting premises to conclusions many steps later. When you replace attention wholesale with Mamba's linear recurrence, these computational mechanisms are disrupted. The hybrid must discover newly introduced paths to the same reasoning outcomes.

That discovery requires explicit examples where reasoning structure is visible and correct:.

Pretraining data, on the other hand, is too noisy and too diffuse. The reasoning signal gets lost. You need concentrated examples of the specific capability you're trying to preserve.

Once we understood the data choice, our distillation method became clear too. We used reverse KL divergence (temperature 1) rather than forward KL. Reverse won consistently. Why? We're training on problems where the teacher has high confidence and clear structure. Reverse KL's mode-seeking behavior encourages the student to commit to those high-confidence predictions. When your teacher is confident and correct, you want your student to be confident too.

This insight is the key to the whole approach: match your distillation data to the capability you're preserving, not the capability you're building.

You can't just swap 40 attention layers for Mamba and hope. We learned this the hard way, and eventually developed a staged distillation procedure to get there reliably.

Stage 1: Identify least-important layers. We used a Leave-One-Out (LOO) analysis on MMLU: remove each layer, replace with identity, then measure the drop. Sort by importance, replace the bottom 25 with Mamba-in-Llama (MIL) initialized mixers. Distill end-to-end. This worked for our H-25 checkpoint.

Industry observers note that stage 2: Progressive conversion beyond 25 layers. LOO broke down past 25 layers because layers unimportant in isolation became critical in combination. To address this, we developed a dynamic heuristic we call MIL-Mamba-Replacement (MMR). For each remaining attention layer, we initialize a Mamba mixer with MIL, run 100 training steps, and record the distillation loss. Layers converging to lower loss are "easier" to replace. This captures training dynamics rather than static importance.

According to recent reports, we progressed incrementally: 25 → 27 → 30 → 34 → 37 → 40 Mamba layers, grouping replacements by MMR scores. Each checkpoint distills from the previous.

According to recent reports, stage 3: End-to-end training on SFT data. After reaching the target Mamba layer count, we did a final SFT pass until reasoning performance stabilized. After 55.9B distillation tokens and 20.9B SFT tokens, this produced our final Apriel-H1-15b-Thinker-SFT model.

The complete efficiency frontier. Each checkpoint shows cumulative training tokens. Our flagship H-30-SFT (released as Apriel-H1-15b-Thinker-SFT) used 76.8B total for 2.1x throughput at 0.76 average score. The aggressively converted H-40 variant used 136.5B tokens for 3.4x throughput. For reference: NVIDIA's Nemotron-Nano-9B-v2 achieves 4.6x at 0.77 score but required training from scratch with orders of magnitude more compute.

Industry observers note that we built all this on Fast-LLM, our open-source training framework. The core architectural principle: large language model transformers should be modular. Attention and Mamba are different implementations of the same "mixing" interface, and can be swapped freely.

Here's a hybrid architecture in Fast-LLM's config format:.

In a recent development, the pattern field specifies layer order. For Apriel-H1-15b-Thinker-SFT: 30 mamba_block, 20 attention_block, placed by importance. That's it.

Distillation is configuration too:.

According to recent reports, fast-LLM handles gradient accumulation, distributed training, tensor parallelism, checkpointing, everything you need for large-scale experimentation. It's open source, and licensed under Apache 2.0. You can reproduce this work because we designed the infrastructure to make it reproducible.

According to recent reports, why release all checkpoints? Because optimal depends on your constraints. H-30 offers the best balance. H-40 maximizes throughput for latency-critical workloads. The intermediate checkpoints let you choose your exact trade-off.

Why do you get different speedups at different context lengths? Mamba's linear complexity advantage grows with sequence length, and attention degrades quadratically.

Industry observers note that why did you only try Mamba? We used Mamba-1 for three reasons: it has a proven distillation track record, has shown strong empirical performance, and was simple to implement in our framework. It let us focus on the data question first.

What were the Mamba hyperparameters? State size 16, DT rank 16, inner dimension 4096. For our GQA setup in Apriel we expanded B (input projection) and x (state) to match total attention heads following M1.

Sources indicate that why didn't you try more advanced conversion methods? We used Mamba-in-Llama initialization and knowledge distillation rather than MOHAWK's multi-stage procedure because the latter didn't show significant advantages in preliminary experiments.

According to recent reports, why did you only SFT the H-30 model? We only applied SFT to H-30 to validate that distilled hybrids can be improved through standard post-training. The other checkpoints are pure distillation but can be fine-tuned similarly.

In a recent development, why didn't you explore RL? This was a scoping decision to isolate the distillation question: can you transfer reasoning via knowledge distillation alone? Answer: yes. But RL should close remaining quality gaps further. We are exploring RL for future iterations.

It has been revealed that did you really show that Apriel-H1 matches full-attention reasoning at similar compute budgets? We didn't do an apples-to-apples comparison between full-attention Apriel and a hybrid trained identically from pretraining forward. That would require repeating all mid-training and post-training of the teacher with the Apriel-H1 architecture, which was beyond our compute budget. What we can claim though is that retrofitting efficiency via distillation is practical and effective, and that the resulting hybrids can be fine-tuned to match or exceed the teacher's reasoning quality.

In a recent development, we've implemented Apriel-H1 in Hugging Face Transformers and vLLM. Transformers integration is straightforward. We ship a new model class with interchangeable attention and Mamba layers. vLLM integration uses their recent Mamba cache operations for continuous batching, prefix caching, and chunked prefill. The vLLM plugin is ready. We are presently waiting for final legal approval to open-source it.

Honest assessment: Deploying hybrids today means rough edges. The tooling is maturing fast but isn't turnkey. You will write custom code, validate numerical behavior carefully, and work around framework limitations. For teams that can absorb that cost, throughput gains are worth it. For those that can't, waiting might be the right call.

Most teams don't have infinite compute for 20T-token pretraining. If you've invested in a strong base model and need efficiency gains, this work shows a practical path: distill into hybrids using high-quality task-specific data that matches the capability you're preserving.

The surprising finding, use reasoning data to distill reasoning, seems obvious in retrospect but contradicts initial intuition. We validated it, explained why it works, and built the infrastructure to make it reproducible.

Models: Apriel-H1 Collection on HuggingFaceTraining framework: Fast-LLM on GitHubTeacher model: Apriel-Nemotron-15B-ThinkerPaper: Apriel-H1: Towards Efficient Enterprise Reasoning Models.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

LLMs have become essential tools for building software. But for Apple developers, integrating them remains unnecessarily painful.

Developers building AI-powered apps typically take a hybrid approach, adopting some combination of:.

It has been revealed that each comes with different APIs, different requirements, different integration patterns. It's a lot, and it adds up promptly. When I interviewed developers about building AI-powered apps, friction with model integration came up immediately. One developer put it bluntly:.

It has been revealed that I thought I'd quickly use the demo for a test and maybe a quick and dirty build but instead wasted so much time. Drove me nuts.

The cost to experiment is high, which discourages developers from discovering that local, open-source models might actually work great for their use case.

Recent findings suggest that today we're announcing AnyLanguageModel, a Swift package that provides a drop-in replacement for Apple's Foundation Models framework with support for multiple model providers. Our goal is to reduce the friction of working with LLMs on Apple platforms and make it easier to adopt open-source models that run locally.

The core idea is simple: Swap your import statement, keep the same API.

Here's what that looks like in practice. Start with Apple's built-in model:.

Now try an open-source model running locally via MLX:.

AnyLanguageModel supports a range of providers:.

Sources indicate that the focus is on local models that you can download from the Hugging Face Hub. Cloud providers are included to lower the barrier to getting started and to provide a migration path. Make it work, then make it right.

When designing AnyLanguageModel, we faced a choice: create a new abstraction that tries to capture everything, or build on an existing API. We chose the latter, using Apple's Foundation Models framework as the template.

In a recent development, this might seem counterintuitive. Why tie ourselves to Apple's choices? A few reasons:.

Foundation Models is genuinely well-designed. It leverages Swift features like macros for an ergonomic developer experience, and its abstractions around sessions, tools, and generation map well to how LLMs actually work.

According to recent reports, it's intentionally limited. Foundation Models represents something like a lowest common denominator for language model capabilities. Rather than seeing this as a weakness, we treat it as a stable foundation (hyuk hyuk). Every Swift developer targeting Apple platforms will encounter this API, so building on it directly means less conceptual overhead.

Recent findings suggest that it keeps us grounded. Each additional layer of abstraction takes you further from the problem you're actually solving. Abstractions are powerful, but stack too many and they become a problem in themselves.

The result is that switching between providers requires minimal code changes, and the core abstractions remain clean and predictable.

Industry observers note that one challenge with multi-backend libraries is dependency bloat. If you only want to run MLX models, you shouldn't have to pull in llama.cpp and all its dependencies.

Industry observers note that anyLanguageModel uses Swift 6.1 package traits to solve this. You opt in to only the backends you need:.

Available traits include CoreML, MLX, and Llama (for llama.cpp / llama.swift). By default, no heavy dependencies are included. You get the base API plus cloud providers, which only require standard URLSession networking.

Industry observers note that for Xcode projects (which don't yet support trait declarations directly), you can create a small internal Swift package that depends on AnyLanguageModel with the traits you need, then add that package as a local dependency. The README has detailed instructions.

Vision-language models are incredibly capable and widely used. They can describe images, extract text from screenshots, analyze charts, and answer questions about visual content. Unfortunately, Apple's Foundation Models framework doesn't presently support sending images with prompts.

Building on an existing API means accepting its constraints. Apple will likely add image support in a future release (iOS 27, perhaps?), but vision-language models are too useful to wait for. So we've extended beyond what Foundation Models offers today.

Here's an example sending an image to Claude:.

Recent findings suggest that we're taking a calculated risk here; we might design something that conflicts with Apple's eventual implementation. But that's what deprecation warnings are for. Sometimes you have to write the API for the framework that doesn't exist yet.

To see AnyLanguageModel in action, check out chat-ui-swift, a SwiftUI chat application that demonstrates the library's capabilities.

Sources indicate that it's meant as a starting point: Fork it, extend it, swap in different models. See how the pieces fit together and adapt it to your needs.

It has been revealed that anyLanguageModel is currently pre-1.0. The core API is stable, but we're actively working on bringing the full feature set of Foundation Models to all adapters, namely:.

In a recent development, this library is the first step toward something larger. A unified inference API provides the scaffolding needed to build seamless agentic workflows on Apple platforms — applications where models can use tools, access system resources, and accomplish complex tasks. More on that soon. 🤫.

We'd love your help making this better:.

We're excited to see what you build 🦾.

Seema Verma, executive vice president and general manager of Oracle Health and Life Sciences, stated the aim is to “monitor performance, identify emerging risks, and coordinate responses across the trial lifecycle.” The offering combines Oracle’s Life Sciences applications, AI-assisted capabilities, connected data services, and cloud infrastructure.

The agents fit into an established clinical trial operations portfolio covering portfolio planning, study startup, electronic trial master file management, and clinical trial management. Those unified applications run through Oracle Cloud Infrastructure and support systems integration, automation, and operational analytics.

Industry observers note that oracle Life Sciences CTMS, its clinical trial management system, centrally tracks study activities, site performance, and regulatory documentation. Interoperability with electronic data capture and electronic trial master file systems supports data integrity and oversight across a research portfolio.

According to recent reports, that application landscape gives context to the emphasis on coordination. Planning, startup, documentation, and trial management already occupy distinct workflows; the agent layer is intended to draw operational intelligence across applications and supported external sources, then present recommendations for review.

The wider Oracle Life Sciences platform serves sponsors, contract research organizations, and research sites. It also spans clinical trial data collection, pharmacovigilance, or drug-safety monitoring, and data intelligence, with embedded AI and analytics supporting study design and execution.

Oracle looks to extend the AI-assisted capabilities into clinical data management, post-trial analytics, trial design, and post-market workflows. Those are roadmap items rather than functions included in the initial early-adopter release, and they would carry agentic assistance beyond the conduct of an active study.

In a recent development, the early-adopter product consequently centers on operational coordination rather than autonomous trial management. Human approval controls execution in the initial release, while Oracle’s roadmap points toward extending that supervised model across a wider set of clinical research and post-market workflows.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that while everyone (and their grandma 👵) is spinning up upcoming ASR models, picking the right one for your use case can feel more overwhelming than choosing your next Netflix show.
  • Most benchmarks focus on short-form English transcription (<30s), and overlook other important tasks, such as (1) multilingual performance and (2) model throughput, which can a be deciding factor for long-form audio like meetings and podcasts.
  • Over the past two years, the Open ASR Leaderboard has become a standard for comparing open and closed-source models on both accuracy and efficiency.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that while everyone (and their grandma 👵) is spinning up upcoming ASR models, picking the right one for your use case can feel more overwhelming than choosing your next Netflix show. As of 21 Nov 2025, there are 150 Audio-Text-to-Text and 27K ASR models on the Hub 🤯.

Most benchmarks focus on short-form English transcription (<30s), and overlook other important tasks, such as (1) multilingual performance and (2) model throughput, which can a be deciding factor for long-form audio like meetings and podcasts.

Over the past two years, the Open ASR Leaderboard has become a standard for comparing open and closed-source models on both accuracy and efficiency. Recently, multilingual and long-form transcription tracks have been added to the leaderboard 🎉.

As of 21 Nov 2025, the Open ASR Leaderboard compares 60+ open and closed-source models from 18 organizations, across 11 datasets.

In a recent preprint, we dive into the technical setup and highlight some key trends in modern ASR. Here are the major takeaways 👇.

Models combining Conformer encoders with large language model (LLM) decoders currently lead in English transcription accuracy. For example, NVIDIA’s Canary-Qwen-2.5B, IBM’s Granite-Speech-3.3-8B, and Microsoft’s Phi-4-Multimodal-Instruct achieve the lowest word error rates (WER), showing that integrating LLM reasoning can significantly boost ASR accuracy.

💡 Pro-tip: NVIDIA introduced Fast Conformer, a 2x faster variant of the Conformer, that is used in their Canary and Parakeet suite of models.

While highly accurate, these LLM decoders tend to be slower than simpler approaches. On the Open ASR Leaderboard, efficiency is measured using inverse real-time factor (RTFx), where higher is better.

Industry observers note that for even faster inference, CTC and TDT decoders deliver 10–100× faster throughput, albeit with slightly higher error rates. This makes them ideal for real-time, offline, or batch transcription tasks (such as meetings, lectures, or podcasts).

Recent findings suggest that openAI’s Whisper Large v3 remains a strong multilingual baseline, supporting 99 languages. However, fine-tuned or distilled variants like Distil-Whisper and CrisperWhisper often outperform the original on English-only tasks, showing how targeted fine-tuning can improve specialization (how to fine-tune? Check out guides for Whisper, Parakeet, and Voxtral).

That remarked, focusing on English tends to reduce multilingual coverage 👉 a classic case of the tradeoff between specialization and generalization. Similarly, while self-supervised systems like Meta’s Massively Multilingual Speech (MMS) and Omnilingual ASR can support 1K+ languages, they trail behind language-specific encoders in accuracy.

⭐ While just five languages are currently benchmarked, we’re planning to expand to more languages and are excited for newly introduced dataset and models contributions to multilingual ASR through GitHub pull requests.

According to recent reports, 🎯 Alongside multilingual benchmarks, several community-driven leaderboards focus on individual languages. For example, the Open Universal Arabic ASR Leaderboard compares models across Modern Standard Arabic and regional dialects, highlighting how speech variation and diglossia challenge current systems. Similarly. the Russian ASR Leaderboard provides a growing hub for evaluating encoder-decoder and CTC models on Russian-specific phonology and morphology. These localized efforts mirror the broader multilingual leaderboard’s mission to encourage dataset sharing, fine-tuned checkpoints, and transparent model comparisons, especially in languages with fewer established ASR resources.

For long-form audio (e.g., podcasts, lectures, meetings), closed-source systems still edge out open ones. It could be due to domain tuning, custom chunking, or production-grade optimization.

It has been revealed that among open models, OpenAI’s Whisper Large v3 performs the best. But for throughput, CTC-based Conformers shine 👉 for example, NVIDIA’s Parakeet CTC 1.1B achieves an RTFx of 2793.75, compared to 68.56 for Whisper Large v3, with only a moderate WER degradation (6.68 and 6.43 respectively).

According to recent reports, the tradeoff? Parakeet is English-only, again reminding us of that multilingual and specialization tradeoff 🫠.

Industry observers note that ⭐ While closed systems still lead, there’s huge potential for open-source innovation here. Long-form ASR remains one of the most exciting frontiers for the community to tackle next!

Given how fast ASR is evolving, we’re excited to see what new architectures push performance and efficiency, and how the Open ASR Leaderboard continues to serve as a transparent, community-driven benchmark for the field, and as a reference for other leaderboards (Russian, Arabic, and Speech DeepFake Detection).

We’ll keep expanding the Open ASR LeaderBoard with more models, more languages, and more datasets so stay tuned 👀.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage News AWS PrivateLink Tunnel Endpoints Open a Whole CIDR Range to Another Account.

Nov 18, 2026 4 min read.

Recent findings suggest that AWS has published a technical walkthrough of tunnel endpoints, a VPC endpoint type launched in September that lets an application in one VPC reach every address in a CIDR range shared from another account, instead of one resource at a time. The provider shares a CIDR-type resource configuration through AWS Resource Access Manager and the consumer creates a tunnel endpoint against it. From then on, anything inside the range is reachable, including resources that did not exist when the share was made.

Bruce Pinsky and Ashish Kumar of AWS frame it as a vendor-access problem, for "a vendor or service provider whose software must reach applications and resources in a customer's network." Until now, that meant a separate PrivateLink resource configuration per database or host, which breaks down when the resources are ephemeral, or the customer does not want to enumerate them. With a CIDR configuration, the customer defines a perimeter in address ranges, and "resources located outside the perimeter can't be reached by the vendor." Two further properties come with the design: the consumer and provider VPCs can use overlapping CIDR blocks, and connections "can start only from the consumer VPC, not from the provider network.".

(Source: AWS Networking & Content Delivery blog).

On the r/aws thread about the September launch, the first question was what this does that VPC peering does not, from a self-described veteran of AWS's advanced networking components. The answers that followed are the use cases: a peering connection exposes the whole VPC in both directions, while a tunnel endpoint shares a subset of the address space in one direction only; one commenter at a bank wrote that "peering with unregulated partners is a massive no-no, the auditors will rip you to shreds for it." Another pointed to clusters that do client-side load balancing, such as self-managed Kafka or Aerospike, which until now needed port-based routing on a Network Load Balancer and a separate port-mapping horizon for connections arriving over an interface endpoint. The same thread drew the line against VPC Lattice itself: Lattice services work at layer 7, tunnel endpoints at layer 4 without a resource configuration per target.

In a recent development, the unusual part is on the consumer side: the application's traffic has to arrive at the tunnel endpoint wrapped in GENEVE, the encapsulation protocol defined in RFC 8926, over UDP port 6081 and in the same Availability Zone. The endpoint strips the header, checks that the inner destination falls inside the shared range, rewrites the source to a resource gateway address, and forwards a plain packet into the provider VPC. Linux can do the wrapping in the kernel. The walkthrough creates an ip link add ... type geneve id 0 device inside its own network namespace with a default route through it, which sends the provider's ranges into the tunnel and leaves the instance's other traffic alone. On the far side, the resources see the resource gateway as the client, so the post advises security groups that reference the gateway's security group or subnet rather than a single address.

The documentation lists the constraints. Inner traffic must be TCP, with UDP permitted only for DNS, so ICMP and ping do not work, and IP fragments are dropped. Private DNS names are not supported on tunnel endpoints. The endpoint's subnets must sit in Availability Zones that overlap with the resource gateway's, or the association reveals as inaccessible. A resource gateway's DNS setting cannot be changed after creation. And the access logs identify the consumer's endpoint but carry no field for the inner source address, so a provider can attribute traffic to a vendor and not to a workload behind that vendor's endpoint. The post also warns that sharing 0.0.0.0/0 grants access to everything the provider VPC can route to, including networks behind VPC peering, Direct Connect or a Site-to-Site VPN, and recommends sharing the narrowest ranges that work.

According to recent reports, both points have been tested in practice. Ryo Suzuki of the Japanese consultancy Classmethod connected two VPCs that both use 10.0.0.0/16 and got HTTP through, but only by running a GENEVE relay as root on the client, by routing a /32 per destination host, or by putting an HAProxy or NAT instance in front, each of which adds a hop or a single point of failure; his conclusion was that "route management according to the number of destinations is required." In a second experiment, he shared 0.0.0.0/0 from a VPC with a NAT gateway and reached the internet from a VPC with no gateway at all, which confirmed AWS's warning from the other side; he judged it workable as a temporary path and "difficult to use in a permanent production setup.".

Pricing is an hourly charge per tunnel endpoint plus a per-GB charge for data processed, under PrivateLink pricing, with the provider side billed per GB through the resource gateway under VPC Lattice pricing, and the feature is available in 28 regions. Terraform support followed from the community: a contributor request opened two days after launch was implemented by another contributor and shipped in version 6.71.0 of the AWS provider, as a Tunnel endpoint type on aws_vpc_endpoint and a cidr_resource block on the Lattice resource configuration.
