📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Starburst Data introduced its Enterprise Context Layer at Launch Point 2026 on November 18, 2026, presenting Context Studio and AI-ready Data Products as a way to give AI agents governed business meaning alongside access to distributed enterprise data.

Sources indicate that starburst says the latest advances to AIDA, its AI Data Assistant, expand the questions agents can answer, the data they can access and the workflows they support, while customers’ own agents can use the same governed context. The intended result is more accurate, consistent and traceable answers from distributed enterprise data.

Enterprise schemas locate and describe data without reliably encoding the rules behind a business question. A case record marked as pending may or may not count as open, and a column name cannot explain how net exposure is calculated or who qualifies as an active customer. Starburst’s Context Studio documentation claims this leaves agents to infer meaning that may be scattered across data products, code repositories, metadata stores, unstructured sources and analysts’ knowledge, producing different answers to the same question.

It has been revealed that context Studio consolidates glossary terms, metrics, business rules, synonyms, join keys and data products into one governed store. Its Context Studio as Code API receives context from repositories and pipelines, while an out-of-the-box Galaxy harvester derives entities from existing Starburst Galaxy data products and query history. The store tracks each entity’s origin. Because every source push describes that connection’s complete current state, an entity omitted from a later push is removed from the store.

Sources indicate that A named steward can review and certify entries through the Context Studio interface or certification API, and agents prioritize certified context. During private preview, however, all context enters as certified while Starburst develops that capability further. AIDA, Claude and other agents supporting Model Context Protocol (MCP), a standard for connecting AI applications to Galaxy data, can use the Context Studio MCP server. They apply certified definitions, metrics, rules and join keys when writing and running queries, with Starburst Galaxy applying the individual user’s access policy each time.

Recent findings suggest that the Launch Point announcement is broader than a first release of Context Studio. Starburst Galaxy’s release notes date private-preview support to October 5, 2026, listing the Galaxy harvester, Context Studio as Code API and MCP access to certified context. The newer development is the Enterprise Context Layer umbrella and the introduction of AI-ready Data Products within it, not the start of Context Studio availability.

In a recent development, context Studio remains in private preview. Organizations need a Galaxy account enrolled in the preview, administrator access to that account and access to the agent or AI client they plan to connect. Starburst requires interested customers to contact their account team for access and current preview status. Usage limits are disclosed during onboarding and may change.

Industry observers note that for enterprises running several agents, the design centralizes business vocabulary and query logic while preserving user-level data controls. The key execution issue is the certification workflow: shared context can already be distributed across MCP clients, but the preview marks every item as certified, leaving steward-controlled review as a central piece still under development.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Hugging Face TRL now officially integrates with RapidFire AI to accelerate your fine-tuning and post-training experiments. TRL people can now discover, install, and run RapidFire AI as the fastest way to compare multiple fine-tuning/post-training configurations to customize LLMs without major code changes and without bloating GPU requirements.

When fine-tuning or post-training LLMs, teams often do not have the time and/or budget to compare multiple configs even though that can significantly boost eval metrics. RapidFire AI lets you launch multiple TRL configs concurrently--even on a single GPU--and compare them in near real time via a newly introduced adaptive, chunk-based scheduling and execution scheme. In internal benchmarks referenced in the TRL page, this delivers ~16–24× higher experimentation throughput than sequentially comparing configs one after another, enabling you to reach much better metrics much faster.

RapidFire AI establishes live three-way communication between your IDE, a metrics dashboard, and a multi-GPU execution backend.

Drop-in TRL wrappers — Use RFSFTConfig, RFDPOConfig, and RFGRPOConfig as near-zero-code replacements for TRL's SFT/DPO/GRPO configs.

Adaptive chunk-based concurrent training — RapidFire AI shards the dataset into a given number of chunks and cycles configs at chunk boundaries to enable earlier apples-to-apples comparisons and also maximize GPU utilization.

Interactive Control Ops (IC Ops) — From the dashboard itself, you can Stop, Resume, Delete, and Clone-Modify, possibly with Warm-Start, any runs in flight to avoid wasting resources on underperforming configs and double-down on better performing configs--no job restarts, no juggling separate GPUs or clusters, no resource bloat.

Clone promising configurations with modified hyperparameters, optionally warm-starting from the parent's weights, all from the live dashboard.

Industry observers note that multi-GPU orchestration — The RapidFire AI scheduler automatically places and orchestrates configs across available GPUs on chunks of data via effcient shared-memory mechanisms. You focus on your models and eval metrics, not plumbing.

Industry observers note that MLflow-based dashboard — Real-time metrics, logs, and IC Ops in one place as soon as you start your experiment. Support for more dashboards such as Trackio, W&B, and TensorBoard coming soon.

Recent findings suggest that rapidFire AI splits your dataset randomly into "chunks" and cycles LLM configurations through the GPUs at chunk boundaries. You get incremental signal on eval metrics across all configs much more rapidly. The automatic checkpointing via an efficient shared-memory-based adapter/model spilling/loading mechanism keeps training smooth, stable, and consistent. Use IC Ops to adapt mid-flight to stop low-performers earlier and clone promising ones with tweaked config knobs, optionally warm-starting from the parent's weights.

Sequential vs. Task Parallel vs. RapidFire AI: The adaptive scheduler maximizes GPU utilization across multiple configs and GPUs. The bottom row shows IC Ops in action—stopping, cloning, and modifying runs mid-flight.

In a recent development, the plan represents a 38% increase in Hi Auto’s footprint at the brands and continues a relationship that began in 2023. The longer contract and larger rollout make voice ordering an ongoing operating layer across the franchise system, with deployment performance now tied to sales and staffing measures as well as order volume.

Industry observers note that hi Auto reports that the system has processed more than 11 million orders at Checkers & Rally’s during 2026 and is handling more than 1.1 million orders a month. Across the deployment, average ticket size has risen 1.1%, while the number of orders needing a crew member to step in has fallen by half since January 2026.

Those measures track different parts of the business case: ticket size reflects sales per order, while crew interventions show where automation still requires human assistance. Evaluating both provides a fuller picture than counting automated transactions alone.

“Checkers & Rally’s challenged us to prove that AI in the drive-thru drives growth, not just efficiency,” remarked Hi Auto CEO and co-founder Roy Baharav.

Sources indicate that the deployment takes orders in English and Spanish and can follow a guest who switches between them within the same order. Checkers & Rally’s states that capability fits the diverse communities its restaurants serve, making language support part of the ordering workflow across different local markets.

The AI Order Taker greets guests, takes and upsells orders, and sends them directly to the restaurant’s point-of-sale (POS) system. Human assistance remains available when a guest needs a team member.

It has been revealed that hi Auto’s product documentation says the platform combines large language models for natural-language processing with in-house audio filtering and automatic speech recognition tailored to drive-thru environments. An audio box connects the system to existing headsets and POS platforms, with HME, PAR and Xenial listed as supported integrations.

The documentation adds that a trained human supervisor steps in when the AI has low confidence. This design separates routine order taking from exception handling, reducing the need for restaurant employees to correct every uncertain exchange while retaining human oversight for difficult conversations.

Across approximately 1,000 stores, Hi Auto reports order completion above 93% and accuracy of 96%. Completion is the percentage of orders sent to the POS without staff intervention, while accuracy is the percentage sent with every item and customization exactly right. These figures cover the company’s broader deployment base rather than Checkers & Rally’s alone.

Industry observers note that for franchise operations, the platform provides centralized control of voice persona, scripts, upsells and regional configurations. Franchisees can adjust menus, limited-time offers and regional offers within brand controls, allowing local variation while maintaining system-wide standards.

According to recent reports, the next phase of the rollout will test whether the reported ticket gains and reduced crew intervention hold across a larger franchise footprint. That makes consistency across restaurants, languages and supervised exceptions the central operational question behind the longer commitment.

  • Product facts are a good place to test whether agreement means accuracy, because the right answer is usually written down by the company that makes the product.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This article is based on findings from Scento’s October 2026 study of how ChatGPT, Gemini and Perplexity answer questions about perfume notes (full method, data and limitations).

Industry observers note that A common safety net in AI agent design is to ask more than one model, or the same model more than once, and trust the answer they agree on. The idea has solid roots. Self-consistency, which samples several reasoning paths and keeps the majority answer, improves accuracy on reasoning benchmarks. Using one model to grade another, studied in Judging LLM-as-a-Judge, reaches high agreement with human raters, although the authors also document position, verbosity and self-enhancement biases.

Product facts are a good place to test whether agreement means accuracy, because the right answer is usually written down by the company that makes the product. We tested it on perfume, and the answer was: only partly.

Sources indicate that the prompt was a single sentence asking for a fragrance’s top, heart and base notes. We sent it for each of 100 perfumes, drawn from 45 houses, to ChatGPT, Gemini and Perplexity on 20 October 2026. All calls ran once, in English, from a US location: 300 in total. Gemini returned 99 answers, as one call ended in a service error.

It has been revealed that for 91 perfumes, the reference was the note list the house publishes on its own site. For the remaining 9, it was a list two authorised retailers agree on. Grading was done by a script that used no language model at all. It mapped every note in each answer onto a 411-note glossary, then compared the result with the reference. When we checked 20 gradings by hand, 17 agreed exactly and 19 within one note. That check was not blind, because the reviewer could see the script’s result.

We measured four things: recall (how many official notes an answer contains), precision (how many of the notes it names are official), exact match (all official notes, nothing extra) and placement (whether each note sits in the right top, heart or base tier).

On recall, the three engines look almost interchangeable. Median recall was 1.00 for each. ChatGPT returned every official note in 82% of answers, Perplexity in 78% and Gemini in 69%.

Agreement on the full answer was much rarer. Of the 99 perfumes all three engines answered, all three returned every official note for 59. All three matched the official list exactly for only 39. At least one engine was exact for 79, and for 20 perfumes none was.

According to recent reports, in about one case in five (20 of the 99 perfumes), all three engines returned every official note, yet at least one of them also added notes that are not on the list. A recall check would have passed all three answers.

The most instructive results were the ones the engines had in common.

It has been revealed that for Jean Paul Gaultier Le Male Elixir, the two agreeing retailers give three notes: lavender on top, tonka bean in the heart, benzoin in the base. ChatGPT, Gemini and Perplexity each produced an identical seven-note pyramid. Each included all three reference notes, put tonka bean and benzoin in each other’s tiers, and added four more. Three separate engines, one identical answer, and that answer departs from the reference in the same places.

For Viktor&Rolf Flowerbomb, the house lists four notes. Gemini and Perplexity both returned the same 11-note pyramid, missed one official note and added eight. Perplexity’s answer then noted that the brand’s current description highlights the four official notes, so it held both versions and led with the older one.

According to recent reports, our data cannot say why the answers match. But the practical point does not depend on the cause. When systems draw on the same pool of web text, a majority vote measures how widely a version has spread, not whether it is current. Agreement between them is weak evidence that the answer matches what the brand itself publishes today.

It has been revealed that other extra notes belonged to one engine alone, and these are exactly what comparison catches. In 32% of its answers Gemini added at least one note that neither of the other engines named, against 10% for ChatGPT and 11% for Perplexity.

Industry observers note that for Prada Infusion de Vétiver, the house lists four notes. ChatGPT and Perplexity returned exactly those four, in exactly the right places. Gemini returned twelve, including eight that no other engine gave, for a precision of 0.33. For Rochas Eau de Rochas, Perplexity matched the ten-note list exactly, while Gemini returned 18 notes, ten of them named by no other engine.

It has been revealed that cross-checking works well here: an outlier stands out against two agreeing answers. That is the asymmetry builders should keep in mind. Disagreement is a useful alarm. Agreement is not a certificate.

Some answers had the right notes in the wrong places. For Montblanc Explorer, ChatGPT matched six of the nine official notes, but only two of those six sat in the correct tier, a placement accuracy of 33%. A check that only asks whether a note appears somewhere in the answer would not see that four of the six are in the wrong tier.

For any agent that turns product facts into decisions, structure carries meaning. The same is true of sizes, compatibility, dosage or ingredients in other categories. An evaluation that checks only whether the facts appear somewhere in the answer will miss this class of mistake.

According to recent reports, answers about designer perfumes carried off-list notes more often than answers about niche ones on all three engines, with gaps of 22 to 32 percentage points. ChatGPT showed the widest split: four in ten of its designer answers included at least one off-list note, compared with fewer than one in ten of its niche answers.

Industry observers note that A short official list gives an engine more room to add notes, so we controlled for list length by pooling all three engines and sorting answers into three bands. Designer answers still carried extras more often in each one: 70% against 31% for lists of five notes or fewer (27 and 29 answers), 61% against 21% for six to eight notes (51 and 42), and 26% against 13% for nine or more (72 and 77). The samples are small, and because each group came from its own set of houses and source pages, we cannot isolate the cause. What the pattern does suggest is that accuracy varies by product segment, and a single figure for a whole catalogue can hide that.

Sources indicate that use consensus to find disagreement, not to confirm truth. Comparing models is a cheap way to flag one-off additions. It cannot detect an answer the models share, so it should not be the last check.

Ground owned facts in an owned source. Where a fact has an owner, such as a manufacturer’s specification, the most reliable path is to retrieve it from a structured record that carries its source page. Open standards make this practical: schema.org Product markup on the page, and the Model Context Protocol for letting agents query a data source directly. Google’s guidance on AI features says structured data should match the visible text on the page, and that no special schema.org markup is needed to appear in those features.

Score precision, exact match and structure, not just recall. An answer that contains every fact plus three invented ones passes a recall test and still misleads the user.

Recent findings suggest that grade deterministically where reference data exists. A rule-based grader compared with structured data is repeatable and auditable, and it does not share a model’s blind spots.

Run more than once. Answers vary from run to run, a point Andrew Lissimore made on this site about measuring AI shopping recommendations. Our study made one call per perfume per engine, so its run-to-run variation is unknown.

Each perfume was asked once per engine, on one day, in English, from one country. Claude and engines without web search were not tested. A note missing from an official list is not automatically wrong, because houses sometimes publish only key notes, so precision is a lower bound on correctness. The grader was tuned on the same 100 perfumes, and the sample is mostly Western designer and niche houses whose lists could be verified.

Within those limits the pattern was consistent. Three engines agreeing tells you that a version of the facts is widely repeated. Only the source tells you whether it is current. So here is the question for anyone whose agent checks itself against a second model: what does your agent do when two models give the same wrong answer?

In a recent development, sebastian Dobrincu is Founder and CEO of Scento, a Paris-headquartered online perfume organization that sells over 3 million perfume decants a year in Europe. Scento designed and ran this study of AI answer accuracy and publishes its perfume note data free of charge for developers and AI agents.

Building Deep Research: How we Achieved State of the Art

📅 24 Nov 2025 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1435 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Research agents are rapidly becoming one of the most vital applications of AI.
  • Industry observers note that the task of building an agent harness is to create a software layer that enhances a model’s runtime execution through context management, tool invocations, loop control, orchestration, and error handling.
  • This requires forecasting how models will evolve, staying optimistic about their progress, limiting assumptions, and avoiding hand-crafted optimizations.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Research agents are rapidly becoming one of the most vital applications of AI. Research is a foundational knowledge-work task: collecting, reading, and synthesizing information underpins everything from writing and decision-making to coding itself. Yet human-driven research is constrained by memory, reading speed, and time. AI research agents, by contrast, can process vast amounts of information, synthesize insights instantly, and scale effortlessly. Because of this, research agents are emerging as a top use case for AI today and will soon become a core subcomponent of broader agentic workflows across content generation, coding, sales, and more. In this post, we share the technical and philosophical lessons we’ve learned building a state-of-the-art research agent, and where we believe the field is headed.

Industry observers note that the task of building an agent harness is to create a software layer that enhances a model’s runtime execution through context management, tool invocations, loop control, orchestration, and error handling. Building applications on top of rapidly improving models is, however, a modern engineering challenge. How can we design software today that absorbs the performance gains from future model releases?

This requires forecasting how models will evolve, staying optimistic about their progress, limiting assumptions, and avoiding hand-crafted optimizations.

It has been revealed that we learned this the hard way seven months ago, when we had to abandon our first attempt at deep research and rebuild the entire system from scratch. The first architecture was complicated and sophisticated (we thought this was a good thing), but its assumptions became bottlenecks when the next generation of models arrived.

Industry observers note that over the last seven months, model capabilities have quietly but meaningfully evolved (especially in their tool-calling abilities). This single optimization focus has pushed us from workflows to agents. We believe future models will be trained to solve the current pain points of agent developers. Every model is ultimately consumed by a harness, so models should evolve in service of that harness. We hope to see models improve in high-recall summarization (for context compression), tool-calling reliability, and concision in writing.

Similarly, tools should evolve to support LLMs and widely adopted agent harnesses. The best tools should perform some context engineering on the tool side, abstracted away from the agent. They should return only the most relevant data instead of dumping large volumes of tokens into the context window. As a tool provider, we’ve invested heavily in our advanced search feature, which has context engineering baked in. This in turn lowers hallucinations and latency for the downstream agent processes.

To build agents that improve over time, we followed a few guiding principles:.

It has been revealed that long-horizon research tasks expose a fundamental challenge in current agent design: the task of maintaining a clean, optimized context window over time. If curating context is not a task the engineer pays close attention to, the agent is almost destined for failure. The following outlines our thinking around this concept within the deep research domain.

Using Tavily’s Advanced Search is the natural first step to take in overcoming this challenge, in that it abstracts away the processing of raw web content and returns only the most relevant content chunks from each source. In leveraging this functionality, we let Tavily Search do the heavy lifting and allow Tavily Research to reap the benefit, gathering the most valuable content in a latency-efficient manner.

According to recent reports, ensuring that the agent does not overfit to a single research thread is the next step towards an effective context-gathering pipeline. It is in this regard that global state persistence and source deduplication is paramount, and in our case, it helps threefold:.

At Tavily, interacting with the web is our bread and butter. Architecting a refined web-retrieval system engineered for deep research was a foundational building block for our deep research agent design as a whole.

Sources indicate that humans research in an inherently unstructured, iterative way. We start by defining the task: what we’re trying to accomplish and what information we need. We next gather data from our sources, extracting the key insights and holding them in short-term memory, letting these distilled thoughts guide our subsequent actions.

This cycle repeats: collect information, distill it, decide what to do next. Only once we’ve gathered enough understanding to produce the final deliverable do we return to the original sources, using them as references to assemble the finished product.

We believe that deep research agents should be designed in a similar manner, in that tool outputs should be distilled into reflections, and only the set of past reflections should be used as context for your tool caller. Similar to humans, it is only at the point when your agent begins to prepare the final deliverable that you must provide the raw information as context, so as to ensure there is no information loss.

According to recent reports, this approach differs from traditional context structuring in a ReAct agent-based architecture. Typically, tool calls and outputs are propagated through the tool calling loop, with previously retrieved/generated tokens being persisted in the context window on each subsequent iteration. This pattern can be seen in LangChain’s Open Deep Research agent implementation, and from a token consumption perspective, it can be modeled by the following quadratic series, where n n n is the amount of tokens the tool calling model is invoked with on each tool calling iteration, and m m m is the number of tool calling iterations.

n+2n+3n+⋯+mn  =  n⋅m(m+1)2n + 2n + 3n + \cdots + mn \;=\; n \cdot \frac{m(m+1)}{2}n+2n+3n+⋯+mn=n⋅2m(m+1)​.

Contrarily, our proposed method of context engineering removes this token propagation (as the knowledge distillations, even when aggregated, are negligible when compared to the quantity of tokens gathered from web) and can be modeled by the following linear series.

n+n+n+⋯+n  =  nmn + n + n + \cdots + n \;=\; nmn+n+n+⋯+n=nm.

When comparing the two approaches, tokens are saved on a per-agent basis by a factor of m+12 \frac{m+1}{2} 2m+1​, and when extrapolating this over a multi-agent system and with consumption at scale, the absolute value of tokens saved becomes even more significant.

Through this methodology, we were able to reduce token consumption by 66% (when compared to Open Deep Research) while achieving SOTA on DeepResearch Bench – the intersection of quality and efficiency in full effect.

Recent findings suggest that building production-grade agents is a balancing act. We leaned into autonomy to maximize performance and quality, while still meeting strict requirements for latency, cost, and reliability.

Recent findings suggest that LLMs are inherently non-deterministic, and we found that giving them guard-railed freedom to reason and iterate produces the strongest results. Autonomy, when gone wrong, can cause agent behavior to go off track. Tools can be called incorrectly, LLMs can overfit to a subtopic, and expected reasoning patterns may break. No single safeguard will catch all of these challenges.

A shift in engineering mindset is required: treat failure modes as core design considerations, not afterthoughts. Simple guardrails like tool-call retries or model cascades help, but proactively anticipating anomalies, reinforcing proper patterns in prompting and edge-case testing is what enables production-grade, long-running agents.

From our experience, it’s better to expose a small, essential toolset to the agent rather than a large, complex one. We were tempted to over-engineer by adding many tools that seemed useful in theory, but in practice this created latest failure modes and made it harder for LLMs to consistently choose the right tool and iterate effectively.

It has been revealed that we used evals to steer our development process but also recognize their shortcomings. LLM-as-a-judge evals are difficult to trust: current models are non‑deterministic, uninterpretable in their reasoning, and can turn into bottlenecks, especially for long‑running agents where a single experiment can take days to complete.

Sources indicate that rather than optimizing for benchmark scores, we optimized for directional feedback. The core question was always: did this change make the agent more reliable and more useful in practice? Evals became a tool for validating that direction, not the optimization target. Intuition and careful agent‑trace monitoring consistently provided higher‑signal feedback than any single eval score. Overall, the best outcome is rarely the highest numerical score. For production systems, improvements like reduced token usage, reliability, lower latency, and fewer failures are more valuable than a one‑point bump on an eval.

According to recent reports, what is r in your solution ? Is it a scratch pad that is updated in the LLM context between each round of research ?

r in the solution is the research insight from previous tool call.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ofqual will propose changes to non-exam assessment in selected A Level subjects and require stronger action against misuse of wearable technology, Chief Regulator Sir Ian Bauckham stated in a letter to leaders at some awarding organisations published on November 18, 2026. The intervention applies to England.

Industry observers note that the forthcoming proposals will cover A Level history and the three A Level English qualifications. Ofqual will also consider changes in other subjects and qualifications where risks to authenticity require action. Awarding organisations have been invited to share their views on the regulator’s direction before any formal consultation.

Bauckham’s concern focuses on work produced without supervision, particularly extended writing. In the full letter, he stated it is increasingly difficult to establish reliably whether such work is entirely the student’s own. He explicitly acknowledged that not all non-exam assessment is inherently vulnerable to AI, while identifying particular risks in some forms of assessment.

“Where we can no longer have sufficient confidence in the authenticity of assessed work, we must consider whether the assessment itself needs to change,” he wrote. That position connects malpractice controls to assessment design: when the conditions surrounding an assessment no longer provide reliable evidence of authorship, detection measures alone may not resolve the underlying problem.

Industry observers note that alongside the assessment proposals, the letter addresses exam security as wearable devices become more sophisticated and AI-enabled. Awarding organisations must take all reasonable steps to protect assessment integrity and ensure that required assessment conditions are implemented effectively and consistently.

Relevant centre staff, including invigilators where appropriate, are expected to receive effective training using clear, consistent and practical resources to identify and respond to wearable-technology misuse. The training should be in place for the summer 2027 exam series. The response cannot rest with invigilators alone, and organisations were asked to consider additional preventive and detection measures.

Sources indicate that responses are requested before November 30, 2026. Bauckham asked organisations to describe their risk assessments, preventive action, support for centres and any further measures they consider necessary. Those planning collective action were also asked to explain the arrangements they will use to coordinate effectively with other awarding organisations.

Industry observers note that the new intervention follows Bauckham’s March 3, 2026 letter, which requested stronger measures against mobile phones and other devices in exam halls and AI misuse in non-exam assessment. The earlier letter reported that 2025 penalties included 1,125 cases in which students lost an entire GCSE or A Level and nearly 2,000 cases in which marks were deducted.

Almost half of approximately 5,000 malpractice cases reported annually over the preceding three years involved students taking mobile phones or other communication devices into exams. Detected AI misuse cases reported to Ofqual remained relatively low at that time, although the letter recorded significant concern among teachers, leaders and others about the real extent of misuse.

In a recent development, ofqual previously asked exam boards to improve awareness of what constitutes misuse and to strengthen deterrence, detection and prevention, including more rigorous candidate and teacher authentication of work. The November letter adds named A Level subjects for possible assessment changes and a specific training timetable for wearable risks.

Ofqual’s direction therefore extends beyond policing individual misconduct. The open question for the forthcoming proposals is which forms of extended writing can remain reliable measures of a student’s own achievement when work is produced without supervision.

Continuous batching from first principles

📅 25 Nov 2025 | ⏱️ 18 min read (3629 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~18 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • TL;DR: in this blog post, starting from attention mechanisms and KV caching, we derive continuous batching by optimizing for throughput.
  • If you've ever used Qwen, Claude, or any other AI chatbot, you've probably noticed something: it takes a while for the first word of the response to appear, and then words appear one-by-one on your screen with (hopefully) a regular and fast-paced frequency.
  • Recent findings suggest that this generation process is computationally expensive: it requires passing the input through billions of parameters for each token generated.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

TL;DR: in this blog post, starting from attention mechanisms and KV caching, we derive continuous batching by optimizing for throughput.

If you've ever used Qwen, Claude, or any other AI chatbot, you've probably noticed something: it takes a while for the first word of the response to appear, and then words appear one-by-one on your screen with (hopefully) a regular and fast-paced frequency. That's because at the heart of it, all LLMs are just fancy next token predictors. An LLM first processes your entire prompt to produce one latest token. Then it keeps adding tokens one by one, each time reading everything that came before, until it decides generation is over.

Recent findings suggest that this generation process is computationally expensive: it requires passing the input through billions of parameters for each token generated. To make these models practical for real-world applications, particularly when serving many consumers simultaneously, researchers and engineers have developed a range of efficient inference techniques.One of the most impactful optimizations is continuous batching, which attempts to maximize performance by processing multiple conversations in parallel and swapping them out when they are done.

To understand how continuous batching works and why it's so effective in high-load serving scenarios, we'll build up from the fundamentals of how LLMs process tokens.

It has been revealed that the attention mechanism is the central piece of how LLMs work. A language model processes text by breaking it down into pieces that we call tokens. We can conceptually think of "tokens" as "words", but sometimes a word might be composed of several tokens. For each token sequence, the network computes a prediction of what the next token should be.

Many operations in the network are token-wise: each token is processed independently, and the output for a given token depends only on that token's content, not on any other tokens in the sequence. Operations like this include layer normalization or matrix multiplication. However, to create connections between words in a sentence, we need operations where tokens can influence each other.

Sources indicate that this is where attention comes in. Attention layers are the only place where different tokens interact with each other. Understanding how a network connects tokens together means understanding attention.

Let's see how this works in practice, in the case where there is only one input prompt.

According to recent reports, consider the initial prompt I am sure this project, tokenized as 7 tokens: [, I, am, sure, this, pro, ject]. The , or "Beginning of Sequence", is a special token we add at the start of the prompt to tell the language model that a newly introduced conversation starts here.

Recent findings suggest that each token is represented inside the network with a vector of length d (the hidden dimension). Therefore, the seven incoming tokens form a tensor xxx with shape [1,7,d]\left[1, 7, d \right][1,7,d]. 1 is the number of sequences, or batch size, which is just one in our case. 7 is the sequence length, and d is the hidden dimension, or the size of each token representation. Going forward, we'll use nnn instead of 7 as the sequence length.

In a recent development, input tensor x x x is then projected by three matrices: the query projection Wq W_q Wq​, the key projection Wk W_k Wk​ and the value projection Wv W_v Wv​. This produces three tensors Q Q Q, K K K and V V V, all of shape [1,n,A] \left[1, n , A \right] [1,n,A], where A A A is the dimension of the attention head. We call them the query, key and value states, respectively. This is represented on the left in the figure below.

Next, tensors Q Q Q and K K K are multiplied together to measure similarity between tokens, producing a tensor of shape [1,n,n] \left[ 1, n , n \right] [1,n,n]. This is why we say that attention has quadratic complexity in sequence length. Computing QKT QK^T QKT requires O(n2d) \mathcal{O} \left( n^2 d \right) O(n2d) operations, so the cost is a square of n n n the sequence length. It is represented on the right in the figure above.

We then apply a boolean attention mask to QKT QK^T QKT to control which tokens can interact, as represented in the figure below. In this figure, the attention mask is a causal mask, meaning each token only interacts with tokens that came before it. This follows the intuition that a cause must come before its consequence, hence the name causal mask. The attention mask is crucial because it dictates all token interactions in the network. Set all attention mask values to False and no token will ever interact with another in the whole network. We'll examine attention masks more closely in a few paragraphs.

Finally, after applying the attention mask, we take a token-wise softmax (which is the same as saying a row-wise softmax) and multiply the result by the value projection V V V to get the output of one attention head, of shape [1,n,A] \left[ 1, n , A \right] [1,n,A]. We offer a visual summary of the whole process in the following figure.

We are going to use a lot of attention visualization in this post, so to simplify things, we are going to condense the figure above just a bit.

According to recent reports, why this matters: In continuous batching, Q Q Q, K K K, and V V V can have different numbers of tokens because, as we'll see, we'll be processing different stages (prefill and decode) at the same time. To make it more general, let's say Q Q Q has shape [1,nQ,A] \left[1, n_Q , A \right] [1,nQ​,A], K K K has shape [1,nK,A] \left[ 1, n_K , A \right] [1,nK​,A], and V V V has shape [1,nV,A] \left[ 1, n_V , A \right] [1,nV​,A].

The attention scores QKT QK^T QKT then have shape [1,nQ,nK] \left[ 1, n_Q , n_K \right] [1,nQ​,nK​], and the attention mask has the same shape since it's applied point-wise to the scores.

In a recent development, after applying the attention mask and row-wise softmax, we multiply by V V V. Since we're multiplying a matrix of shape [1,nQ,nK] \left[ 1, n_Q , n_K \right] [1,nQ​,nK​] by one of shape [1,nV,A] \left[ 1, n_V , A \right] [1,nV​,A], the inner dimensions must match: nK=nV n_K = n_V nK​=nV​. This means V V V and K K K always have the same length, so we can simplify our visualizations by only showing K K K.Don't worry if this seems abstract: the figures will make it concrete.

Sources indicate that furthermore, since we know that the attention mask is applied to QKT QK^T QKT, we know they have the same shape. Instead of representing the attention scores, we will represent the attention mask in its place. Finally, since Q Q Q, K K K and V V V are direct projections of x x x, no need to represent x x x. This gives the simplified figure where we only represent Q Q Q, K K K and the attention mask:.

This representation also underlines how we can read an attention mask.

We read the mask row-by-row, which is the same as reading token-by-token: each row corresponds to one token's attention computation. A green square at position (row i, column j) means True: token j can influence token i. A white square means False: no interaction allowed.

Recent findings suggest that for example, look at the third row for token "am". The "I" column is green, so "I" influences the computation of "am". The "pro" column is white, so "pro" doesn't influence "am" . This is causal masking at work: future tokens can't affect past ones.

The last layer of the model outputs a token prediction for each input token. In our context, generating the continuation of a single prompt, we only care about the next token prediction from the last token. The last token is "ject" in the figure above, and the associated prediction is "will".

Industry observers note that the process we just described, where we take an entire input sequence, pass it through multiple attention layers and compute a score for the next token, is called prefill. This is because, as we'll see in a moment, much of the computation we performed can be cached and reused – hence, we are prefilling the cache. Thanks to the use of this cache, sequence generation can proceed using much less compute in a phase called decoding. In the decoding phase, generating one fresh token will be much faster than the initial full-sequence computation. Let's see why.

To continue generation, we begin a new forward pass, which would naively look like this:.

According to recent reports, to compute the attention scores of the latest token, we still need the key and value projections of the previous tokens. So we need to repeat the matrix multiplication of the old tokens (in grey in the figure above) with Wk W_k Wk​ and Wv W_v Wv​ to retrieve a result that was already computed once before. In other terms, we are wasting compute. Let's see how we can avoid that.

Right off the bat, we notice that the last token does not impact the attention calculation of the other tokens:.

It has been revealed that this follows the idea of the causal mask: since "will" comes after all previous tokens, it does not change their attention calculation. For text generation, causal attention is by far the most common, so we will focus on that case from now on. Keep in mind that non-causal attention schemes can also be used, especially when dealing with images. Considering we only need the next-token prediction for the "will" token, we can simplify the attention mechanism by only computing the output for this token.

Moreover, we already computed the K K K and V V V states for the tokens "", … , "ject" during the previous forward pass: if they have been stored, we do not need to recompute them again. This is the KV cache: the list of key and value states created during generation. It essentially allows one to reduce the compute cost of generating token n+1 n+1 n+1 from O(n2) \mathcal{O} \left( n^2 \right) O(n2) to O(n) \mathcal{O} \left( n \right) O(n) by avoiding recomputation of key and value projections, while paying a memory cost of O(n) \mathcal{O} \left( n \right) O(n).

In the figure above, only the tokens in white are computed: instead of computing the keys and values for 8 tokens, we compute them for 1. You can see that through KV caching, a lot of compute is saved.You can check this post for more visualizations of KV caching, or this one for a practical implementation example.

In a recent development, let's be a bit more specific about the cache size, because it's a good opportunity to examine the shapes present in our model. For a model with L \mathcal L L attention layers and H H H attention heads with head dimension A A A, the total cache size needed to store one token will be 2∗L∗AH 2 *\mathcal L * AH 2∗L∗AH with a factor of 2 2 2 to account for both K K K and V V V.For instance, Llama-2-7B with L=32 \mathcal{L}=32 L=32 layers, H=32 H=32 H=32 heads, and A=128 A=128 A=128 requires 2×32×128=8,192 2 \times 32 \times 128 = 8,192 2×32×128=8,192 values per token per layer. With float16 precision, this takes 2AH×2 2AH \times 2 2AH×2 bytes =16 = 16 =16 KB in memory.

KV caching is useful when we want to generate the next token, which is a stage we call decoding. But it can also be useful in the prefill stage, when we process the initial prompt and have many input tokens. Especially when there are large initial prompts that don't fit in GPU memory all at once.

In a recent development, up till now, we have looked at an example of prefill where we have n=7 n=7 n=7 tokens, but in practice initial prompts can be much longer. For instance, when using Cursor, you can add your repository to the prompt, where it acts as context: this significantly increases the prompt size. In such cases, the memory needed to store the activations for n n n tokens can be larger than the available memory on the GPU. Thus we cannot perform prefill in a single forward pass: we have to split the prefill in chunks. This is called chunked prefill, and it's going to be one of the components needed to enable efficient inference.

Let's pretend that the available memory is very constrained, and that we can only pass m=4 m=4 m=4 tokens per forward pass. If we have an initial prompt with n=7 n = 7 n=7 tokens, we need to split it in ⌈n/m⌉=2 \lceil n /m \rceil = 2 ⌈n/m⌉=2 chunks (rounding up 7/4 = 1.75 to 2). We illustrate the example below using the same n n n and m m m notations:.

Recent findings suggest that we can do that thanks to the KV cache. We store the KV states during the first prefill split, and during the second prefill split, we prepend the stored KV states to the fresh KV states. We also adapt the attention mask accordingly. Visually, it looks like we split the non-chunked prefill in the middle.

The key insight: cached KV states let us process the prompt incrementally without losing information.

Although we showed here an example where we split the prefill into 2 chunks, chunked prefill can be used to split the prefill in any way we want, adapting flexibly to memory constraints.

We are now finally equipped with all the tools we need to understand Continuous Batching.

According to recent reports, in our previous examples we have only considered the case of batch size one, i.e. we only generate tokens for one prompt at a time. In the context of evaluation or model serving, we want to generate tokens for a large number of prompts. To increase the throughput, which is the number of tokens generated per second, the best course of action is to generate tokens in parallel for a batch of several prompts.

To batch prompts together, the naive way is to add an axis to both input tensors: token sequence and attention mask. However, this comes with a constraint on the shape of the inputs: we need all prompts to have the same length, because tensors must be rectangular. To achieve this, we usually add padding on the left so the new token prediction always comes from the rightmost token. We also modify the attention mask of each prompt accordingly, as shown below:.

where the padding tokens are coloured in orange. Then we can perform the forward pass as we used to, with the added dimension of the batch size. This is called batched generation: efficient for same-length prompts, but wasteful when lengths vary.It is illustrated below, through 4 steps of generation: one prefilling step (at the top) and 3 decoding steps (below each "Forward pass" lines).

where means "End Of Sequence", this is a special token to indicate the model has reached the end of generation for the corresponding sequence.

According to recent reports, the drawback of batched generation is that if one prompt finishes generation before the other one by generating an token, all further generated tokens are useless. And this goes on until the longest request of the batch finishes. Of course, we can remove the prompts that have reached an token from the batch and save some compute and memory, but saving resources is not the goal here: throughput is.

According to recent reports, instead of just removing the finished prompt from the batch, we can replace it with a prompt that's waiting for generation. We will call this dynamic scheduling, or dynamic batching. Dynamic scheduling is great to maintain throughput while ensuring any token generated by a forward pass is relevant. But because of the way we batched prompts together, it has a major drawback: we need a lot of padding when swapping prompts. That's because the newly-inserted prompt needs to go through prefill while the other prompts are decoding one token at a time. So there is almost as much padding as there are tokens in the newly-inserted prompt.

The problem becomes even worse when batch size increases and initial prompts are long. The padding cost grows quadratically with both batch size and prompt length. If we have a batch of B B B prompts that are in decoding phase and one finishes, dynamically introducing a prompt of n n n initial tokens in the batch requires (n−1)(B−1) (n-1)(B-1) (n−1)(B−1) padding tokens. For instance, with B=8 B=8 B=8 and n=100 n=100 n=100, we'd need 99×7=693 99 \times 7 = 693 99×7=693 padding tokens!

Sources indicate that furthermore, practical optimizations like CUDA graphs or torch.compile require static tensor shapes. This forces us to pad all prompts to a fixed maximum length, dramatically increasing the padding waste.

It has been revealed that at this point, our main problem is padding, which is a consequence of the axis we added to batch sentences together. Thus, the ideal would be to get rid of this axis entirely, a radical rethinking of batching. If we do so, the only way to batch prompts together is to concatenate them:.

Industry observers note that but we don't want tokens from prompt 0 to interact with the tokens of prompt 1! Luckily for us, we have a way to control how tokens interact with one another: the attention mask. How we do this is displayed below:.

In a recent development, although we use different tints of green to illustrate the different parts of the attention mask, this is still a boolean mask with only greens for True and white for False. This way of batching prompts together is called ragged batching (because sequence lengths are 'ragged' or uneven), and it offers the benefit of added throughput without introducing the need for padding tokens.

Industry observers note that in the figure above, we use ragged batching to combine two full prompts together, but we can batch as many as memory allows. The only limit is m m m, the number of tokens we can fit in a batch, with m m m depending on the available memory on the GPU.

It has been revealed that ragged batching is one of the key components of continuous batching. To maximize throughput, we can combine prefill and decoding sequences following an algorithm like this:.

Dynamic scheduling is the final piece that contributes to the continuous batching technique: we remove finished prompts from the batch as soon as they are done, and replace them with latest chunked prompts that correspond to incoming requests.

This combination of ragged batching and dynamic scheduling is called continuous batching, and it's the technique that powers modern LLM serving systems.

Continuous batching combines three key techniques to maximize throughput in LLM serving:.

Recent findings suggest that by removing the batch dimension and using attention masks to control token interactions, continuous batching allows mixing prefill and decode phases in the same batch, dramatically improving efficiency for serving multiple requests. This is why services like ChatGPT can handle thousands of concurrent users efficiently.

According to recent reports, in the next article in this series, we make continuous batching much more efficient by introducing asynchronous batching. Read it here!If you'd like to see a deep dive on other continuous batching topics, please let us know in the comments!

Thanks for the article! I'd like to add one note: the primary reason we need chunked prefill isn't the memory constraint (otherwise we could simply solve it with Flash Attention). The more practical reason is that a long prefill blocks all decode requests in the batch. Chunking it lets decode requests make progress between chunks. Moreover, since prefill chunks make the forward pass compute-bound, decode tokens can piggyback on the same batch at nearly zero marginal cost - they're just extra rows in an already large matmul. This turns memory-bound decode-only batches into better-utilized compute-saturating ones. See the SARATHI paper for details.

Diffusers welcomes FLUX-2

📅 25 Nov 2025 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2864 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, FLUX.2 is the recent series of image generation models from Black Forest Labs, preceded by the Flux.1 series.
  • 🚨 FLUX.2 is not meant to be a drop-in replacement of FLUX.1, but a newly introduced image generation and editing model.
  • FLUX.2 can be used for both image-guided and text-guided image generation.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, FLUX.2 is the recent series of image generation models from Black Forest Labs, preceded by the Flux.1 series. It is an entirely new model with a new architecture and pre-training done from scratch! In this post, we discuss the key changes introduced in FLUX.2, performing inference with it under various setups, and LoRA fine-tuning.

🚨 FLUX.2 is not meant to be a drop-in replacement of FLUX.1, but a newly introduced image generation and editing model.

FLUX.2 can be used for both image-guided and text-guided image generation. Furthermore, it can take multiple images as reference inputs, while producing the final output image. Below, we briefly discuss the key changes introduced in FLUX.2.

Industry observers note that first, instead of two text encoders as in Flux.1, it uses a single text encoder — Mistral Small 3.1. Using a single text encoder greatly simplifies the process of computing prompt embeddings. The pipeline allows for a max_sequence_length of 512. Instead of using a single-layer output for the prompt embedding, FLUX.2 stacks outputs from intermediate layers, which have been known to be more beneficial.

FLUX.2 follows the same general multimodel diffusion transformer (MM-DiT) + parallel DiT architecture as Flux.1. As a refresher, MM-DiT blocks first process the image latents and conditioning text in separate streams, only joining the two together for the attention operation, and are thus referred to as “double-stream” blocks. The parallel blocks then operate on the concatenated image and text streams and can be regarded as “single-stream” blocks.

The key DiT changes from Flux.1 to FLUX.2 are as follows:.

Time and guidance information (in the form of AdaLayerNorm-Zero modulation parameters) is shared across all double-stream and single-stream transformer blocks, respectively, rather than having individual modulation parameters for each block as in Flux.1.

According to recent reports, none of the layers in the model use bias parameters. In particular, neither the attention nor feedforward (FF) sub-blocks of either transformer block use bias parameters in any of their layers.

It has been revealed that in Flux.1, the single-stream transformer blocks fused the attention output projection with the FF output projection. FLUX.2 single-stream blocks also fuse the attention QKV projections with the FF input projection, creating a fully parallel transformer block:.

Note that compared to the ViT-22B block depicted above, FLUX.2 uses a SwiGLU-style MLP activation rather than a GELU activation (and also doesn’t use bias parameters).

A larger proportion of the transformer blocks in FLUX.2 are single-stream blocks (8 double-stream blocks to 48 single-stream blocks, compared to 19/38 for Flux.1). This also means that single-stream blocks make up a larger proportion of the DiT parameters: Flux.1[dev]-12B has ~54% of its total parameters in the double-stream blocks, whereas FLUX.2[dev]-32B has ~24% of its parameters in the double-stream blocks (and ~73% in the single-stream blocks).

FLUX.2 uses a larger DiT and Mistral3 Small as its text encoder. When used together without any kind of offloading, the inference takes more than 80GB VRAM. In the following sections, we show how to perform inference with FLUX.2 in more accessible ways, under various system-level constraints.

Before you try out the following code snippets, make sure you have installed diffusers from main and have run hf auth login.

The above code snippet was tested on an H100, and it isn’t sufficient to run inference on it without CPU offloading. With CPU offloading enabled, this setup takes ~62GB to run.

Consumers who have access to Hopper-series GPUs can take advantage of Flash Attention 3 to speed up inference:.

You can check out the supported attention backends (we have many!) here.

According to recent reports, using bitsandbytes, we can load the transformer and text encoder models in 4-bit, allowing owners of 24GB GPUs to use the model locally. You can run this snippet on a GPU with ~20 GB of free VRAM.

Notice that we're using a repository that contains the NF4-quantized versions of the FLUX.2 DiT and the Mistral text encoder.

Sources indicate that due to the modular design of a Diffusers pipeline, we can isolate modules and work with them in sequence. We decouple the text encoder and deploy it to an Inference Endpoint. This helps us with freeing up the VRAM usage for the DiT and VAE only.

Recent findings suggest that ⚠️ To use the remote text encoder, you need to have a valid token. If you are already authenticated, no further action is needed.

Sources indicate that the example below uses a combination of local and remote inference. Additionally, we quantize the DiT with NF4 quantization through bitsandbytes.

You can run this snippet on a GPU with 18 GB of VRAM:.

In a recent development, for GPUs with even lower VRAM, we have group_offloading, which allows GPUs with as little as 8GB of free VRAM to use this model. However, you'll need 32GB of free RAM. Alternatively, if you're willing to sacrifice some speed, you can set low_cpu_mem_usage=True to reduce the RAM requirement to just 10GB.

You can check out other supported quantization backends here and other memory-saving techniques here.

To check how different quantizations affect an image, you can play with the playground below or access it as standlone in the FLUX.2 Quantization experiments Space.

According to recent reports, FLUX.2 supports using multiple images as inputs, allowing you to use up to 10 images. However, keep in mind that each additional image will require more VRAM. You can reference the images by index (e.g., image 1, image 2) or by natural language (e.g., the kangaroo, the turtle). For optimal results, the best approach is to use a combination of both methods.

FLUX.2 supports advanced prompting techniques like structured JSON prompting, precise hex color control, and multi-reference image editing. Aside for the added control, this also allows for flexibility in changing specific attributes while maintaining others overall the same.For example, let's start with this json as the base schema (taken from the official FLUX.2 prompting guide):.

Building up on that, let's turn it into a prompt for a shot of a good old fashion walkman on a carpet (simply pass this prompt to your chosen diffusers inference example from above):.

Now, let's change the color of the carpet to a specific teal-blue shade (#367588) and add wired headphones plugged into the walkman:.

The carpet color now matches the hex code provided, and the headphones have been with small changes to the overall scene.

Check out the official prompting guide for more examples and details.

Being both a text-to-image and an image-to-image model, FLUX.2 makes the perfect fine-tuning candidate for many use-cases! However, as inference alone takes more than 80GB of VRAM, LoRA fine-tuning is even more challenging to run on consumer GPUs. To squeeze in as much memory saving as we can, we utilize some of the inference optimizations described above for training as well, together with shared memory saving techniques, to substantially reduce memory consumption. To train it, you can use either the diffusers code below or Ostris' AI Toolkit.

We provide both text-to-image and image-to-image training scripts, for the purpose of this blog will focus on a text-to-image training example.

Many of these techniques complement each other and can be used together to reduce memory consumption further. However, some techniques may be mutually exclusive, so be sure to check before launching a training run.

Please make sure to check out the README for prerequisites before starting training.

Industry News: Pentera Opens Early Access to Agentic Web App and API Pentesting

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (898 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Unite

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Pentera has moved Pentera Apps, its agentic web application and API penetration-testing product, into early availability.
  • Pentera reported beta findings involving unpaid e-commerce checkouts, account takeovers through broken access control and multifactor-authentication bypass, and customer-data extraction through SQL injection in an unauthenticated API.
  • In a recent development, the release follows the selected-customer beta introduced in Pentera’s July 29, 2026 announcement.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Pentera has moved Pentera Apps, its agentic web application and API penetration-testing product, into early availability. The November 18, 2026 announcement said more than 60 customers had tested it in beta.

Pentera reported beta findings involving unpaid e-commerce checkouts, account takeovers through broken access control and multifactor-authentication bypass, and customer-data extraction through SQL injection in an unauthenticated API. Those cases span payment logic, user permissions and API input handling, showing the product’s intended focus on application behavior as well as familiar vulnerability classes.

In a recent development, the release follows the selected-customer beta introduced in Pentera’s July 29, 2026 announcement. General availability was then targeted for the fourth quarter of 2026; the latest schedule places it in the first quarter of 2027.

It has been revealed that the product documentation describes an attack engine that maps application behavior and tests workflows under different user roles and permissions. Specialist agents handle individual attack classes, adjust payloads as the application responds, and generate and run exploit code. Confirmed weaknesses can be linked into paths extending from applications and APIs into internal networks, Active Directory and cloud identity-and-access-management systems.

Sources indicate that testing can start from a URL without source-code access, although credentials and documentation can deepen coverage. The system maps routes, hidden parameters and documented or undocumented APIs, with support for REST, GraphQL and WebSocket interfaces. It also tests authenticated workflows behind single sign-on, multifactor authentication and OAuth. Tests can run on demand, on a schedule or when endpoints, authentication or permissions change, with incremental retesting limited to what changed.

In a recent development, context comes from the Validation Grid, which holds asset profiles, validated findings, threat-actor techniques and signals from across the technology stack. Customers can add earlier penetration-test reports and environment documentation. Pentera states this material guides the agents’ investigation, while the execution harness determines which actions can run against the target.

According to recent reports, before execution, the control plane checks targets, authorization, credentials and testing policies; invalid configurations stop a test before traffic is sent. Pentera indicates testing can target live production applications using non-destructive payloads within approved scope, and users can stop a test at any time. Deterministic checks confirm exploitability and dedicated validator agents review the result, with conflicting signals left inconclusive instead of becoming findings.

For data handling, Pentera notes sensitive information is removed before the context required for testing is sent to AI models. Its enterprise agreements with model providers provide for zero retention and prohibit training on customer data. Test credentials are held in memory during execution and discarded afterward, while customer data is processed and stored in an assigned EU or US region.

It has been revealed that findings can include proof of exploitation, request-and-response records, an execution trace, reproduction steps and a replayable script. Pentera Apps does not repair the weaknesses itself. Pentera Resolve assigns each finding to the responsible team under the organization’s service-level agreement, tracks remediation by that team or integrated workflows, and triggers another attack-path run to confirm that the exposure is closed.

Industry observers note that the product takes code-analysis and scanner findings as inputs for runtime testing rather than replacing those tools. It also does not replace manual penetration testing or bug bounties; its role is continuous validation between engagements and as applications change. Web application and API testing joins Pentera’s existing network, cloud and identity validation products, and the firm describes the combined offering as the only all-attack-surface exposure-validation platform.

Recent findings suggest that pentera prepares a live demonstration on December 1, 2026, at 11:00 a.m. ET, in which an agent will attack an e-commerce application. Planned demonstrations include workflow reasoning, chained weaknesses, refusals at scope boundaries and replayable exploit evidence. One application will be selected for the live test; organizations that own or are authorized to test a proposed application could submit it through the Call for Apps until November 23, 2026.

According to recent reports, the release makes the operating boundary clear: AI agents can generate and execute attacks, but the customer defines the scope, the harness controls execution and validators determine what becomes a finding. For AppSec teams, the practical question is whether those controls, replayable evidence and retesting can turn continuous autonomous testing into completed fixes without adding another stream of unverified alerts.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage News Vercel Releases UI SDK for Agents to Compose UI from Reusable Behaviors.

Nov 18, 2026 2 min read.

Sources indicate that vercel has released UI SDK, an open-source TypeScript library that treats keyboard navigation, focus, selection, popups, and drag and drop as reusable behaviors rather than details buried inside finished components. Vercel UI SDK is published on GitHub as vercel-labs/ui and is currently in beta.

The behaviors live in @ui-sdk/core. Vercel says it built more than 50 of them, including createPopup, createSelection, createTypeahead, createRovingFocus, createReorder, createResize, createViewport, createListbox, createChange, createFocusRecovery, and createVirtualizer. A developer, or more often an agent, combines those helpers inside definePrimitive, which declares a component's state, API, and slots once. Framework adapters then render the same primitive through createParts in React, Vue, Svelte, Solid, or as Web Components. The parts are unstyled and expose attributes and CSS variables. The same behaviors also back a starter library of more than 50 unstyled components, from Color Picker, Token Input, and Command to Calendar, Tree, and OTP Input, with the same part names in all five adapters.

UI SDK is meant to be used by agents, not only written by them. The ui-sdk skill, installed with npx skills add vercel-labs/ui --skill ui-sdk, points an agent at the Markdown docs shipped in the installed packages. At runtime, createAgent, imported from the matching framework package such as @ui-sdk/react/agent, exposes snapshot, act, and query so an agent can read component state and call actions through the component API, without screenshots. Apps can approve or refuse those steps, and change callbacks receive a source of "agent" and may cancel a change. registerTools can expose the same methods to a browser's built-in agent through WebMCP, when the browser provides document.modelContext.

Developers already have several headless libraries at this layer, including Radix UI, Base UI, React Aria, Ark UI and its Zag.js state machines, and Headless UI. shadcn/ui sits one level above those primitives as a copy-into-your-repo component kit. UI SDK aims lower, at composable behaviors shared across frameworks, and adds a first-class agent bridge. The changelog thanks the teams behind Radix, Base UI, React Aria, shadcn/ui, Nuxt UI, and Geist. Vercel has not said whether shadcn/ui will be rebuilt on UI SDK.

Rahim, a product engineer at Mux who built Vidstack, wrote after reading the source:.

According to recent reports, this is so genuinely cool. I love how it's been packaged up. So elegant @shadcn and @shuding! I'll be studying this for a while. 1. createAgent is an "agent bridge" which gives a snapshot, act, and query tool. It allows agents to interact with the actual UI components directly 2. Change callbacks know when the agent made the change (details.source === "agent"), and the app can refuse it with cancel (I love this).

A developer identified as Stefan looked at the repository and asked how the idea compares with existing headless libraries:.

I tried looking at the repo a bit but I’m not sure I quite understand the value prop of this versus something like Base UI. Is the thought process that we should be thinking about UIs/components as combinations of behaviours?

In a recent development, UI SDK is in beta as 0.1.0-beta.1, licensed under the Apache License 2.0, and subject to Vercel's public beta terms; the APIs, documentation, and behavior may change before general availability. Install @ui-sdk/core plus the adapter for your framework, for example npm install @ui-sdk/react @ui-sdk/core, which requires React 19 or later. The Vue, Svelte, and Solid adapters document peer ranges of Vue 3.5, Svelte 5.33, and Solid 2 from 2.0.0-rc.14. Setup details are in the documentation.

#34350. AI Products in 2027: Buyers Will Pay for Completed Work
