AI Products in 2027: Buyers Will Pay for Completed Work

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2282 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Unite

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A buyer does not wake up wanting more AI interactions.
  • Those questions will shape AI product strategy in 2027.
  • Recent findings suggest that outcome pricing is already established.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A buyer does not wake up wanting more AI interactions. They want the service request resolved, the qualified lead handed over or the accounts reconciled. Yet those ordinary outcomes contain awkward questions. When is the job finished? Who decides? What happens when it reopens tomorrow?

Those questions will shape AI product strategy in 2027. Charging for completed work is appealing because it sounds close to customer value. Making that promise precise enough to put on an invoice is where the real product work begins.

Recent findings suggest that outcome pricing is already established. Sierra described its model in 2024. Salesforce offers several Agentforce purchasing models, including actions, conversations, licenses, and help-agent resolutions. Zendesk introduced automated resolution tiers in May 2026. These are materially different units, even when each is presented as a way to align spending with value.

It has been revealed that the companies followed here are Fin/Intercom, Salesforce, Zendesk and Sierra. Their approaches put the same purchasing questions in different forms: what work is finished, what the buyer can verify and which costs remain around the result.

It has been revealed that the next expansion of outcome pricing will follow the work buyers can describe clearly enough to dispute. Sales qualification, internal IT service and back-office reconciliation are plausible territory because each has recognizable milestones. In 2027, vendors in this article's cohort will add newly billable categories in those areas. A message sent or a tool called will not be enough; the offering will have to name the completed milestone for which the customer pays.

According to recent reports, the underlying product problem is to find a unit small enough to attribute and valuable enough to price. “Improve customer relationships” is too broad to settle an individual charge. “Validate eligibility and route a qualified prospect according to these rules” is narrower, with an observable completion state. That precision also exposes the cases where a superficially successful action has little business value.

It has been revealed that fin offers a revealing baseline. Its current outcomes documentation distinguishes resolutions, configured Procedure handoffs, qualifications, and disqualifications. A configured handoff can be billable; an ordinary escalation triggered by a request for a human is treated differently. Therefore, neither “outcome” nor “handoff” can safely be translated into “the customer’s whole problem was solved.”.

In its March 2026 explanation of the change, Intercom argues that an agent can perform useful work before a human confirmation step. That is a coherent product position. It also means buyers need to specify whether they are purchasing autonomous resolution or a completed subtask in a larger process. The distinction should survive into the reporting interface and the contract.

Industry observers note that my forecast follows the incentive created by that distinction. A supplier that can reliably complete one bounded milestone can enter workflows where the final decision remains human. Expansion will depend on attribution: a call that is booked, a request that is fulfilled, or a reconciliation exception that is correctly classified must correspond to an agreed event. Products will struggle where the event can be counted more easily than its value can be established.

It has been revealed that watch for pricing pages that define newly billable milestones in sales, employee service, and back-office work. The important detail is the event that triggers payment, particularly when an agent completes only part of a larger process. Expanding the word 'outcome' without clarifying what work the buyer receives would weaken the commercial argument.

Product leaders should define the smallest result a customer can recognize, verify, and value before choosing an outcome meter. Buyers should map that result to the work that remains for employees. A qualified lead, completed handoff, and resolved customer problem can all have value, but their prices and performance measures need to reflect their different roles.

It has been revealed that sooner or later, a customer will open an AI invoice and ask why a particular case appears on it. That moment makes verification part of the product. I expect more of the cohort's suppliers to let buyers inspect individual billable events, see how they were classified and challenge a mistake. A pricing model built around outcomes needs a shared account of what happened, especially when the supplier and customer disagree.

A result meter is also a system of judgment. It may infer that a problem was resolved because the customer stopped replying, apply a classifier, or record that a configured sequence ended at a handoff. Each method can be useful. Each can also diverge from the buyer’s understanding of a completed job.

It has been revealed that the differences are visible in existing documentation. Zendesk’s resolution-tier description claims its automated-resolution unit concerns requests resolved without escalation to a human. Fin’s pricing FAQ includes configured handoffs among its outcome types. Comparing the headline price of these units without comparing their definitions would obscure what is being purchased.

Customers already have some visibility. Fin’s Procedure reporting distinguishes handoff outcomes, while usage controls expose limits and the complications of conversations whose state changes over time. The forecast is for further verification capability, not the invention of billing dashboards.

The next useful step is an event record that connects the invoice to the work: which customer request was handled, what event triggered a charge, which policy classified it, and what happens if the result is later corrected. A buyer should be able to distinguish an incorrect classification from a legitimate charge for a narrower contracted milestone. Those are different disagreements and require different remedies.

In a recent development, there is a commercial reason to expect progress. A supplier can make a strong outcome promise only if it can resolve disputes without re-investigating every conversation manually. Sierra’s 2026 discussion of outcome pricing explicitly acknowledges the operational and contractual complexity of attribution. I read that as evidence of the work needed behind the pricing model, rather than evidence that the industry has settled on a common definition.

Industry observers note that look for billing tools that let customers trace a charge to an individual event, understand its classification, and challenge an error. Stronger evidence will include a clear process for handling later corrections or changes in conversation state. More elaborate aggregate dashboards would add less value if customers still cannot explain a disputed charge.

According to recent reports, procurement, finance, and the team operating the agent should agree on a shared definition of completion. Before scaling, inspect a sample of billed events and establish how disputed classifications will be reviewed. This connects product performance to the invoice and gives both sides a practical way to resolve disagreements as workflows become more complex.

Recent findings suggest that an assistant can make the first step faster and still leave the organization with more work. Escalation, checking and reopened cases can consume the apparent saving. In 2027, stronger customer accounts will make the whole workflow visible: a material reduction in handling time or cost, with service quality preserved and the difficult cases still included. That evidence will tell buyers more than an impressive demonstration of the easiest part of the job.

It has been revealed that this is the hardest forecast in the article because public measurement is often thinner than the product claim. A high automation rate does not reveal whether the remaining cases became harder. A lower cost per conversation can coexist with more conversations per resolved problem. Faster initial handling may be offset by later correction or repeat contact.

Sources indicate that there is evidence that AI can improve useful work in particular settings. The NBER working-paper version of Generative AI at Work studied a support-assistant deployment and reported higher issues resolved per hour, with substantial variation across worker experience. That concerns human workers using assistance, not a direct estimate of the economics of today’s autonomous agents. Its value here is the choice to measure resolved work and examine heterogeneous effects.

There is also a warning against treating perceived speed as measured value. METR’s early-2025 developer study found a slowdown in its particular experienced-developer setting. Its February 2026 enhancement explains why later measurements became difficult to interpret because of selection, task choice, and changing work patterns. The later update does not establish that every developer is slower—or that the earlier result remains a current universal estimate.

The product lesson is to measure the complete operating loop. A useful cost numerator includes agent fees, relevant platform and infrastructure expense, human review, escalations, and rework. The denominator should count cases that meet a stated completion standard over a stated observation window. For a time measure, all human handling associated with those cases belongs in scope, including the correction queue.

According to recent reports, that operating view is consistent with Measuring Agents in Production, whose revised 2026 study emphasizes controllable systems and reliability challenges. τ²-Bench supplies a complementary research reminder: completing a support task can depend on coordinating with a user who also changes the environment. A fluent answer and a completed workflow are different evaluation targets.

Sources indicate that watch for customer reports that follow cases through escalation, reopening, and human correction, rather than stopping at the first automated response. Results with a stated baseline, observation period, and quality measure will be the most informative. Higher automation rates accompanied by more repeat contacts or heavier exception handling would challenge the forecast's economic premise.

Industry observers note that judge an agent against the full operating cost of completing the customer's job. Include review, rework, escalations, platform expense, and the time employees spend maintaining the workflow. A controlled pilot should establish whether savings persist when those costs are counted and whether the remaining human workload becomes more difficult.

Outcome pricing sounds like a clean replacement for software subscriptions, but the supplier still has a platform to run and customers with very different usage patterns. I expect hybrid bills to remain common within this cohort at the end of 2027: a charge for results alongside seats, platform access or consumption. The useful purchasing question is what the complete arrangement costs at the customer's expected volume and case mix.

Industry observers note that this is a continuation forecast, and deliberately so. The broader adoption of outcome meters does not require all software economics to become outcome-only. Buyers still use inboxes, reporting systems, knowledge infrastructure, connectors, and administrative controls. Suppliers can price those capabilities separately while charging an agent for completed work.

According to recent reports, the existing baseline makes this plausible. Intercom’s pricing distinguishes helpdesk seats and Fin usage; its standalone Fin route has a different structure, so the seat component should not be attributed to every Fin buyer. Salesforce’s pricing page exposes multiple purchasing units and configurations. Zendesk’s plans combine service-platform packaging with automated-resolution allowances and additional capacity. Buyers must compare the configuration they would actually purchase.

The strategic consequence is that a cheaper advertised outcome may not produce a cheaper completed case. A lower unit price can sit beside a higher platform commitment or more human handling. A higher unit price can be attractive if it removes enough downstream work. The correct comparison depends on the full workflow and an explicit accounting boundary.

Recent findings suggest that my high confidence rests on this coexistence, not on any prediction that a particular vendor will raise prices. The competing incentive is simplification: a supplier could absorb more supporting costs into its outcome unit to reduce procurement friction. If enough vendors do that, this forecast will fail even if outcome pricing itself becomes more popular.

It has been revealed that follow the complete purchasing configuration as outcome charges expand. Separate seat, platform, or consumption fees may remain even when the agent is advertised around a completed result. Clearer bundles that absorb those supporting costs into a single outcome unit would weaken the forecast that hybrid pricing remains prevalent across the selected vendors.

Build a cost model around your expected mix of usage, successful outcomes, human handling, and fixed commitments. Compare the same deployment scope across suppliers, including the supporting software the team still needs. The advertised price of an outcome is a starting point for that analysis; the cost of a completed case determines whether the product is worthwhile.

In a recent development, the strongest AI products will make the buyer's definition of success visible inside the service. That includes the awkward cases, the correction process and the work people still perform. A completed outcome can be a powerful commercial unit. It earns that role when both sides can recognize it without needing the sales team to explain the invoice.

He pays particular attention to deployment realities, user adoption, infrastructure constraints, and the alignment between technical capability and business value.

#34349. Breaking: Transformers v5: Simple model definitions powering the AI ecosystem

📅 01 Dec 2025 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (2029 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: Transformers v5: Simple model definitions powering the AI ecosystem

📅 01 Dec 2025 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2029 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Transformers' version v4.0.0rc-1, the initial release candidate for version 4, was released on November 19th, 2020.
  • Today, as we launch v5, Transformers is installed more than 3 million times each day via pip - up from 20,000/day in v4 🤯.
  • The ecosystem has expanded from 40 model architectures in v4 to over 400 today, and the community has contributed more than 750,000 model checkpoints on the Hub compatible with Transformers, up from roughly 1,000 at the time of v4.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Transformers' version v4.0.0rc-1, the initial release candidate for version 4, was released on November 19th, 2020. Five years later, we now release v5.0.0rc-0.

Today, as we launch v5, Transformers is installed more than 3 million times each day via pip - up from 20,000/day in v4 🤯. Altogether, it has now surpassed 1.2 billion installs!

The ecosystem has expanded from 40 model architectures in v4 to over 400 today, and the community has contributed more than 750,000 model checkpoints on the Hub compatible with Transformers, up from roughly 1,000 at the time of v4.

This growth is powered by the evolution of the field and the now mainstream access to AI. As a leading model-definition library in the ecosystem, we need to continuously evolve and adapt the library to continue being relevant. Reinvention is key for longevity in AI.

We’re fortunate to collaborate with many libraries and apps built on transformers, in no specific order: llama.cpp, MLX, onnxruntime, Jan, LMStudio, vLLM, SGLang, Unsloth, LlamaFactory, dLLM, MaxText, TensorRT, Argmax, among many other friends.

For v5, we wanted to work on several notable aspects: simplicity, training, inference, and production. We detail the work that went into them in this post.

The first focus of the team was on simplicity. Working on transformers, we see the code as the product. We want our model integrations to be clean, so that the ecosystem may depend on our model definitions and understand what’s really happening under the hood, how models differ from each other, and the key features of each upcoming model. Simplicity results in wider standardization, generality, and wider support.

Transformers is the backbone of hundreds of thousands of projects, Unsloth included. We build on Transformers to help people fine-tune and train models efficiently, whether that’s BERT, text-to-speech (TTS), or others; to run fast inference for reinforcement learning (RL) even when models aren’t yet supported in other libraries. We're excited for Transformers v5 and are super happy to be working with the Hugging Face team!

Sources indicate that transformers, at the core, remains a model architecture toolkit. We aim to have all recent architectures and to be the “source of truth” for model definitions. We’ve been adding between 1 - 3 new models every week for 5 years, shown in the timeline below:.

We’ve worked on improving that model-addition process.

Over the past year, we’ve heavily pushed our modular design as a significant step forward. This allows for easier maintenance, faster integration, and better collaboration across the community.

Sources indicate that we give a deeper overview in our Maintain the Unmaintainable blog post. For brevity, we aim to achieve a much easier model contribution process, as well as a lower maintenance burden. One metric we can highlight is that the number of lines of code to contribute (and review), drop significantly when modular is used:.

While we respect the “One model, one file” philosophy, we continue introducing some abstractions making the management of common helpers simpler. The prime example of this is the introduction of the AttentionInterface, which offers a centralized abstraction for attention methods. The eager method will remain in the modeling file; others, such as FA1/2/3, FlexAttention, or SDPA, are moved to the interface.

Over the past couple of years, the increasing amount of 0-day support for upcoming model architectures and standardization of attention handling has helped to simplify our support for post-training modern LLMs.

Sources indicate that we’re building tooling to help us identify which existing model architecture a newly introduced model resembles. This feature uses machine learning to find code similarities between independent modeling files. Going further, we aim to automate the conversion process by opening a draft PR for the model to be integrated into our transformers format. This process reduces manual effort and ensures consistency.

According to recent reports, we’ve significantly refactored the modeling and tokenization files. Modeling files have been greatly improved thanks to the modular approach mentioned above, on top of standardization across models. Standardization contributes to abstracting most of the tools that don’t make up a model, so that the modeling code only contains the relevant parts for a model’s forward/backward passes.

Alongside this work, we’re simplifying the tokenization and processing files: going forward, we’ll only focus on the tokenizers backend, removing the concept of “Fast” and “Slow” tokenizers.

Recent findings suggest that we'll use tokenizers as our main tokenization backend, just as we do for PyTorch-based models. We’ll offer alternatives for Sentencepiece or MistralCommon backed tokenizers, which will be non-default but will be supported. Image processors will now only exist with their fast variant, which depends on the torchvision backend.

Finally, we’re sunsetting our Flax/TensorFlow support in favor of focusing on PyTorch as the sole backend; however, we're also working with partners in the Jax ecosystem to ensure we have compatibility between our models and this ecosystem.

Industry observers note that with its v5 release, transformers is going all in on PyTorch. Transformers acts as a source of truth and foundation for modeling across the field; we've been working with the team to ensure good performance across the stack.

We're excited to continue pushing for this in the future across training, inference, and deployment.

-- Matt White, Executive Director, PyTorch Foundation. GM of AI, Linux Foundation.

Training remains a massive focus of the team as we head into v5: whereas previously we would focus heavily on fine-tuning rather than pre-training/full-training at scale, we’ve recently done significant work to improve our support for the latter as well.

Supporting pre-training meant reworking the initialization of our models, ensuring that they worked at scale with different parallelism paradigms, and shipping support for optimized kernels for both the forward and backward passes.

Going forward, we’re excited to have extended compatibility with torchtitan, megatron, nanotron, as well as any other pre-training tool that is interested in collaborating with us.

According to recent reports, we continue collaborating closely with all fine-tuning tools in the Python ecosystem. We aim to continue providing model implementations compatible with Unsloth, Axolotl, LlamaFactory, TRL and others in the PyTorch ecosystem; but we are also working with tools such as MaxText, in the JAX ecosystem, to have good interoperability between their frameworks and transformers.

All fine-tuning and post-training tools can now rely on transformers for model definitions; further enabling Agentic use-cases through OpenEnv or the Prime Environment Hub.

We’re putting a significant focus on inference for v5, with several paradigm changes: the introduction of specialized kernels, cleaner defaults, new APIs, support for optimized inference engines.

In a recent development, similarly to training, we’ve been putting some effort in packaging kernels so that they’re automatically used in case your hardware and software permits it. If you haven’t heard of kernels before, we recommend taking a look at this doc.

Alongside this effort, we ship two new APIs dedicated to inference:.

It has been revealed that we see this as a major step forward for use-cases such as evaluation, where a great number of inference requests are done simultaneously. We don’t aim to do specialized optimizations like the dedicated inference engines (vLLM, SGLang, TensorRT LLM). Instead, we aim to be perfectly inter-compatible with these, as detailed in the next section.

It has been revealed that the Transformers backend in vLLM has been very enabling to get more architectures, like BERT and other encoders, available to more consumers. We've been working with the Transformers team to ensure many models are available across modalities with the best performance possible. This is just the start of our collaboration: we're happy to see the Transformers team will have this as a focus going into version 5.

-- Simon Mo, Harry Mellor at vLLM.

Industry observers note that standardization is key to accelerating AI innovation. Transformers v5 empowers the SGLang team to spend less time on model reimplementation and more time on kernel optimization. We look forward to building a more efficient and unified AI ecosystem together!

Industry observers note that recently, we've been working hand in hand with the most popular inference engines for them to use transformers as a backend. The value added is significant: as soon as a model is added to transformers, it becomes available in these inference engines, while taking advantage of the strengths each engine provides: inference optimizations, specialized kernels, dynamic batching, etc.

Sources indicate that we've also been working very closely with ONNXRuntime, llama.cpp and MLX so that the implementations between transformers and these modeling libraries have great interoperability. For example, thanks to a significant community effort, it's now very easy to load GGUF files in transformers for further fine-tuning. Conversely, transformers models can be easily converted to GGUF files for use with llama.cpp.

According to recent reports, the Transformers framework is the go-to place for reference AI model implementations. The framework plays a crucial role in enabling modern AI across the entire stack. The team and the community behind the project truly understand and embrace the spirit of the open-source development and collaboration.

The same is true for MLX, where the transformers' safetensors files are directly compatible with MLX's models.

It has been revealed that it’s hard to overstate the importance of Transformers (and datasets, tokenizers, etc) to the open-source and overall AI ecosystem. I can’t count the number of times I’ve personally used Transformers as a source-of-truth.

In a recent development, finally, we’re pushing the boundaries of local inference and are working hand-in-hand with the executorch team to get the transformers models to be available on-device. We’re expanding the coverage to multimodal models (vision, audio) through optimum.

Quantization is quickly emerging as the standard for state-of-the-art model development. Many SOTA models are now released in low-precision formats such as 8-bit and 4-bit (e.g., gpt-oss, Kimi-K2, Deepseek-r1), hardware is increasingly optimized for low-precision workloads, and the community is actively sharing high-quality quantized checkpoints. In v5, we're making quantization a central focus of Transformers support, ensuring full compatibility with all major features, and delivering a reliable framework for training and inference.

We introduce a significant change to the way we load weights in our models; and with this, we move to quantization being a first-class citizen.

Our collaboration with the Transformers team was highly productive, marked by their proactive code reviews, feedback, and technical expertise. Their support was crucial in integrating TorchAO, expanding quantization features, and improving documentation for broader adoption in the V5.

In a recent development, we're excited that v5 has made quantization a first-class citizen. It provides the foundation for bitsandbytes to better support key features like TP and MoEs, and also makes it easier to integrate newly introduced quantization methods.

-- Matthew Douglas & Titus von Koeller, bitsandbytes.

The overarching theme of this version 5 release is “interoperability”. All refactors, performance improvements, and standardization are aligned with this theme. v5 plays nicely and end-to-end with the growing ecosystem: train a model with Unsloth/Axolotl/LlamaFactory/MaxText deploy it with vLLM/SGLang, and export it to llama.cpp/executorch/MLX to run locally!

In a recent development, version 5 is undeniably an accomplishment of the past five years by a very large number of people in our community. We also see it as a promise, and as a beacon of the direction we want to go.

Sources indicate that we took it as an opportunity to clean up the toolkit and isolate what mattered; we now have a clean slate on top of which to build. Thanks to the many changes from the community and team, improvements in performance, usability, and readability, will be simpler to ship.

Now that v5.0.0's first RC is out there, we'll be eagerly awaiting your feedback. Please check our release notes for all the technical details, and we'll be awaiting your feedback in our GitHub issues!

We Got Claude to Fine-Tune an Open Source LLM

📅 04 Dec 2025 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1934 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • We gave Claude the ability to fine-tune language models using a new tool called Hugging Face Skills.
  • In a recent development, claude Code can use "skills"—packaged instructions, scripts, and domain knowledge—to accomplish specialized tasks.
  • Recent findings suggest that the model trains on Hugging Face GPUs while you do other things.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We gave Claude the ability to fine-tune language models using a new tool called Hugging Face Skills. Not just write training scripts, but to actually submit jobs to cloud GPUs, monitor progress, and push finished models to the Hugging Face Hub. This tutorial shows you how it works and how to use it yourself.

In a recent development, claude Code can use "skills"—packaged instructions, scripts, and domain knowledge—to accomplish specialized tasks. The hf-llm-trainer skill teaches Claude everything it needs to know about training: which GPU to pick for your model size, how to configure Hub authentication, when to use LoRA versus full fine-tuning, and how to handle the dozens of other decisions that go into a successful training run.

With this skill, you can tell Claude things like:.

Recent findings suggest that the model trains on Hugging Face GPUs while you do other things. When it's done, your fine-tuned model appears on the Hub, ready to use.

This isn't a toy demo. The skill supports the same training methods used in production: supervised fine-tuning, direct preference optimization, and reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards. You can train models from 0.5B to 70B parameters, convert them to GGUF for local deployment, and run multi-stage pipelines that combine different techniques.

Hugging Face skills are compatible with Claude Code, Codex, and Gemini CLI. With integrations on the way for Cursor, Windsurf, and Continue.

This repo includes gemini-extension.json to integrate with the Gemini CLI.

You have to authenticate to your Hugging Face account with a write-access token so that the job can create a model repo.

Configure Hugging Face MCP Server to use your write token by sending it in either the HF_TOKEN or Authorization: Bearer HTTP Headers.

For Claude Code: claude mcp add --transport http hf-skills https://huggingface.co/mcp?bouquet=skills --header "Authorization: Bearer $HF_TOKEN".

Let's walk through a complete example. We'll fine-tune a small model to see the full workflow, then explore more advanced capabilities.

Start with a simple and clear instruction to fine tune a specific model.

The coding agent analyzes your request and prepares a training configuration. For a 0.6B model on a demo dataset, it selects t4-small—enough GPU for this model size and the cheapest option available.

The open-r1/codeforces-cots dataset is a dataset of codeforces problems and solutions. It is a good dataset for instruction tuning a model to solve hard coding problems.

Recent findings suggest that this works for vision language models too! You can simply run "Fine-tune Qwen/Qwen3-VL-2B-Instruct on llava-instruct-mix".

Before your coding agent submits anything, you'll see the configuration:.

According to recent reports, this is your chance to adjust anything. Change the output repo name, pick different hardware, or ask Claude to modify training parameters. Once you approve, the agent submits the job.

For example, you can ask the agent to try a test run:.

After submission, you get job details:.

In a recent development, the skill includes Trackio integration, so you can watch training loss decrease in real-time. Jobs run asynchronously so you can close your terminal and come back later. When you want an update:.

Then the agent fetches the logs and summarizes progress.

When training completes, your model is on the Hub:.

Recent findings suggest that that's the full loop. You described what you wanted in plain English, and the agent handled GPU selection, script generation, job submission, authentication, and persistence. The whole thing cost about thirty cents.

In a recent development, the skill supports three training approaches. Understanding when to use each one helps you get better results.

Sources indicate that SFT is where most projects start. You provide demonstration data—examples of inputs and desired outputs—and training adjusts the model to match those patterns.

According to recent reports, use SFT when you have high-quality examples of the behavior you want. Customer support conversations, code generation pairs, domain-specific Q&A—anything where you can show the model what good looks like.

The agent validates the dataset, selects hardware (a10g-large with LoRA for a 7B model), and configures training with checkpoints and monitoring.

According to recent reports, for models larger than 3B parameters, the agent automatically uses LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation) to reduce memory requirements. This makes training 7B or 13B models feasible on single GPUs while preserving most of the quality of full fine-tuning.

DPO trains on preference pairs—responses where one is "chosen" and another is "rejected." This aligns model outputs with human preferences, typically after an initial SFT stage.

Use DPO when you have preference annotations from human labelers or automated comparisons. DPO optimizes directly for the preferred response without needing a separate reward model.

DPO is sensitive to dataset format. It requires columns named exactly chosen and rejected, or a prompt column with the input. The agent validates this first and reveals you how to map columns if your dataset uses different names.

According to recent reports, you can run DPO using Skills on vision language models too! Try it out with openbmb/RLAIF-V-Dataset. Claude will apply minor modifications but will succeed in training.

GRPO is a reinforcement learning task that is proven to be effective on verifiable tasks like solving math problems, writing code, or any task with a programmatic success criterion.

The model generates responses, receives rewards based on correctness, and learns from the outcomes. This is more complex than SFT or DPO, but the configuration is similar.

The agent selects hardware based on your model size, but understanding the tradeoffs helps you make better decisions.

Sources indicate that for tiny models under 1B parameters, t4-small works well. These models train swiftly—expect $1-2 for a full run. This is perfect for educational or experimental runs.

For small models (1-3B), step up to t4-medium or a10g-small. Training takes a few hours and costs $5-15.

For medium models (3-7B), you need a10g-large or a100-large with LoRA. Full fine-tuning doesn't fit, but LoRA makes these very trainable. Budget $15-40 for production.

For large models (7B+), this HF skills job is not suitable.

When testing a workflow, start small:.

The coding agent configures minimal training—enough to verify your pipeline works without real cost.

Sources indicate that always run a demo before committing to a multi-hour production job. A $0.50 demo that catches a format error saves a $30 failed run.

Dataset format is the most common source of training failures. The agent can validate datasets before you spend GPU time.

The agent runs a quick inspection on CPU (fractions of a penny) and reports:.

If your dataset needs transformation, the agent can show you how:.

The agent provides mapping code and can incorporate it directly into your training script.

Real-time monitoring helps you catch problems early. The skill configures Trackio by default—after submitting a job, you can watch metrics at:.

In a recent development, this shows training loss, learning rate, and validation metrics. A healthy run shows steadily decreasing loss.

Ask the agent about status anytime:.

If something goes wrong, the agent helps diagnose. Out of memory? the agent suggests reducing batch size or upgrading hardware. Dataset error? The agent identifies the mismatch. Timeout? The agent recommends longer duration or faster training settings.

After training, you might want to run your model locally. The GGUF format works with llama.cpp and dependent tools like LM Studio, Ollama, etc.

The agent submits a conversion job that merges LoRA adapters, converts to GGUF, applies quantization, and pushes to Hub.

According to recent reports, we've shown that coding agents like Claude Code, Codex, or Gemini CLI can handle the full lifecycle of model fine-tuning: validating data, selecting hardware, generating scripts, submitting jobs, monitoring progress, and converting outputs. This turns what used to be a specialized skill into something you can do through conversation.

The skill is open source. You can extend it, customize it for your workflows, or use it as a starting point for other training scenarios.

#34343. DeepMath: A lightweight math reasoning Agent with smolagents

📅 04 Dec 2025 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (943 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

DeepMath: A lightweight math reasoning Agent with smolagents

📅 04 Dec 2025 | ⏱️ 5 min read (943 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • DeepMath is an aligned math reasoning agent built on Qwen3-4B Thinking and fine-tuned with GRPO (Group Relative Policy Optimization).
  • We evaluate DeepMath on four math datasets: MATH500, AIME, HMMT, and HLE, and show that:.
  • 🤖 The math agent alone reduces output lengths by up to 66%, while often improving accuracy.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

DeepMath is an aligned math reasoning agent built on Qwen3-4B Thinking and fine-tuned with GRPO (Group Relative Policy Optimization). Instead of verbose text, the model emits tiny Python snippets for intermediate steps, runs them in a secure sandbox, and folds the results back into its reasoning, reducing errors and output length. The agent is implemented using the smolagents library.

We evaluate DeepMath on four math datasets: MATH500, AIME, HMMT, and HLE, and show that:.

🤖 The math agent alone reduces output lengths by up to 66%, while often improving accuracy.

⚡ GRPO training improves the agent performance even further, in almost all benchmarks.

👉 Code and evaluation scripts: https://github.com/IntelLabs/DeepMath 👉 Model: https://huggingface.co/Intel/deepmath-v1.

Large language models (LLMs) have advanced reasoning capabilities, but mathematical problem-solving remains challenging; chain-of-thought traces can be lengthy and prone to arithmetic mistakes. Recent works[^1][^2] demonstrate that small models can reach strong performance, and other studies[^3] investigate tool use to improve reliability. What those papers generally do not emphasize is reducing trace verbosity or explicitly training models to prefer short, computation-oriented traces executed in a constrained, auditable environment.

Offload deterministic computation to a safe executor.

Train models to prefer concise, computation-oriented traces over verbose text.

DeepMath tackles this by combining a small Python executor with a fine-tuned LLM, enabling concise, computation-driven reasoning. The model learns to generate short Python snippets, which are executed in a sandbox and reintegrated into the context. GRPO fine-tuning encourages this behavior by rewarding correctness and encouraging shorter outputs.

Figure 1: The vLLM client and server were modified to use the DeepMath agent in generating the candidates, while using the vLLM backend.

Agent Interface: During inference, the model can output normal tokens or special agent calls containing Python snippets.

Execution: Snippets run in a sandboxed environment with strict safety constraints (no file I/O, no network, timeouts).

Concision: Replace multi-line textual calculations with short, focused snippets.

Determinism & Safety: Enforce strict execution limits.

Interpretability: Snippets are readable and auditable.

Figure 2: Output example where python code is generated, evaluated and the answer is inserted into the trace and used for context.

We fine-tune the model using GRPO, a reward-based optimization that balances:.

Accuracy Reward: +1 for correct answers.

Using code snippets: +1 for generating code snippets, weighted 10:1 vs. the accuracy reward.

Length reduction: shorter lengths are encouraged by limiting the GRPO completion candidates to 5k tokens.

Temperature Scheduling: We implemented linear temperature scheduling (T=1.2 → T=0.7) to balance exploration and stability during training. This approach aims to enhance experimentation during the initial training phases, subsequently reducing the temperature as we refine our proficiency in the skill.

In-context Learning: we include 4 solved examples where the trace contains agent calls and executor outputs, so the model learns the syntax and the call/response pattern.

Industry observers note that dataset: we used the Tool-Integrated Reasoning (TIR) subset of the OpenMathReasoning dataset. Note that GRPO only uses the problem, not the solution in the data. This dataset was chosen to ensure the problems benefit from the external tool.

We benchmarked DeepMath against baselines on four datasets. Metrics include:.

majority@16: robustness across samples, as used in previous math reasoning works, see references.

In a recent development, we compare a baseline configuration (Qwen3-4B-Thinking-2507, no agenting) with our DeepMath model. As ablation, we evaluate the agentic framework we developed running with the untrained Qwen3 model, denoted by +Agent. Additionally, we examine whether the GRPO training (for agentic use) improves non-agentic inference, denoted by +GRPO. Thus the two ablations are independent, not additive.

According to recent reports, we observe the agentic inference reduces output lengths, with mixed accuracy results. The DeepMath model is both GRPO-trained and run in agentic mode, and shows the highest accuracy with shortened traces. We conclude both GRPO training and agentic inference are needed for best results.

Key Insight: DeepMath reduces output length by up to 66% while improving accuracy on challenging datasets.

Accuracy: Offloading computation reduces arithmetic errors.

Efficiency: Shorter outputs mean faster inference and easier interpretability.

Safety: Sandbox execution mitigates risks of running arbitrary code.

Sources indicate that deepMath demonstrates a practical and lightweight way to combine a small executor with an LLM and to train the model to prefer short, computation-driven traces. Offloading deterministic computation reduces arithmetic and numerical errors and shortens traces, and GRPO fine-tuning further encourages concise, correct answers. The result is a more accurate and more interpretable math-solving agent without requiring a massive model or heavyweight external tools.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Vero Security declared on November 18, 2026 an $11 million seed round led by TLV Partners, alongside the launch of AISecurityEngineering.org, an open community for the emerging discipline of securing enterprise AI tools and agents.
  • GTM Capital, Maple Capital and angel investors also participated.
  • Industry observers note that vero reports that multiple Fortune 500 companies already use its platform.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Vero Security declared on November 18, 2026 an $11 million seed round led by TLV Partners, alongside the launch of AISecurityEngineering.org, an open community for the emerging discipline of securing enterprise AI tools and agents.

GTM Capital, Maple Capital and angel investors also participated. Vero stated it will use the funding to advance its AI Security Engineering platform, expand coverage across enterprise AI technologies and security workflows, and grow its go-to-market presence in the United States.

Industry observers note that vero reports that multiple Fortune 500 companies already use its platform. Founded in 2025 by CEO Elad Tessler and CTO Daniel Meirov, the tech giant brings together Tessler’s experience leading product at Astrix Security and Meirov’s work as Sightfull’s first employee, where he led R&D and product. The pair met in Unit 8200, where they co-led a cyber operations unit of more than 100 people.

Industry observers note that “CISOs have seen enough dashboards and tables that tell their teams what’s wrong and leave the work to them. AI Security Engineering deserves a better operating model, designed for AI rather than borrowed from other areas of security,” Tessler remarked.

At the center of the platform is the AI Runtime Governor, which Vero indicates inspects supported prompts, tool calls and agent actions when an action is attempted. It is designed to enforce approved policies during execution, including stopping a coding agent from reading secrets it has no reason to touch, blocking actions that violate security policies and preventing malicious skills or prompt injection from triggering unauthorized behavior.

In a recent development, vero’s product documentation describes coverage across endpoint, browser, SaaS and cloud environments. The platform discovers AI tools, agents, connected systems, configurations and permissions, identifies misconfigurations, and connects through existing endpoint, device-management and identity tools, so employees have nothing new to install.

Recent findings suggest that security teams decide which changes Vero can handle automatically. The platform implements approved controls, coordinates remediation with relevant owners, verifies completion and keeps protections aligned as the environment evolves. When a change requires a new risk decision, the responsible security professional receives the analysis and a recommended action.

In a company-supplied example, a new Fortune 1000 customer set a policy that only developers could connect AI agents to corporate code repositories or let them execute code. Vero notes that policy became more than 15 controls across coding agents, MCP servers, skills, identities and runtime actions within minutes.

According to recent reports, the staffing context comes from the 2026 Security Organizational Design Benchmark Report, produced by IANS and Artico Search using data from more than 1,400 CISOs and security staff. Among organizations with at least $10 billion in revenue, 65% had a head of AI security: 18% had a dedicated role and 47% had added the responsibility to an existing job. At organizations below $1 billion, 44% had a head of AI security, but only 6% had made it a dedicated role.

GTM Capital mentioned it invested after a structured evaluation with its community of Fortune 500 CIOs and CISOs, who worked directly with Vero before the firm committed.

The community’s free roadmap requires no sign-up and currently offers nine tracks with 259 topics, covering how AI agents work, threats, inventory, configuration, identity, runtime defenses, drift monitoring and incident response. Member note-sharing, online teardowns, in-person meetups and credentials are listed as forthcoming, while tracks on running an agent security program and red-teaming agents are marked as coming soon.

Vero builds and funds the site under a public charter stating that the curriculum contains no product material and that member names are not provided to its sales organization.

The seed round therefore supports two connected efforts: a commercial system intended to turn policies into continuously updated controls, and a vendor-funded curriculum for the people responsible for setting those policies. Vero’s early enterprise deployments provide a direct test of whether automation can reduce the ongoing work of AI security while preserving human review of risk decisions.

Once they found such a feature table, all they do is a point-in-wise join, wherein they take a unique ID, in this case, user ID, and some timestamp, and they do a time-wise join on it. In a recent development, when we looked at this, we said, we can help in two places. One is building that feature table, and the other is doing the time-wise join. That is what we set out to achieve. That was a feature table. That feature table is built by another fact log or an immutable log. This is just the searches that have happened over a period of time. By looking at this, it is just very clear that there is one data frame and the other data frame. We figured out we can actually just use Spark ML transformer, which did the feature translation between.

This is how it looked in its entirety. There were immutable fact logs, which is just log of search events that have happened in the past. We asked people to write reusable feature encoders that converted into a feature table. Once we had that, all anybody has to do is just go look at the initial dataset and do a time-wise join on it. We tried to do something similar to online as well. There were event streams. We asked people to write feature mappers in Scala, and that became enriched streams. From there, there was a centralized team which took all these features, put it into Cassandra, and then served it via an API. There were a couple of problems with this approach. One was parity. Data was different between online and offline. The computation was different from online and offline. Then there were performance problems because of the amount of data that we were processing in offline.

Backfilling or recomputation was hard. In the second attempt, we decided, let's fix data and computational parity together. The way we fixed data parity was we introduced the concept of timelines. Timelines is nothing but a time-ordered sequence of events for a user. User searched, user clicked, user booked, things like that. The idea was, let's build this timeline equally or approximately in the same way for both online and offline. Then that way, once we have that, we can just write computation once and then use the timeline. That was a substantial picture. This is how the timelines were built. Those are the search, clicks, and immutable events. They got materialized into Hadoop. We built timeline builders separately. It's a duplicate effort, but it was managed by a central team. That timeline was operating separately for online and offline. They synced the data or the timelines into Cassandra and HDFS. The only difference between these two timelines were the Cassandra timelines were trimmed. Unlike the MVA, TVA, we actually didn't trim timelines for saving the universe. We trimmed timelines in Cassandra for saving the space.

Recent findings suggest that this is how we used timelines for computational parity. We had a full timeline in HDFS, a trimmed timeline in Cassandra. We asked people to write centralized shared feature libraries. These are things that can be used to compute features, things like sum, count, large scale, and all those typical things was written by a centralized team. It also allowed extension. Anybody could come in and write in the feature that is not already there. In online or in real time, when an application wanted some inference, they would go to a feature store API and ask, can you give me this feature? What it would do is go into Cassandra, pick up the timeline for that specific user or use case, and then build that feature on the fly with these shared libraries. The same happened on the training side or on offline. That stack was Python, because scientists were using Python.

It has been revealed that we had a wrapper, which had a feature computation library wrapper. What it did was, whenever the scientist wanted a feature, it submitted a Spark job. In that Spark job, we actually did the same thing. We typically achieved what we wanted to do, both data and feature parity. The problem was, ML scientists were not familiar with writing features in Java, and that created a dependency between engineering and ML science. Secondly, in the previous one, the Cassandra timelines, computing features on the fly was costly, expensive, because it took more than 90 milliseconds or so to actually just fetch the data. It was not suitable for most of the use cases. Then we noted, ok, third attempt. Forget feature computation, we'll just focus on feature storage and serving. Let people deal with feature computation. We didn't care how features are computed, as long as we knew where to pick the features from.

If it was pre-computed, ok, we'll go to a data lake of sorts. If it is real time, we'll go to Kafka. Then we built a feature store. In the feature store, there was an ingestor component, which knew about these multiple data sources, and pulled that data, and stored it into an online store, and served it via an API. In this API, there was no on-the-fly computation. It was just a simple lookup, because features were already computed. The same pipeline, what it also did was sync data into offline, so that MLS can use it for retraining purposes, and for also other analysis. This feature store also had other benefits, like it had feature registry, feature monitoring, and so on. In essence, after three attempts, this is what we learned. It's a multidimensional problem, and we don't have an answer. Currently, for the pre-computation and real time, we currently have three systems, and we are always looking for one more system. That wraps the second layer.

Recent findings suggest that now in that third layer, we are moving away from infrastructure to business impact. I want to give you a high-level tour of all the ML platforms that we have, and then dive into one of them. This is the platform that we have. One is GenAI platform. It's the newest kid in the block. What it does is it enables any team to actually safely build generative AI experiences. It provides tools and infrastructure and foundational capabilities like guardrails, evaluation, orchestration out of the box. Things like PII detection, PII masking, everything comes out of the box. The product teams can focus just on product innovation and not on LLM plumbing. Let's look at a few use cases there, what we have. The trip planning, which is just a conversational experience where someone can go talk in natural language and get recommendations, that's powered by GenAI. We have smart filters.

Recent findings suggest that if you were ever on Booking.com, you would see hundreds of filters on the left, and it is hard for anyone to know which to pick. We have a text box where you can type it, and that translated into the right filters and sorters. The third is review summaries. That provides, based on the last reviews, a quick snapshot of pros and cons. The next is property Q&A. This actually enables instant answers to any property-specific questions, and it is grounded on reviews, past Q&A, and that is also powered by GenAI. There are many interesting things under the platform, but we are not going to cover it today.

GenAI is good, but to generate data, we actually want good content. That's where content intelligence comes in. What it does is it provides surfaces like good, high-quality content that are usable. This platform analyzes every image and text. It actually adds metadata or enriches that metadata. For example, if it is images, it adds themes, tags, and looks for any harmful content. If it is text, it looks for, for example, sentiments or topics that have been discussed. This also supports the reviews. Because most of the things happen in the background, like fraud detection is also taken care of by this content intelligence. One example that you see, anytime you see a gallery on Booking.com, it is probably powered by this content intelligence. Recent findings suggest that there's a platform for that. It also does reviews. It detects topics on the reviews and summarizes it at the property level. This is a platform that we are going to dig in, so I'll park it here. When I say multi-vertical, I'm referring to accommodations, flights, attractions, and so on. Those kinds of recommendations come from this platform. The goal of this platform is to say, maximize value for travelers, partners, and the business. That wraps all the platforms.

Let's jump into ranking platform. Ranking is a three-way optimization problem. We need choice and value for customers. We need exposure and growth for the partners. We also need efficiency and revenue for business. If we show irrelevant results, the travelers are going to be annoyed. If we show poor visibility, partners are going to be frustrated. If any one of them is annoyed for too long, I'm going to get my salary re-ranked. It's a three-way optimization problem. Back then in 2005, we had the formula for ranking hotels look like this. It was simple. It was just a simple function, which took bookings and views, and a random tiebreaker in case there were two hotels which had the same rank. The formula evolved over time. We introduced cancellations. It was taking consideration of seasonality. What is the distance of the hotel from the center? What is the number of views the hotel is getting?

Availability of the hotel. The average ranking in the locality. What is the visitor traffic? Guest reviews. These are just some flavors of what are the factors we considered. Back then, ranking actually was computed offline using simple Perl cron scripts every night, and then the scores were dumped into MySQL, and we used it in real time. Around 2016, we actually tried to replace the ranking formula with machine learning, and we failed miserably. The handcrafted formula was undefeatable. We could not beat it for a long time, like one and a half years or so. This formula cannot be beaten. The reasons were many fold. The primary reason was that the ideal model that we wanted to train the model on, and the massive amount of data that we had was not actually helpful when Spark kept exploding. The memory of Spark was not sufficient. What we did was we cut corners, we made some approximations, and we succeeded. In true Booking sense, we ran an experiment, and it was successful.

Next, we wanted to tackle personalized ranking, and there was a problem. This is what it looked like. The ranking scores was calculated offline until then. It was put into MySQL, and an availability engine read that MySQL data, loaded it into memory. The responsibility of this availability engine was that it needs to search the availability and prices of millions of properties. Because of the amount of data that this engine had, it used a scatter-gather pattern. It had a coordinator and 24 shards. Each of those shards actually worked on a subset of the data. When a request came in from the user, it came to the availability engine via a search orchestrator, and the request landed there. The request contained something like this. Where does the user want to search on? When? Then, what is the party size? Then, what are the filters and preferences of the user?

According to recent reports, the coordinator accepted that request and then distributed the work to the workers. Workers went on to do their job. They actually looked into the subset of the data that they had, took the data out, and then they used the ranking scores that were preloaded into memory to do the sorting. After they did the sorting, they supplied the results back to the coordinator. Coordinator aggregated all the information from the workers and re-sorted the results and gave the results back to the search. This is what was happening. If you wanted to personalize, meaning that every user gets a specific set of results, what we had to do was take the ranking logic out of this availability engine, get rid of those static scores at the bottom, and then replace it with a service. That's what we wanted to do. There were two problems. The first problem was, if there were 1,000 requests for the availability engine, it meant that the new service is going to get 24,000 requests because it was sitting behind the fanout, behind the shards. Secondly, the availability engine was operating at super low latency, and that also meant that this new service plus the network hop to the model and the model's time all needs to be well within the time of that service. It's basically a high throughput, low latency problem, and we managed to crack it. These are the numbers from 2024. That ranking service that you saw in the previous slide, that green box that was introduced new, is able to solve 100,000 requests per second with a p99.9 latency of 100 milliseconds. The average is way low. It's like 40, 50 milliseconds or so.

I want to share one more thing before I wrap up the evolution story. Experiments at Booking typically run for two to four weeks, but this meant that we couldn't actually train or run models. We wanted to move faster, knowing well that if we actually put in a bad ranking model upfront, it is going to cost all of us, like travelers, partners, and business. What we did was we introduced interleaving. This is how it worked. Typically, for an A/B testing, we actually take the people and split them across two groups, and then we show different search results for them, which was coming from different ranking models. In interleaving, what we did was we didn't show two groups, we didn't split the groups, we just showed the same results for all users.

Recent findings suggest that those results were coming from merged data, meaning we would train a couple of models, in this case, two models, red and blue. We trained the model, and each of these models gave a list of results. Then we would somehow need to merge it. One simple example could be, take the top one from here, top one from here, merge it. Then keep alternating it. It's just a team draft approach. Then once you have done, you present that to all users across the service. Then you check offline, ok, from which list did the user interact more? Was it from model A or from model B? That gives us the answer. Why it was useful was we could suddenly run more variants. On the right side, it doesn't have to be two. We can even run eight different models that are actually interleaving the results for search. That is, we can run more variants that was like 10 times speed-up than what we are used to with A/B testing.

According to recent reports, we could use it with less traffic because interleaving is super sensitive to customer preferences, and we can get signals faster. The way we use it now, interleaving and A/B, is that we train a bunch of models, we pre-select it with interleaving, we pick up a winner, and then we take the winner and then do proper A/B testing. We have optimized both speed, while not losing scientific rigor.

Recent findings suggest that I started the talk by saying that experiment laid the foundation in general for data-driven decision-making. You can see that, still, it continues to underpin what we do every day. With that, that concludes the evolution story.

Secondly, we wanted to centralize all kinds of AI-related governance, security, quality, and all those things. We wanted to centralize that.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Supermicro revealed on November 18, 2026 that the first systems in its new all-flash storage family based on sixth-generation AMD EPYC 9006 processors are now shipping, led by a Petascale server with PCIe Gen 6 connectivity and as much as 3.93 PB of flash in a 2U chassis.

Supermicro reports a sequential-read bandwidth gain of up to 100% over PCIe Gen 5 for the fresh servers, its first storage products to implement PCIe Gen 6. The systems are aimed at high-performance computing, AI training and inference. The initial Petascale server uses AMD’s SP7 platform, and more storage products are planned as AMD introduces SP8 CPU versions.

Chief business officer Vik Malyala said the systems are intended to keep storage in step with current CPU and GPU clusters, while the Data Center Building Block Solutions architecture allows customization for those workloads and provides software-defined-storage partners with validated systems.

Recent findings suggest that the chassis accommodates as many as 32 E3.S NVMe SSDs and reaches its maximum capacity with 122 TB drives. Networking can be built around as many as four x16 high-performance cards, with the balanced I/O design intended to let customers adapt the system to different fabrics and workloads.

Sources indicate that the hardware is intended to supply the sustained bandwidth needed for AI data lakes, large-scale analytics and high-throughput storage networking. That connects the drive density to the networking side of the system: capacity alone does not address how quickly data can move between storage and the rest of an AI cluster.

It has been revealed that validation covers Supermicro’s CloudDC, GrandTwin and Hyper families and software from Hammerspace, IBM, MinIO, Nutanix, Scality, VAST Data, VDURA and WEKA for AI-scale deployments. The partner statements show the hardware being positioned across several storage architectures rather than as a single fixed stack.

Vincent Hsu, IBM Fellow, vice president and CTO of IBM Storage, mentioned AI inference spans data ingest, model loading, retrieval and KV cache, and that IBM Storage Scale on the newly introduced Petascale server is designed to support the entire pipeline while maximizing GPU-utilization efficiency, with headroom for performance and capacity growth.

Other partners outlined different data-management approaches. Hammerspace’s Data Platform can fold the Petascale flash into one global namespace that also includes a customer’s existing lower-cost capacity systems. WEKA’s distributed NeuralMesh software runs across the upcoming server without hardware tiers, while VDURA’s platform can present Supermicro’s all-flash and HDD systems within one namespace.

The hardware adds denser flash and higher-bandwidth I/O, while the validated software layer determines how that capacity is organized and delivered to each stage of an AI workload.

This approach extends Sequel’s original product rather than replacing it. Webinars remain available, while each event supplies activity that can inform later content, follow-up and website experiences.

  • Reminder: llama.cpp server is a lightweight, OpenAI-compatible HTTP server for running LLMs locally.
  • In a recent development, this feature was a popular request to bring Ollama-style model management to llama.cpp.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

llama.cpp server now ships with router mode, which lets you dynamically load, unload, and switch between multiple models without restarting.

Reminder: llama.cpp server is a lightweight, OpenAI-compatible HTTP server for running LLMs locally.

In a recent development, this feature was a popular request to bring Ollama-style model management to llama.cpp. It uses a multi-process architecture where each model runs in its own process, so if one model crashes, others remain unaffected.

Start the server in router mode by not specifying a model:.

This auto-discovers models from your llama.cpp cache (LLAMA_CACHE or ~/.cache/llama.cpp). If you've previously downloaded models via llama-server -hf user/model, they'll be available automatically.

You can also point to a local directory of GGUF files:.

It has been revealed that on the first request, the server automatically loads the model into memory (loading time depends on model size). Subsequent requests to the same model are instant since it's already loaded.

Returns all discovered models with their status (loaded, loading, or unloaded).

All model instances inherit settings from the router:.

According to recent reports, all loaded models will use 8192 context and full GPU offload. You can also define per-model settings using presets:.

The built-in web UI also supports model switching. Just select a model from the dropdown and it loads automatically.

We hope this feature makes it easier to A/B test different model versions, run multi-tenant deployments, or simply switch models during development without restarting the server.

Industry observers note that AI agents are rapidly becoming essential for building intelligent applications, but creating robust, adaptable agents that scale across domains remains a challenge. Many existing frameworks struggle with brittleness, tool misuse, and failures when faced with complex workflows.

CUGA (Configurable Generalist Agent) was designed to overcome these limitations. It's an open-source, AI Agent that combines flexibility, reliability, and ease of use for enterprise use cases. By abstracting orchestration complexity, CUGA empowers developers to focus on domain requirements rather than the internals of agent building. And now, with its integration into 🚀Hugging Face Spaces🚀, experimenting with CUGA and open models has never been easier.

CUGA is a configurable, general-purpose AI agent that supports complex, multi-step tasks across web and API environments. It has achieved state-of-the-art performance on leading benchmarks:.

🥇 #1 on AppWorld - a benchmark with 750 real-world tasks across 457 APIs.

🥈 Top-tier on WebArena (#1 from 02/25 - 09/25) - showcases CUGA Computer Use capabilities with a complex benchmark for autonomous web agents across application domains.

We're also continuing to innovate with upcoming experimental capabilities, including:.

Figure 1: CUGA Agentic Architecture.

The CUGA architecture begins with the user's message flowing into a chat layer that interprets intent and constructs the user's goal, based on context. A task planning and control component then decomposes this goal into structured subtasks, tracked programmatically through a dynamic task ledger. This ledger supports re-planning when needed, ensuring robust execution. Subtasks are delegated to specialized agents, such as the API agent, which uses an inner reasoning loop to generate pseudo-code instructions before invoking code in a secure sandbox. The system leverages a tool registry that goes beyond MCP protocols to parse and understand tool capabilities, enabling precise orchestration. Once all steps are completed, the final response is returned to the user, delivering reliable, policy-aligned outcomes.

Sources indicate that CUGA works best when inference is fast. When each call takes seconds, delays compound and force a tradeoff between agent capability and user experience. Running on high-performance inference platforms like Groq shows how fast inference fundamentally expands what agent architectures can achieve.

CUGA is fully open source, under the Apache 2.0 license, and you can find us at cuga.dev.

By embracing open models, CUGA aligns with the Hugging Face ethos of democratizing AI-giving developers the freedom to choose models that best fit their needs, whether for experimentation or production.

CUGA has been tested with a variety of open models, including gpt-oss-120b and Llama-4-Maverick-17B-128E-Instruct-fp8 (both hosted on Groq). Our Hugging Face Space uses gpt-oss-120b, with the model hosted on Groq, offering a rapid response time for LLM calls.

It has been revealed that groq runs open models on its custom‑built LPUs, which are designed for AI inference and optimal for repeated agent inferences required by CUGA's architecture, enabling planning, execution, and validation steps to finish fast. The result is strong cost and performance: open models are ~80-90% cheaper than closed alternatives; Groq's OpenAI-compatible APIs meet production latency needs, and CUGA stays fully configurable across models, providers, and deployment topologies.

Recent findings suggest that to make agent development even more accessible, CUGA integrates with Langflow, an open-source visual programming interface for building LLM-powered workflows. Its intuitive drag-and-drop interface reduces the barrier to entry for those who prefer low-code solutions.

According to recent reports, starting with Langflow 1.7.0, CUGA ships with its own widget, enabling users to assemble complex, multi-tool agents visually and deploy with a click. Give it a try at langflow.org.

Sources indicate that we've launched a CUGA demo on Hugging Face Spaces to give you a taste of what's possible. This demo showcases a small CRM system and equips CUGA with 20 preconfigured tools for handling sales related data queries and API interactions through the API Agent. To make experimentation even more powerful, the demo provides access to workspace files, enabling you to use predefined policies.

Give it a try on Hugging Face Spaces and share your feedback!

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that it has become increasingly challenging to assess whether a model’s reported improvements reflect genuine advances or variations in evaluation conditions, dataset composition, or training data that mirrors benchmark tasks. The NVIDIA Nemotron approach to openness addresses this by publishing transparent and reproducible evaluation recipes that make results independently verifiable.

Sources indicate that NVIDIA released Nemotron 3 Nano 30B A3B with an explicitly open evaluation approach to make that distinction clear. Alongside the model card, we are publishing the complete evaluation recipe used to generate the results, built with the NVIDIA NeMo Evaluator library, so anyone can rerun the evaluation pipeline, inspect the artifacts, and analyze the outcomes independently.

According to recent reports, we believe that open innovation is the foundation of AI progress. This level of transparency matters because most model evaluations omit critical details. Configs, prompts, harness versions, runtime settings, and logs are often missing or underspecified, and even small differences in these parameters can materially change results. Without a complete recipe, it’s nearly impossible to tell whether a model is genuinely more intelligent or simply optimized for a benchmark.

Industry observers note that this blog shows developers exactly how to reproduce the evaluation behind Nemotron 3 Nano 30B A3B using fully open tools, configurations, and artifacts. You’ll learn how the evaluation was run, why the methodology matters, and how to execute the same end-to-end workflow using the NeMo Evaluator library so you can verify results, compare models consistently, and build transparent evaluation pipelines of your own.

Recent findings suggest that developers and researchers need evaluation workflows they can rely on, not one-off scripts that behave differently from model to model. NeMo Evaluator provides a unified way to define benchmarks, prompts, configuration, and runtime behavior once, then reuse that methodology across models and releases. This avoids the common scenario where the evaluation setup quietly changes between runs, making comparisons over time difficult or misleading.

Recent findings suggest that model outputs can vary by inference backend and configuration, so evaluation tools should never be tied to a single inference solution. Locking an evaluation tool to one inference solution would limit its usefulness. NeMo Evaluator avoids this by separating the evaluation pipeline from the inference backend, allowing the same configuration to run against hosted endpoints, local deployments, or third-party providers. This separation enables meaningful comparisons even when you change infrastructure or inference engines.

Recent findings suggest that many evaluation pipelines work once and then break down as the scope expands. NeMo Evaluator is designed to scale from quick, single-benchmark validation to full model card suites and repeated evaluations across multiple models. The launcher, artifact layout, and configuration model support ongoing workflows, not just isolated experiments, so teams can maintain consistent evaluation practices over time.

In a recent development, transparent evaluation requires more than final scores. Each evaluation run produces structured results and logs by default, making it easy to inspect how scores were computed, understand score calculations, debug unexpected behavior, and conduct deeper analysis. Each component of the evaluation is captured and reproducible.

Recent findings suggest that by releasing Nemotron 3 Nano 30B A3B with its full evaluation recipe, NVIDIA is providing a reference methodology that the community can run, inspect, and build upon. Using the same configuration and tools brings consistency to how benchmarks are selected, executed, and interpreted, enabling more reliable comparisons across models, providers, and releases.

Open evaluation means publishing not just the final results, but the full methodology behind them, so benchmarks are run consistently, and results can be compared meaningfully over time. For Nemotron 3 Nano 30B A3B, this includes open‑source tooling, transparent configurations, and reproducible artifacts that anyone can run end‑to‑end.

Sources indicate that neMo Evaluator is an open-source library designed for robust, reproducible, and scalable evaluation of generative models. Instead of introducing yet another standalone benchmark runner, it acts as a unifying orchestration layer that brings multiple evaluation harnesses under a single, consistent interface.

Under this architecture, NeMo Evaluator integrates and coordinates hundreds of benchmarks from many widely used evaluation harnesses, including NeMo Skills for Nemotron instruction-following, tool use, and agentic evaluations, as well as the LM Evaluation Harness for base model and pre-training benchmarks, and many more (full benchmark catalog). Each harness retains its native logic, datasets, and scoring semantics, while NeMo Evaluator standardizes how they are configured, executed, and logged.

Recent findings suggest that this provides two practical advantages: teams can run diverse benchmark categories using a single configuration without rewriting custom evaluation scripts, and results from different harnesses are stored and inspected in a consistent, predictable way, even when the underlying tasks differ. The same orchestration framework used internally by NVIDIA’s Nemotron research and model‑evaluation teams is now available to the community, enabling developers to run heterogeneous, multi‑harness evaluations through a shared, auditable workflow.

This variance reflects the probabilistic nature of LLMs rather than an glitch with the evaluation pipeline. Modern evaluation introduces several sources of non‑determinism: decoding settings, repeated trials, judge‑based scoring, parallel execution, and differences in serving infrastructure. All of which can lead to slight fluctuations.
