#34248. Breaking: Put the AI in the Work, Not Next to It

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1272 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dev ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: Put the AI in the Work, Not Next to It

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1272 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that most companies I meet now have an AI demo.
  • It lives in a slide, a sandbox, or a tool that sits beside the work.
  • In a recent development, the useful test is simpler than a feature list.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that most companies I meet now have an AI demo. Fewer have AI in the actual job.

A demo is easy to recognise. It lives in a slide, a sandbox, or a tool that sits beside the work. People try it, nod, and then go back to the spreadsheets, the inboxes, and the visits that still run the way they did last year. The intelligence is nearby. It is not in the process.

In a recent development, the useful test is simpler than a feature list. Does the system change an outcome inside the work, before a person has to notice? If the answer is no, you do not have an AI capability yet. You have a demonstration.

According to recent reports, I have spent a lot of time on the other side of that line, building systems that have to hold up in regulated enterprises, in field teams, and in support queues. Across twenty-seven builds, the pattern that keeps proving itself is this: put the AI in the work, not next to it.

It has been revealed that here is what that looks like in practice. I will stay with anonymised examples from real delivery, and I will not add numbers or stories that are not in the work itself.

A large pharmaceutical manufacturer, with 1,200+ employees, was running its entire people operation across disconnected spreadsheets, manual payroll, and fragmented HR tools. Every report took hours to assemble. Attrition was going undetected. Compliance was a risk.

Industry observers note that the useful response was not an HR chatbot parked next to the existing mess. It was a single AI-powered platform covering the complete employee lifecycle, from first application to final settlement. Seventeen module groups. 130+ features. 25+ embedded AI capabilities. Ten user roles. A 24-week roadmap in four delivery phases.

It has been revealed that the AI sat inside the work. Resume parsing at acquisition. Predictive time-to-hire. Appraisal bias detection and succession risk scoring. Workforce management with real-time anomaly detection. A learning system with AI-personalised paths. An executive view that surfaced KPIs, attrition flags, and compliance alerts.

The moment I come back to is this one. When a department's attrition risk score climbs, the platform flags it automatically and surfaces a retention recommendation before a single resignation letter arrives. That is not a demo. That is the job, happening earlier than a person would have caught it.

The same idea indicates up in support.

In a recent development, A support operation needed to handle high inbound message volume on WhatsApp without scaling headcount in a straight line, while keeping response quality and a clean handoff to human agents. Volume was growing faster than the team could hire against it.

The build was an AI-assisted automation layer on WhatsApp Business, delivered in twelve weeks. Common queries were recognised and resolved end to end, without an agent touching the conversation. Edge cases routed to a human with the conversation context intact, so the customer never had to repeat themselves. The resolution flow was tuned against the real query mix, so automation absorbed the repetitive volume and agents kept the complex work.

On the automated flows, first response moved from minutes to seconds. A large share of repetitive queries resolved without agent involvement, in line with mature support-automation deployments. Again, the intelligence was not a separate assistant that a tired agent might remember to open. It was in the queue, doing the repetitive part of the job, and stepping aside when the job needed a person.

Field work is a third version of the same lesson.

A major FMCG brand needed merchandising teams to execute in-store standards consistently across hundreds of retail touchpoints. The familiar problem was this: what actually happened in store looked nothing like the plan on paper.

It has been revealed that the response was a mobile-first field execution platform. Merchandisers select the store format, and the platform loads the mandatory SKUs, shelf share targets, planograms, and scoring rules automatically. Four pillars get tracked on each visit, with photo proof: distribution, shelf share, planogram, and pricing. On visit completion, the total score calculates automatically, broken down by pillar, and syncs to management dashboards in real time. The configuration was built to deploy across food, beverage, personal care, and home care without rebuilding, and to be ready for more than one brand and more than one market from day one.

There is no large language model in that story that I need to wave at you. There is a score that used to be assembled later, if it was assembled at all, and that now exists at the shelf, while the visit is still the work in front of the merchandiser. The system is in the visit, not in a report that arrives after the window to fix the store has closed.

If I stand back from these builds, and from the rest of the twenty-seven, a few practical rules hold.

According to recent reports, put the intelligence where the decision actually happens. In people operations, that is inside the lifecycle, not in a side tool. In support, that is inside the conversation. In the field, that is inside the visit.

Build for the job that already exists, then let the AI change the timing of it. Attrition risk before the resignation. A first response in seconds, not minutes. A store score at the end of the visit, not at the end of the week.

Recent findings suggest that treat integration and governance as part of the product, not as a later phase you will get to. In the same body of work, a multi-site quality system and a laboratory system were taken from kickoff to go-live in 135 days, with audit trails and the controls those environments require. A regulatory information system for a multi-country pharmaceutical operation was made production-ready in twelve weeks by customising an existing platform rather than rebuilding it, with maker-checker controls so the same user cannot create and approve. Twenty-two third-party systems have been delivered with zero critical-path slippage, including SAP and SSO across regulated estates. This is unglamorous, and it is usually the reason an AI feature can actually run.

It has been revealed that and when the date is fixed, treat the date as the brief. A national campaign stack, designed, built, and deployed for a UAE-wide scan-and-win promotion across all emirates, went live in two weeks. An animated, five-chapter product story, built inside an existing single-page site, was delivered in ten days across three phases. Launch dates are not a mood. They are a constraint the work has to meet.

None of this requires you to start with a model. It requires you to start with the job: the resignation you want to see coming, the message you want resolved, the shelf you want to be able to score before the merchandiser leaves the aisle. Then you place the AI there.

Industry observers note that it is also the kind of work I build: enterprise systems, field tools, and automation designed so the intelligence sits inside the process. I write more about brand, growth, and this kind of building at usmanakhan.com.

If you already have an AI demo, keep it if it helps people see what is possible. Just do not stop there. Move the same intelligence into the job, and let it change an outcome before a person has to notice.

That is when AI stops being a slide, and starts being the work.

Transformers.js v4: Now Available on NPM!

📅 09 Feb 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1195 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • We're excited to announce that Transformers.js v4 is now available on NPM!
  • The biggest change is undoubtedly the adoption of a upcoming WebGPU Runtime, completely rewritten in C++.
  • According to recent reports, in addition to better operator support (for performance, accuracy, and coverage), this new WebGPU runtime allows the same transformers.js code to be used across a wide variety of JavaScript environments, including browsers, server-side runtimes, and desktop applications.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We're excited to announce that Transformers.js v4 is now available on NPM! After a year of development (we started in March 2025 🤯), we're finally ready for you to use it.

The biggest change is undoubtedly the adoption of a upcoming WebGPU Runtime, completely rewritten in C++. We've worked closely with the ONNX Runtime team to thoroughly test this runtime across our ~200 supported model architectures, as well as many new v4-exclusive architectures.

According to recent reports, in addition to better operator support (for performance, accuracy, and coverage), this new WebGPU runtime allows the same transformers.js code to be used across a wide variety of JavaScript environments, including browsers, server-side runtimes, and desktop applications. That's right, you can now run WebGPU-accelerated models directly in Node, Bun, and Deno!

According to recent reports, we've proven that it's possible to run state-of-the-art AI models 100% locally in the browser, and now we're focused on performance: making these models run as fast as possible, even in resource-constrained environments. This required completely rethinking our export strategy, especially for large language models. We achieve this by re-implementing upcoming models operation by operation, leveraging specialized ONNX Runtime Contrib Operators like com.microsoft.GroupQueryAttention, com.microsoft.MatMulNBits, or com.microsoft.QMoE to maximize performance.

For example, adopting the com.microsoft.MultiHeadAttention operator, we were able to achieve a ~4x speedup for BERT-based embedding models.

Developing a latest major version gave us the opportunity to invest in the codebase and tackle long-overdue refactoring efforts.

Sources indicate that until now, the GitHub repository served as our npm package. This worked well as long as the repository only exposed a single library. However, looking to the future, we saw the need for various sub-packages that depend heavily on the Transformers.js core while addressing different use cases, like library-specific implementations, or smaller utilities that most users don't need but are essential for some.

In a recent development, that's why we converted the repository to a monorepo using pnpm workspaces. This allows us to ship smaller packages that depend on @huggingface/transformers without the overhead of maintaining separate repositories.

In a recent development, another major refactoring effort targeted the ever-growing models.js file. In v3, all available models were defined in a single file spanning over 8,000 lines, becoming increasingly difficult to maintain. For v4, we split this into smaller, focused modules with a clear distinction between utility functions, core logic, and model-specific implementations. This new structure improves readability and makes it much easier to add new models. Developers can now focus on model-specific logic without navigating through thousands of lines of unrelated code.

In v3, many Transformers.js example projects lived directly in the main repository. For v4, we've moved them to a dedicated repository, allowing us to maintain a cleaner codebase focused on the core library. This also makes it easier for consumers to find and contribute to examples without sifting through the main repository.

According to recent reports, we updated the Prettier configuration and reformatted all files in the repository. This ensures consistent formatting throughout the codebase, with all future PRs automatically following the same style. No more debates about formatting... Prettier handles it all, keeping the code clean and readable for everyone.

Thanks to our newly introduced export strategy and ONNX Runtime's expanding support for custom operators, we've been able to add many new models and architectures to Transformers.js v4. These include popular models like GPT-OSS, Chatterbox, GraniteMoeHybrid, LFM2-MoE, HunYuanDenseV1, Apertus, Olmo3, FalconH1, and Youtu-LLM. Many of these required us to implement support for advanced architectural patterns, including Mamba (state-space models), Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA), and Mixture of Experts (MoE). Perhaps most importantly, these models are all compatible with WebGPU, allowing owners to run them directly in the browser or server-side JavaScript environments with hardware acceleration. We've released several Transformers.js v4 demos so far... and we'll continue to release more!

Industry observers note that we've migrated our build system from Webpack to esbuild, and the results have been incredible. Build times dropped from 2 seconds to just 200 milliseconds, a 10x improvement that makes development iteration significantly faster. Speed isn't the only benefit, though: bundle sizes also decreased by an average of 10% across all builds. The most notable improvement is in transformers.web.js, our default export, which is now 53% smaller, meaning faster downloads and quicker startup times for users.

Version 4 also adds new library features that make it easier to build robust, production-ready applications.

It has been revealed that the new ModelRegistry API is designed for production workflows. It provides explicit visibility into pipeline assets before loading anything: list required files with get_pipeline_files, inspect per-file metadata with get_file_metadata (quite useful to calculate total download size), check cache status with is_pipeline_cached, and clear cached artifacts with clear_pipeline_cache. You can also query available precision types for a model with get_available_dtypes. Based on this new API, progress_callback now includes a progress_total event, making it easy to render end-to-end loading progress without manually aggregating per-file updates.

In a recent development, we also added new environment controls for model loading. env.useWasmCache enables caching of WASM runtime files (when cache storage is available), allowing applications to work fully offline after the initial load.

env.fetch lets you provide a custom fetch implementation for use cases such as authenticated model access, custom headers, and abortable requests.

Finally, logging is easier to manage in real-world deployments. ONNX Runtime WebGPU warnings are now hidden by default, and you can set explicit verbosity levels for both Transformers.js and ONNX Runtime. This update, also driven by community feedback, keeps console output focused on actionable signals rather than low-value noise.

According to recent reports, A frequent request from users was to extract the tokenization logic into a separate library, and with v4, that's exactly what we've done. @huggingface/tokenizers is a complete refactor of the tokenization logic, designed to work seamlessly across browsers and server-side runtimes. At just 8.8kB (gzipped) with zero dependencies, it's incredibly lightweight while remaining fully type-safe.

This separation keeps the core of Transformers.js focused and lean while offering a versatile, standalone tool that any WebML project can use independently.

We've made several quality-of-life improvements across the library. The type system has been enhanced with dynamic pipeline types that adapt based on inputs, providing better developer experience and type safety.

Additionally, we've added support for larger models exceeding 8B parameters. In our tests, we've been able to run GPT-OSS 20B (q4f16) at ~60 tokens per second on an M4 Pro Max.

We want to extend our heartfelt thanks to everyone who contributed to this major release, especially the ONNX Runtime team for their incredible work on the newly introduced WebGPU runtime and their support throughout development, as well as all external contributors and early testers.

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1090 w)
📖 Baca

Breaking: Telecom Core Network Software: The Key Components Every Mobile Operator Needs and Where to Start

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1090 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • You open a vendor list for core network software and meet a wall of acronyms: HSS, MME, PGW, PCRF, ePDG and more.
  • 3GPP defines SGi as the reference point between the PDN Gateway and the packet data network.
  • Recent findings suggest that 3GPP specifies the split of the gateway functions into control plane and user plane in TS 23.214.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

You open a vendor list for core network software and meet a wall of acronyms: HSS, MME, PGW, PCRF, ePDG and more. Which ones do you actually have to deal with? We walk through what each part of a mobile core does, how the standard relates it to the fifth-generation core, and what to settle before you talk to a vendor. Which of these functions you run yourself depends on your operator model.

3GPP defines SGi as the reference point between the PDN Gateway and the packet data network. That network may be an operator external public or private network or an intra-operator network.

Recent findings suggest that 3GPP specifies the split of the gateway functions into control plane and user plane in TS 23.214. The specification covers the control and user plane separation of the Serving Gateway and the PDN Gateway, and it lets you place the control plane and the user plane separately.

Functions of a 4G core in the 3GPP architecture.

In home-routed roaming, S8 connects the SGW in the visited network with the PGW in the home network. When the SGW and the PGW are in the same network, S5 connects them: without roaming, or in roaming with local breakout, where the PGW is in the visited network.

According to recent reports, follow one phone as it joins the network. The MME handles NAS signalling and talks to the HSS over S6a, which carries subscription and authentication data. The data session runs through the SGW and the PGW, and the PGW allocates the IP address of the UE. For policy, the PCRF sends quality of service (QoS) rules and charging rules over Gx to the PCEF in the PGW, and the PCEF applies them.

The PGW and the SGW may be implemented in one physical node or in separate nodes. Our test lab uses classic EPC with plane separation by the Control and User Plane Separation (CUPS) model, built from the MME, the HSS, the SGW and the PGW with the PCEF. Use the table as a map of the functions in a 4G core.

According to recent reports, voice and Wi-Fi rely on functions around the core. Voice over LTE runs on the IP Multimedia Subsystem (IMS). GSMA IR.92, the IMS Profile for Voice and SMS, defines a minimum mandatory set of 3GPP features for IMS-based telephony and for IMS-based and SGs-based SMS over LTE. Wi-Fi access relies on an evolved Packet Data Gateway (ePDG) for untrusted access or a Trusted WLAN Access Gateway (TWAG) for a trusted WLAN.

Sources indicate that who decides which path a network takes? In a non-roaming scenario, 3GPP leaves the choice to the home operator. Whether a non-3GPP IP access network is used as trusted or untrusted is not a characteristic of the access network. An operator typically makes that choice for Wi-Fi it controls. For your list, note which of the two Wi-Fi access types you initiative to offer.

In a recent development, for its policy references to the EPC policy standard TS 23.203, TS 23.503 states that the PCRF maps to the Policy Control Function (PCF) in the 5G core. It states that the PCEF maps to the combination of the Session Management Function (SMF) and the User Plane Function (UPF).

In a recent development, for the PGW and the MME the specifications describe interworking. These are the combined PGW-C + SMF and UPF + PGW-U functions, and the optional N26 interface between the MME and the Access and Mobility Management Function (AMF).

Policy mappings that TS 23.503 states for its references to TS 23.203.

In a recent development, in the 5G core, the PCF provides policy rules to control plane functions to enforce them. The SMF handles session management and UE IP address allocation, and the UPF is the external PDU session point of interconnect to the data network.

It has been revealed that one more term for 5G radio. EN-DC (E-UTRA-NR Dual Connectivity) connects the phone to one eNB as master node and one en-gNB as secondary node, and the eNB is connected to the EPC via S1. The 3GPP overview page adds that the Non-Stand Alone architecture, which uses the existing LTE and EPC, is also known as EN-DC.

Industry observers note that start from what you already run and what you need: decide which functions you operate and list the interfaces they require. Then choose the generation and access types, agree how the core connects to billing and policy, and test on your own side.

In a recent development, this order is a suggestion from our team, and step 4 is where our lab experience comes in. In our test lab, the PCEF communicates with the PCRF and the OCS over Diameter on the Gx and Gy interfaces. If your billing and policy systems come from other vendors, put their names and interfaces on your list before the first call.

Compare vendors against your own interface list. Ask which 3GPP interfaces the software terminates and how control and user plane are separated. Ask how it connects to billing and policy systems and whether it works next to the functions you keep.

Questions to ask a core network software vendor.

According to recent reports, we suggest checking these six points when you compare vendors. Add your own rows for the functions you keep, and use the list when you talk to us, too.

Industry observers note that an operator sends a request through the form on a product page. We contact the operator to specify the task, provide access to the documentation and answer questions.

We build seven products for mobile networks: Stingray PGW, Stingray ePDG, Stingray TWAG, Stingray PCRF Proxy, Stingray GTP-C Proxy, LBS and Stingray PCEF.

It has been revealed that in our solution, the PCEF function runs as a separate module of Stingray Service Gateway. This is why we can also supply our PGW on its own: it then works with a PCEF made by other vendors. Stingray TWAG is a software gateway for mobile network operators and mobile virtual network operators. It lets them build a TWAN, a trusted Wi-Fi access network based on the 3GPP standard. Stingray GTP-C Proxy lets you combine PGWs from different vendors into shared pools.

These products are separate pieces of mobile network software; this article describes the 3GPP functions, not our product set.

Specifications used (3GPP Release 19): TS 23.002, TS 23.214 and TS 23.401.

Also used: TS 23.203, TS 23.402, TS 23.501, TS 23.503, TS 32.240 and TS 37.340.

#34241. Breaking: From three apps to one monorepo

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (610 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dev ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: From three apps to one monorepo

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (610 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that epicstock is a photo stock marketplace where buyers license photos straight from the photographers who took them.
  • The storefront is public and the admin is not.
  • Sources indicate that the API had to be separate too, and strong enough to carry every transaction: orders, payments, downloads and photographer payouts.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that epicstock is a photo stock marketplace where buyers license photos straight from the photographers who took them. A client asked for a storefront in the style of Unsplash or Alamy, selling digital products, with an admin panel to run part of the business. Putting the panel inside the storefront project was the obvious shortcut, and the wrong one. This post explains how the work split into three pieces in one repository, what that bought, and what it did not fix.

The storefront is public and the admin is not. Mixing them in one project and one domain made every admin feature a risk for the shop, and every shop change a risk for the admin. The panel needed its own domain.

Sources indicate that the API had to be separate too, and strong enough to carry every transaction: orders, payments, downloads and photographer payouts. Both frontends call it, so it could not belong to either one.

The work therefore split into a storefront (apps/web), an admin (apps/admin) and an API (apps/api). They stayed in one repository because they share a lot: UI components, business logic and domain references such as licence types, store names and photo statuses. With separate repositories, that code would be copied or published as packages, and the copies would drift apart.

The root pnpm-workspace.yaml declares two globs:.

Each app is a folder under apps/:.

Turborepo fans out every command to all the workspaces. pnpm build builds the whole repository, and --filter scopes a command to one package when only one changed. Each app still owns its own wrangler.toml and deploys to Cloudflare on its own, so the monorepo does not merge the three runtimes into one.

Four packages carry the contract between the apps:.

According to recent reports, the typed client matters most where it replaces plain strings. Some admin calls to the API were still plain strings.

In a recent development, in a smoke test of the admin panel on 2026-09-07, saving a photographer's fee amount returned a 404. The dialog called fetch("/api/admin/photographers/:id/fee-amount") with a relative path. The admin app has no app/api folder and no rewrites, so the request went to the admin's own origin and never reached the worker. Two other admin calls had the same problem: paying a payout and enabling two-factor authentication.

Recent findings suggest that the fix sent all three through the typed client, with credentials included. Now a wrong route is a type error, and pnpm check:types reports it before the code runs.

In a recent development, the bug existed inside the monorepo. Putting the apps in one place did not prevent it. Sharing the client did.

Recent findings suggest that deploys are still manual. pnpm deploy:manual deploys the web app, then the API, then the admin. CI does not run it. Database migrations are hand-written SQL files, applied by hand, and a migration has to land before the code that depends on it.

A shared package also means one change can reach three apps. That is the point of the layout, and it is also the risk. The checks that catch it are pnpm check:types across every workspace, the linter, and the dead-code and duplication reports. They run because someone runs them.

Recent findings suggest that I would keep the shared types, the validators and the typed client. They turned a runtime 404 into a type error, and that is the cheapest kind of bug to find.

The repository puts the three apps where you can see them change together. It does not make a change safe on its own. The types, the checks and the deploy order do that.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • AI agents often perform impressively in controlled research settings, yet struggle when deployed in real-world systems where they must reason across multiple steps, interact with real tools and APIs, operate under partial information, and recover from errors in stateful, permissioned environments—highlighting a persistent gap between research success and production reliability.
  • OpenEnv is an open-source framework from Meta and Hugging Face designed to address this challenge by standardizing how agents interact with real environments.
  • In this post, we explore how OpenEnv works in practice, why calendars serve as a powerful benchmark for real-world agent evaluation, and what our findings reveal about the current limitations of tool-using agents.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI agents often perform impressively in controlled research settings, yet struggle when deployed in real-world systems where they must reason across multiple steps, interact with real tools and APIs, operate under partial information, and recover from errors in stateful, permissioned environments—highlighting a persistent gap between research success and production reliability.

OpenEnv is an open-source framework from Meta and Hugging Face designed to address this challenge by standardizing how agents interact with real environments. As part of this collaboration, Turing contributed a production-grade calendar management environment to study tool-using agents under realistic constraints such as access control, temporal reasoning, and multi-agent coordination.

In this post, we explore how OpenEnv works in practice, why calendars serve as a powerful benchmark for real-world agent evaluation, and what our findings reveal about the current limitations of tool-using agents.

In a recent development, openEnv is a framework for evaluating AI agents against real systems rather than simulations. It provides a standardized way to connect agents to real tools and workflows while preserving the structure needed for consistent and reliable evaluation.

OpenEnv uses a gym-oriented API (reset, step, action, observations) like OpenAI's Gymnasium. Also, OpenEnv uses a standard MCP tool call interface to connect to envs which provides a consistent interface across domains and simulation to production environments.

The environments maintain state across multiple actions—enabling long-horizon reasoning—and can connect directly to real APIs and tools such as browsers, code repositories, or calendars. This shifts evaluation from "Can this work in a controlled demo?" to "Can this operate reliably in the real world?".

Calendar systems are deceptively complex. While scheduling a meeting seems simple, real-world calendar management requires agents to reason over time, permissions, multiple users, and incomplete information—often across several dependent steps. These properties make calendars a powerful testbed for evaluating tool-using agents outside controlled simulations.

In a recent development, to ground OpenEnv in this kind of realistic, demanding use case, Turing built a production-grade calendar management environment referred to as the Calendar Gym. Rather than simulating scheduling in the abstract, it exposes agents to the same constraints they would face in real calendar systems: Access Control Lists across people and calendars, limited visibility into other users' state, and multi-step workflows where actions must be chained in the correct order. Agents interact with a rich set of calendar operations—from listing calendars to modifying events and permissions—and must handle failed actions, incorrect assumptions, and missing permissions. Each session runs in an isolated environment, enabling reliable comparisons across runs.

Below is a code example of how to use the Calendar Gym. We explore the environment, discover available tools, list calendars, create an event, and print the result.

In a recent development, below is an excerpt of what the Calendar Gym returns when you call ListToolsAction. Each entry includes the tool name plus an input schema (what arguments the tool accepts).

Evaluating agents in the Calendar Gym revealed consistent patterns which were common across multiple domains. While agents often perform well on individual game like actions, reliability breaks down as tasks become longer, more ambiguous, and more constrained.

It has been revealed that multi-step reasoning is the primary bottleneck. Agents struggle to correctly chain actions across longer workflows, suggesting that benchmarks need to test sustained reasoning over multiple dependent steps—not just single tool calls.

Ambiguity significantly degrades performance. Agents achieved close to 90% success on tasks with explicit calendar identifiers, but success dropped to roughly 40% when the same tasks were phrased using natural language descriptions. Building stronger lookup and validation into agent loops—rather than relying on the LLM to resolve references unaided—appears essential.

Recent findings suggest that correct tool choice isn't enough. Across failed interactions, more than half of errors stemmed from malformed tool arguments or incorrect ordering, even when the right tool was selected. Reliable agent behavior depends as much on execution quality and structured feedback as on tool selection—environment design matters.

These challenges are not unique to scheduling and calendars. They reflect broader limitations that emerge whenever agents operate in changing systems over long periods of time, and they point toward evaluation frameworks that test permissions, partial observability, and multi-step workflows together.

OpenEnv provides a foundation for testing agents under realistic conditions, and the Calendar Gym demonstrates how seemingly simple domains can surface deep challenges in reasoning, ambiguity resolution, and tool use. By evaluating agents where failure is measurable and constraints are real, we gain clearer insight into what it takes to build agents that operate reliably in production.

Recent findings suggest that for a deeper dive into the Calendar Gym's design, benchmarking methodology, and quantitative results, explore the full technical article on Turing's site. To explore a clone of the Calendar Gym, visit the Calendar Gym space.

Sources indicate that in practice, tool integrations rarely fail in dramatic ways; they fail in small, predictable ones. When wiring up MCP tools to real APIs (like calendar operations), we encountered a handful of recurring concerns.

Below are three common failure modes we’ve seen in production, along with representative error payloads and mitigation strategies. These examples illustrate not just what can go wrong, but how structured errors can help agents recover gracefully.

According to recent reports, the agent calls a valid tool (e.g. events_insert), but the arguments do not match the declared JSON schema.

We can mitigate this by providing one canonical example of a correct 'events_insert' call in your prompt. Return structured validation errors so the model can repair and retry instead of failing silently.

The tool call is syntactically correct, but the API rejects it due to insufficient permissions.

According to recent reports, we can mitigate this by clearly documenting the required OAuth scopes. Return structured, actionable remediation steps so the agent can guide the user instead of retrying the same failing call. Clearly document required OAuth scopes. Return structured, actionable remediation steps so the agent can guide the user instead of retrying the same failing call.

The event is rejected by the API, or it is created at an unexpected time.

Recent findings suggest that we can mitigate this by standardizing on RFC3339 with explicit timezone offsets (e.g. 2026-02-11T09:30:00-05:00). Include at least one correct datetime example in your documentation to anchor model behavior and reduce repair retries.

Tech Report: The Weekly Operating Rhythm That Scaled My Consulting Firm Past Chaos

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1297 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that there is a stage in a consulting firm where everyone is busy and nobody can tell you, in one minute, how the business is actually doing.
  • It has been revealed that earlier in my career, as a partner, I helped grow a software consulting manufacturer from about $6M to $60M in under three years, and later I founded and ran a fully remote consultancy.
  • Here is how that consulting firm weekly operating rhythm works, and how to start one without turning it into another long meeting.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that there is a stage in a consulting firm where everyone is busy and nobody can tell you, in one minute, how the business is actually doing. Pipeline lives in someone's inbox. Delivery status lives in a project tool nobody outside the team opens. Cash lives in accounting. People issues live in private chats. The leadership team finds out about problems when they explode. The week is a string of ad-hoc meetings, each one trying to put out a fire that started days earlier.

It has been revealed that earlier in my career, as a partner, I helped grow a software consulting manufacturer from about $6M to $60M in under three years, and later I founded and ran a fully remote consultancy. Growth at that pace does not leave room for managing by surprise. The habit that kept us oriented was not a complicated dashboard. It was a one-page weekly operating rhythm that looked at the same four things every week: pipeline, delivery, cash and people.

Here is how that consulting firm weekly operating rhythm works, and how to start one without turning it into another long meeting.

Firefighting feels like leadership because it is visible and urgent. A client is unhappy, so you jump on a call. A deal is slipping, so you rewrite the proposal at night. Someone is overloaded, so you move them at the last minute. You go home exhausted and convinced you ran the firm that day.

What you actually did was react to the last thing that shouted the loudest. The quieter problems keep growing: a thin pipeline two months out, a project that is drifting, an invoice that has been sitting, a strong engineer who is quietly miserable. By the time they shout, your options are worse.

A weekly rhythm does not eliminate surprises. It makes the crucial things visible on a schedule, while you still have time to act.

The page is deliberately short. If it takes more than a few minutes to patch, it will not get updated. I want one owner for the page, usually me or a general manager, and each section has a named person who supplies the facts before we meet.

The four sections stay the same.

Pipeline. What is in play this week and this month? Which deals moved forward, which stalled, and where are we thin further out? The point is not to re-run every sales conversation. The point is to see whether next month's work is actually there, and whether we are selling work we cannot staff.

Recent findings suggest that delivery. Which engagements are on track, which are at risk, and what would change the risk this week? I want names, dates and the real blocker, not a traffic-light color with no explanation. If a project needs a decision from leadership, it belongs here, not in a side chat that leadership might miss.

Cash. What came in, what is overdue, what is going out, and is there a timing gap we should face now? You do not need a full finance review every week. You do need to know whether a late invoice, a surprise cost or a slow month is about to become a problem. In a services firm, cash is often a lagging picture of delivery and sales discipline.

It has been revealed that people. Who is overloaded, who is underused, who is at risk of leaving, and where do we have a hiring or bench gap? This is the section firms skip, and it is usually where the damage shows up last and costs the most. A weekly look at load, morale and upcoming rotations prevents the conversation that starts with "how did we not see this.".

It has been revealed that if something does not fit one of those four, it is either not a weekly operating problem or it needs to be translated into one of them. A new tool, a conference, a random idea: park it. Do not let it crowd out the page.

According to recent reports, the page is the work product. The meeting exists only to make decisions the page cannot make by itself.

Keep it short and regular, the same day and time every week. In a remote firm, a written patch can come first, with a brief call to resolve the open questions. If a topic needs a long debate, schedule that debate separately. The weekly rhythm is not the place to redesign the firm.

Recent findings suggest that every item should arrive with a proposed next step. "Project X is at risk" is a status. "Project X is at risk because the client has not signed the change request, and I need a decision by Thursday on whether we pause the extra work" is something a leadership team can act on.

Write the decisions down on the same page. Who will do what, by when. The following week starts by checking those items before anything new is added. That loop is what replaces firefighting. People stop raising the same alarm in three different chats because they know there is a place where it will be seen and closed.

The rhythm fails when it becomes a dumping ground.

In a recent development, do not review every ticket or every lead. Summaries only. Do not add a fifth, sixth and seventh section because each function wants its own slide. Do not use the meeting to re-litigate a single account for forty minutes. Do not collect vanity metrics that nobody uses to make a decision.

Recent findings suggest that and do not let the page get stale. A weekly operating rhythm with last month's numbers is theater. If a section owner cannot update it before the review, the fix is to make that section lighter, not to skip the week.

Recent findings suggest that once the rhythm is real, the rest of the week gets quieter, at least for leadership. You still handle true emergencies the day they happen. You stop treating every surprise as an emergency, because you know it will have a place within a few days. Sales, delivery, finance and team leads also start coming with exceptions, not tours of everything they did.

According to recent reports, in my experience, this is also how you notice tradeoffs early: a deal that would overload a team, a delivery risk that should change an invoice conversation, a people problem that should change what you are willing to sell. The four sections are useful on their own. They are more useful when you look at them together, on one page, every week.

According to recent reports, you do not need new software to do this. A single shared document is enough.

In a recent development, this week, write the four headings, add the few facts you already have, and schedule a thirty-minute review with the people who own sales, delivery, cash and the team. End that first review with no more than a handful of decisions, written down. Do the same thing next week, and cut anything that felt like theater.

Recent findings suggest that chaos in a growing consulting firm is often just notable information arriving too late, in too many places. A one-page weekly operating rhythm will not run the firm for you. It will keep pipeline, delivery, cash and people in the same conversation, on a cadence you can actually keep, which is usually the difference between scaling and scrambling.

Short links you can edit after they're printed: 302s, a 2-second cache, and not counting Facebook's crawler

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (617 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that I build iBuat.Link, a link manager for small businesses that sell through WhatsApp, Instagram and marketplaces.
  • Industry observers note that doing that well comes down to three small decisions in the redirect path.
  • Industry observers note that the first instinct for a URL shortener is 301 Moved Permanently: it's the "SEO-friendly" redirect, and browsers love it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that I build iBuat.Link, a link manager for small businesses that sell through WhatsApp, Instagram and marketplaces. The feature people care about most sounds boring: change where a short link or a printed QR code goes, after it's out in the world. A seller prints 2,000 boxes with a QR code, the marketplace listing behind it gets taken down, and the code has to open something else by tomorrow.

Industry observers note that doing that well comes down to three small decisions in the redirect path. None of them are clever, but each one was a bug before it was a decision.

Industry observers note that the first instinct for a URL shortener is 301 Moved Permanently: it's the "SEO-friendly" redirect, and browsers love it. That's exactly the problem. Browsers cache a 301 aggressively, sometimes for as long as the user keeps their profile. Change the destination in the dashboard and anyone who clicked before keeps landing on the old page, and you can't reach their cache to fix it.

So every redirect is a 302, and it says out loud that it must not be cached:.

Sources indicate that private, no-store also keeps CDNs and corporate proxies from holding on to it. The cost is one extra request to us on every click, which is the whole point: the decision about where to send someone is made fresh each time.

If every click hits the database, a link that goes viral turns into a primary-key lookup storm. If you cache for minutes, edits feel broken ("I changed it, why does it still open the old page?").

The compromise is a tiny read-through cache in front of the lookup, with a TTL of two seconds:.

A burst of a thousand clicks in a second costs one query. An edit is visible within two seconds everywhere, and immediately in the process that handled it. Nobody has ever noticed two seconds, and the database graph stopped spiking.

It has been revealed that note what's cached: the link row, not the redirect. Everything that decides the answer is evaluated on each request against that row: an expiry date is compared with the clock every time, so an expired link stops exactly on time, and a link with a click limit reads a fresh count. Switching a link off follows the same two-second rule as an edit.

It has been revealed that the first time a link ran in a Facebook ad, the click count looked fantastic. Then we split it by user agent. A large share of the "clicks" were facebookexternalhit, the bot Facebook sends to build a link preview, plus WhatsApp's own preview fetcher (WhatsApp/2.x), plus the usual crawlers.

Those requests still get redirected (a preview with no title looks broken), but they're counted separately and never use up the owner's monthly click quota:.

Two details that took a while to get right:.

The last lesson is about ordering. Quota checks, analytics writes and fraud scoring all happen after the destination is known, and none of them can stop the redirect. If the analytics write fails because the database is slow during a traffic spike, the error is logged and the visitor still lands where they were going.

A visitor scanning a QR code on a box doesn't know or care that the seller is out of quota this month. The link has to work.

That's the whole trick behind editable links: no permanent redirects, a cache short enough that nobody notices it, and honest numbers about who actually clicked. If you're curious how it looks from the user's side, the dynamic vs static QR codes post explains it without any code.

According to recent reports, tl;dr: We built an agent skill that teaches coding agents how to write production CUDA kernels. The agents produced working kernels for both, with correct PyTorch bindings and benchmarks, end to end.

Writing CUDA kernels is hard. Writing CUDA kernels that correctly integrate with transformers and diffusers is harder. There are architecture-specific memory access patterns, vectorization strategies, warp shuffle reductions, and a dozen integration pitfalls that trip up even experienced developers. It is exactly the kind of specialized, high-stakes problem where agent skills shine.

We gave coding agents the domain knowledge they need, like which GPU architecture to target, how to structure a kernel-builder project, when to use shared memory versus registers, and how to write PyTorch bindings. The agents did the rest. If you have used the LLM training skill or read We Got Claude to Teach Open Models, the pattern will feel familiar: package domain expertise into a skill, point the agent at a problem, and let it work.

The Kernel Hub solved the distribution of custom hardware kernels. You can load pre-compiled kernels from the Hub with a single get_kernel call. No builds, no flags. However, someone still needs to write the kernels. That is the gap this skill fills.

CUDA kernel development has a brutal surface area:.

This is domain knowledge that gets lost in documentation tabs and Stack Overflow answers. An agent skill packages it into context that loads on demand.

First, let's show how to use the skill right away, then we'll dive into the details of how we benchmarked the kernels.

Sources indicate that first, we compare the isolated RMSNorm kernel performance against the PyTorch baseline. This is the main speedup in the optimized pipeline.

Average speedup: 1.88x and a bandwidth efficiency: 34.7% of H100 theoretical (3,350 GB/s).

Next, we compare the end-to-end video generation performance of the optimized kernels against the baseline (no compile) and the torch.compile baseline.

RMSNorm accounts for ~5% of total compute in LTX-Video. The remaining time is spent in attention, linear projections, and VAE decode. The 6% end-to-end speedup from a single kernel type is consistent with that profile.

It has been revealed that the agent built an RMSNorm kernel for Qwen3-8B, a large language model from transformers with 65 RMSNorm modules across 32 layers. The full example is at examples/qwen3_8b/. We optimized the RMSNorm kernel for H100. Both benchmarks were run on H100 80GB HBM3 at precision BFloat16.

Average speedup: 1.94x and a bandwidth efficiency: 22.3% of H100 theoretical (3,350 GB/s).

Speedup scales with sequence length: 1.58x at 128 tokens, 2.47x at 8192 tokens. For long-context inference, the custom kernel roughly halves RMSNorm latency.

author is { id: number; name: string }, and books is:.

Sources indicate that the compiler reads the query. rating is a string because round(avg(...)) returns numeric, and it's nullable because of the LEFT JOIN. reviews isn't nullable because of the coalesce. count(*) and rank() return int8, so they're bigint.

Sources indicate that A statement is an Effect, and yield* runs .exec(). There's also execTakeFirst() (fails with NoResultError), execTakeFirstOrNone(), execCount() and stream(). Errors and the SqlClient requirement show up in the type:.

Transactions use the client's withTransaction, and the same sql works inside it:.

Industry observers note that it needs effect 4.1.3+ and TypeScript 7.1+ (the native compiler). It also works with @effect/sql-sqlite-node and @effect/sql-mysql2.

The schema is a TypeScript type. You can write it by hand or generate it:.

Significant statements can run into the compiler's limits. sql.as() lets you type those yourself.

#34229. Tech Report: Rumble-2-Flash: an open 0.5B speech model for 40+ languages

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 2m • 📖 Standard (447 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: Rumble-2-Flash: an open 0.5B speech model for 40+ languages

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (447 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that today we're open sourcing Rumble-2-Flash under the Apache 2.0 license.
  • audio accepts a local path, a URL, a NumPy array, or a list of these.
  • Rumble-2-Flash uses the Qwen3-ASR architecture for day-0 support.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that today we're open sourcing Rumble-2-Flash under the Apache 2.0 license. It's a 0.5B-parameter speech recognition model for 40+ languages that competes with models 3-60x its size.

audio accepts a local path, a URL, a NumPy array, or a list of these.

Rumble-2-Flash uses the Qwen3-ASR architecture for day-0 support. If your stack runs Transformers or vLLM, it runs Rumble-2-Flash, with no forked runtime or trust_remote_code.

To find out how small a model could get before accuracy dropped off, we distilled Rumble-2, our larger production model, into it with on-policy distillation. The student doesn't train on transcripts the teacher wrote. It transcribes the audio itself, and the teacher grades that transcript token by token: at every position, it gives its own probability for what should come next, and the student learns to match it. Because the student learns from its own outputs, it gets corrected on exactly the mistakes it makes, with feedback on every token instead of one score per clip.

Recent findings suggest that on-policy distillation normally requires teacher and student to share a tokenizer, and ours don't: choosing Qwen3-ASR meant taking its vocabulary too. GOLD removes that restriction. It merges tokens where the two tokenizers split the text differently, so both models are compared over the same text. Tokens that exist in both vocabularies are compared directly, and the rest by their sorted probabilities.

Sources indicate that on the Open ASR Leaderboard multilingual track, Rumble-2-Flash averages a 6.96% error rate across Chinese, German, French, Italian, Spanish, Portuguese, Hindi, Dutch and English. That's better than Meta's omniASR-LLM 7B, a model 15x larger, and ahead of Whisper large-v3. On the English track it averages 6.6% WER.

Rumble-2-Flash is also fast. Its throughput depends on how full the batches are: on the larger datasets in HF's Open ASR Leaderboard, where batches stay full, it reaches over 7,000 RTFx. That's an hour of audio in about half a second.

Clean audio is easy. Phone calls are compressed and noisy, and often have speakers with very different accents. On AppTek's call-centre benchmark (302 hours of helpline calls, 14 English accents, scored with AppTek's own script), Rumble-2-Flash reaches 7.86% WER, on par with NVIDIA's Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe (30B) at 7.78%. That's well ahead of Qwen3-ASR 0.6B (8.7%), from the same model family, and close to Qwen3-ASR 1.7B (7.4%), the only model in the comparison that does better.

The weights are on the Hub at Reson8/Rumble-2-Flash. It's also available through our API.

We're very curious what you'll build with it. Tell us in the Discussions tab what you've made, what you like, and what you'd like to see changed in a next version.

#34228. Why my first CPU benchmark was too noisy to use, and how I fixed it

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 2m • 📖 Standard (442 w)
📖 Baca
Hardware & Chips ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dev ↗ Open Full Page

Why my first CPU benchmark was too noisy to use, and how I fixed it

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (442 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Dev

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • My first benchmark numbers looked reasonable, until I ran the same thing twice and got different answers.
  • All numbers come from the repo's README (including its "First attempt (archived)" section) and results/archive_summary.json in cpu-inference-bench.
  • I started by running ResNet-18 on PyTorch, ONNX Runtime and OpenVINO with default settings on a laptop CPU (Intel i7-12650H).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

My first benchmark numbers looked reasonable, until I ran the same thing twice and got different answers. This post is about how I found out why, and what I changed before trusting any number.

All numbers come from the repo's README (including its "First attempt (archived)" section) and results/archive_summary.json in cpu-inference-bench.

I started by running ResNet-18 on PyTorch, ONNX Runtime and OpenVINO with default settings on a laptop CPU (Intel i7-12650H). To check repeatability I ran each configuration twice. In 12 of 18 repeated rows, the two identical runs differed by more than 5%, up to 48.27% for one row (PyTorch, 12 threads, batch 1). The results were not usable as a comparison, so I archived them.

In a recent development, A laptop has package power and thermal limits, so the clock changes during a run. Without control over that, a difference of a few percent between frameworks would be within the noise.

Sources indicate that the first attempt used default frequency scaling, so the clock was free to move. This CPU has a sustained package power limit of 45 W and a short-term limit of 115 W, and power and thermal limits like these can change the clock during a run. Background services and other processes sharing the cores can add noise as well.

In a recent development, the data from that attempt is archived locally and is not in the public repo, so I can't show its per-run frequencies or temperatures here. Instead of guessing which factor dominated, I changed the setup so that each one is either controlled or visible: every repeat now records the package temperature, the mean and minimum P-core frequency, and the kernel's thermal-throttle counters.

According to recent reports, I capped the P-cores at 3000 MHz and ran a small pilot. Two of four rows still raised the kernel's thermal-throttle counters, so I chose 2600 MHz as a clock the cores could sustain.

In a recent development, speedup ratios are printed only between two stable rows. Unstable rows are shown and marked, not dropped.

With these controls, ResNet-18 INT8 vs FP32 at batch 1 came out at 2.34× (PyTorch), 2.74× (ONNX Runtime) and 3.48× (OpenVINO, 2.6 ms). Five of 36 BERT rows and 2 of 18 ResNet rows (both FP32) were still unstable, and the README states so.

Thermal counters do not detect power-limit throttling, so I also checked the frequency columns. A VPN client was running during all runs and I did not measure its effect. This is one laptop and one campaign.

The code was written with Claude Code; the methodology, decisions and verification are mine.

Originally published at diyor.dev.

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (719 w)

Tech Report: A Trusted Software Dependency Was Compromised. What Should You Review Next?

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (719 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Four engineering questions for investigating third-party software exposure.
  • On 16 November 2026, attackers exploited a vulnerability in Optimizely Web Experimentation, allowing them to impersonate customer customers and inject malicious JavaScript into legitimate website scripts.
  • In a recent development, researchers at Report URI identified 188 affected scripts across 178 organisations, including major international brands.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Four engineering questions for investigating third-party software exposure.

On 16 November 2026, attackers exploited a vulnerability in Optimizely Web Experimentation, allowing them to impersonate customer customers and inject malicious JavaScript into legitimate website scripts.

In a recent development, researchers at Report URI identified 188 affected scripts across 178 organisations, including major international brands. The malicious code was capable of stealing payment information, manipulating cryptocurrency transactions and targeting browser-accessible information.

Optimizely has since fixed the vulnerability and removed the injected code. Its forensic investigation remains ongoing.

But containing the incident doesn't automatically establish what happened on every affected website.

If your application loads a compromised third-party component, how do you establish what it could access and whether anything was actually exposed?

Here are four questions engineering teams should investigate.

Start by identifying which applications and pages loaded the affected component.

For the Optimizely incident, the reported exposure window was 07:51–22:24 UTC on 16 November, although individual customer exposure windows may differ.

It has been revealed that optimizely has confirmed that Web Experimentation was affected, rather than its other experimentation products. Customers should confirm their individual exposure status and window directly with Optimizely.

What to establish: Which pages loaded the script, when it was active and whether visitors could have received the malicious version.

Historical deployments, tag-manager configurations, archived script responses and browser monitoring records can help reconstruct that picture.

Knowing that a script was present doesn't tell you what it could do.

Third-party JavaScript running in a website's context may be able to interact with page content, form fields, browser-readable storage and outbound requests, subject to browser security controls.

For this incident, researchers observed malicious capabilities including payment-card skimming and cryptocurrency address manipulation.

That makes the execution context particularly vital.

Payment details entered inside properly isolated third-party payment iframes are generally inaccessible to scripts running on the parent page. Optimizely's initial investigation also identified that distinction.

What to establish: The information and functionality available to the script, not simply whether the dependency existed.

Importantly, browser-level exposure does not automatically mean an organisation's backend infrastructure was compromised.

This is where understanding the wider architecture becomes useful.

A third-party script may be supplied by an external organisation but execute within the context of your own website. That creates a trust relationship worth examining.

Review the controls that determine what it can reach and where information can travel.

According to recent reports, content Security Policy (CSP): Does your policy restrict executable scripts and outbound connections? Are directives overly permissive?

Data flows: Which payment, authentication and customer-information workflows operate on affected pages?

Isolation: Are sensitive interactions separated from third-party scripts through appropriate browser and application boundaries?

A dependency might have legitimate access to an application while still creating exposure if that access is broader than necessary.

What to establish: Which safeguards were present, whether they were effective and what an attacker could potentially reach through the affected component.

Industry observers note that an architecture diagram can help identify potential exposure. It cannot prove that malicious code executed or that information was stolen.

Incident investigations need historical evidence.

It's useful to separate findings into three categories:.

The absence of suspicious logs is not necessarily proof that nothing happened. Some browser-side activity may not appear in server-side monitoring.

For affected Optimizely customers, preserving relevant logs, reviewing payment activity and following the vendor's incident guidance should be immediate priorities.

Industry observers note that traditional incident response remains essential. Teams still need to contain threats, preserve evidence, investigate indicators of compromise and assess any notification obligations.

Architectural understanding supports that work by showing how an affected component relates to the wider application.

It helps answer questions such as:.

At Veriom, we're building technology that maintains a living model of software architecture across code, cloud and infrastructure, helping engineering teams understand dependencies, data flows and trust boundaries.

According to recent reports, that context can help teams investigate and prioritise structural risks. It doesn't replace browser forensics, incident response or specialist security testing.

When a trusted dependency is compromised, start with four questions:.

According to recent reports, A dependency inventory tells you what software you're using. Understanding how that software interacts with the rest of your system helps you assess what a compromise could actually affect.

For teams looking to improve their architectural visibility, explore Veriom.

#34221. For Creamier, Crispier Grilled Cheese, Make It Disneyland-Style

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (556 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Foodrepublic ↗ Open Full Page

For Creamier, Crispier Grilled Cheese, Make It Disneyland-Style

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (556 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foodrepublic

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, is there anything more magical than a visit to Disneyland in sunny, beautiful Anaheim, California?
  • According to recent reports, disney actually released the recipe during COVID for its grilled cheese sandwich, which features three different cheeses, as well as a garlic mayo spread for the outside.
  • Sources indicate that you might use butter when making your grilled cheeses, but trust us, switching to mayo is the move because it is scientifically disposed to create a more even, crisper crust.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, is there anything more magical than a visit to Disneyland in sunny, beautiful Anaheim, California? While the kids might associate this theme park with their favorite Disney characters or the delightful rides and themed areas, many adults make the pricey trek with an additional consideration in mind: the food. In the theme park where Doritos were first served, one can't-miss creation is the Grilled Cheese Sandwich found at the Jolly Holiday Bakery Cafe (as well as Woody's Lunch Box at Walt Disney World in Florida). If you wanted to replicate its creamy, crispy goodness at home, you might already have the ingredients in your fridge: You'll just need cream cheese for the inside and mayonnaise for the outside.

According to recent reports, disney actually released the recipe during COVID for its grilled cheese sandwich, which features three different cheeses, as well as a garlic mayo spread for the outside. There's cheddar and provolone, but the cream cheese is the star, as it gets oh-so-gooey and decadent when it melts down, and it adds a slight tang that will make your tongue take immediate interest.

Sources indicate that you might use butter when making your grilled cheeses, but trust us, switching to mayo is the move because it is scientifically disposed to create a more even, crisper crust. Think about it: You can spread it easily in an even layer without worrying about tearing the bread, as you might with butter. And the inclusion of garlic is a master stroke that introduces even more flavorful depth to what is, essentially, a simple sandwich.

Using cream cheese as a filling and mayonnaise as an outer agent of browning is just one way to achieve the grilled cheese of your dreams. While you should absolutely try these two ingredients, we have a few other ideas that can help you achieve the upgraded Disney Parks-inspired sandwich. The first? Cream cheese is just one of three cheeses that go into this toastie; you'll likely use sliced provolone, but at least for the cheddar, you should grate your own. Blocks of cheese that are grated simply melt better than the pre-shredded variety because there are additional ingredients in the latter that help to keep it from clumping, which prohibits it from melting as wonderfully. If you're going to the trouble of including cream cheese to up the gooey-factor, you might as well go full-tilt where the cheddar is concerned. Disney also includes a bit of cream in its cream cheese blend, which will undeniably enhance the richness of the sandwich and keep things gooey for longer. One tablespoon per quarter cup of cream cheese is more than enough.

To ensure that the sandwich gets its crispiest crust, too, it's important that you don't drop it into the skillet until the pan is fully heated through(though you can still sprinkle salt onto the pan if you want a little extra seasoning). This is so that the golden outsides can start crisping immediately. At the same time, though, you don't want to have the heat turned up too high — a nice medium to medium-low will do the trick. Any hotter and the outside will burn before the cheese has an opportunity to melt all the way through — not the kind of crispness we're seeking.

The Hardest McDonald's Item To Prepare, According To One Former Worker

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (523 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foodrepublic

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that there are quite a few challenges, actually, when it comes to working at McDonald's.
  • And there's the fact that there isn't a mold; it's all hand-stacked, with many different parts, including three buns, two burger patties, a slice of cheese, pickles, onion, and lettuce.
  • Peruse any discussion board where McDonald's employees are chatting about what their least favorite menu item is to make, and aside from Big Macs (which get plenty of mentions), the Quarter Pounder (and its variants) comes up quite frequently.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that there are quite a few challenges, actually, when it comes to working at McDonald's. There's a lot of time management involved, as well as customer service and interaction, to say nothing of the physical fatigue from being on your feet for hours. Then there's the actual assembly of the food itself, and while the burger chain with nearly 42,000 locations across the globe has automated many facets of its kitchen, for the most part, employees must still work the machines and put the sandwiches together. So all this begs the question: Is there a menu item that is the hardest to prepare? Food Republic spoke with Tristen Epps-Long, who won Season 22 of "Top Chef" and who is actually a former McDonald's chef, and in his opinion, the dubious honor belongs to the Major Mac.

His reasoning? "It's multi-layered," he remarked. And there's the fact that there isn't a mold; it's all hand-stacked, with many different parts, including three buns, two burger patties, a slice of cheese, pickles, onion, and lettuce. "It was just a bit more hand work," Epps-Long told us. It seems other McDonald's employees agree with our expert, too, as one person on Reddit reported they had a coworker almost quit after receiving an order for 12 Big Macs at once. It is worth noting, though, that Epps-Long did mention that, after a while, Big Macs can lose their undesirable status; you just have to get the hang of making them.

Peruse any discussion board where McDonald's employees are chatting about what their least favorite menu item is to make, and aside from Big Macs (which get plenty of mentions), the Quarter Pounder (and its variants) comes up quite frequently. It's understandable; the QP is the only McDonald's burger that's cooked fresh, not frozen, so there would be an extra layer of food safety that employees would have to follow in order to prevent cross-contamination with the raw beef product.

Sources indicate that on the dessert side, the apple pies seem to be a pain to make as well, as one employee on Reddit recounted how the sweet treats take six minutes in the deep fryer, which is apparently long enough to start doing other tasks, but not long enough to finish the tasks before the pies are done. That individual must work at an overseas location as apple pies are baked in the USA. The McFlurries appear to be another annoying menu item to make, likely because the process is so hands-on; unlike the burgers, which get cooked on a timed clam shell grill, employees have to hold the McFlurry cup during every step.

In a recent development, now, at the other end of the spectrum, Tristen Epps-Long shared that he found the Egg McMuffin to be one of the easiest things to make, which is slightly surprising, as there are quite a few different elements to it. However, on Reddit, a commenter remarked that the easiest thing for them to make is the plain burgers or cheeseburgers, and this apparently resonated with their peers because the statement has 43 upvotes.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Customers are reporting overnight battery drain and charging errors on the high-tech, pedal-by-wire TM-B e-bike.
  • Customers are reporting overnight battery drain and charging errors on the high-tech, pedal-by-wire TM-B e-bike.
  • Also, the mobility startup that spun out of Rivian last year, has run into another speed bump.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Customers are reporting overnight battery drain and charging errors on the high-tech, pedal-by-wire TM-B e-bike.

Customers are reporting overnight battery drain and charging errors on the high-tech, pedal-by-wire TM-B e-bike.

Also, the mobility startup that spun out of Rivian last year, has run into another speed bump. The organization was already struggling to get its first e-bikes to customers due to a litany of supply chain headaches and the complexity of building a futuristic bike powered almost entirely by software. Now there is a upcoming wrinkle, the company noted in an email sent this week to customers, informing them that their wait just got a little longer.

In a recent development, also remarked it identified “a few software-based issues, such as charging behavior,” affecting some of the Launch Edition versions of its TM-B bikes. As a result, it was pausing customer deliveries until it could work out a solution.

“Our team is hard at work on a firmware patch to address these issues so that every TM-B owner can enjoy the full product experience we aspire to, beginning with your very first ride,” the email reads.

Industry observers note that the issues were already popping up on the Also subreddit, where customers were reporting batteries draining overnight for no apparent reason, in some cases dropping from 70 percent to 40 percent or lower over a couple of days. Others noted that the parasitic drain would trigger a “bike concern detected” or “install battery to ride” error on the bike’s display. Trying to plug the battery in would often fail because the bike wouldn’t recognize the battery installed, they said.

It has been revealed that also has paused customer deliveries until it can fix the problem. The organization said it had almost shipped out all of its Launch Edition bikes, after which it planned on transitioning to its Performance Edition. But now that timeline will be delayed beyond what Also previously communicated to its customers who are still waiting on their deliveries, Michele Mehl, senior PR manager at Also, says in an email to The Verge.

In a recent development, “The team recognizes this means a delay for customers who have already waited longer than expected, but believes it’s the right decision to ensure every TM-B delivers the full product experience we aspire to,” Mehl added. The company plans on sending another update on the delay on November 24th.

It’s been clear from the beginning that Also took on an enormous challenge when it set out to build one of the most high-tech, logistically complex e-bikes ever made. The USB-C chargeable batteries, which are available in either 538Wh or 808Wh packs, are supposed to offer up 100 miles of range. But the 240W power delivery exceeds current regulatory guidelines, forcing Also to work with standards groups to establish new safety and testing protocols.

Sources indicate that in addition, the bike is powered by a pedal-by-wire system, which means there’s no mechanical connection between the pedaling and the movement of the bike. Instead, the rider pedals a generator motor on the crank, which replenishes the battery; a separate traction motor at the rear wheel is software-driven via a Gates Carbon belt drive.

Last month, when I asked Also President Chris Yu whether the company bit off more than it can chew with this bike, he pushed back:.

According to recent reports, I don’t look at it that way at all. If we were to revisit the design, I would do the exact same thing. The largest untapped opportunity isn’t cyclists who already tolerate the current bike experience. It’s the massive demographic of people intrigued by leaving the car behind who haven’t opted in yet. Their hesitations are consistent: fear of theft, avoiding maintenance every two months, wanting seamless navigation and audio, and needing to carry a child without having to buy three different bikes.

Solving those pain points requires a baseline of technology. Just like in automotive EVs, once you use software to personalize the ride and eliminate friction, people opt in. The majority of people attending our test rides haven’t ridden a bicycle in 10 or 15 years. Our goal wasn’t to go overboard; it was determining the minimum amount of innovation needed to create an experience as frictionless as stepping into a Tesla Model Y or Rivian R2.
